Brand demand should be less elastic than category demand, because a brand includes fewer possible purchases than the category.
Brand and category demand should have equal elasticity, because both purchases satisfy the same basic need.
Brand demand can be elastic only if the entire category is a luxury, because generic substitutes cannot change necessity status.
items.feedback: Elasticity depends on the defined choice set.

items.stem: A product has no close substitutes today but represents a large budget share. What is the best conclusion?
options: Few substitutes establish inelastic demand; budget share changes spending levels but cannot affect responsiveness.
Few substitutes restrain responsiveness while a large budget share encourages adjustment; estimate their combined effect in this market.
The large budget share establishes elastic demand; the absence of substitutes changes price but cannot affect responsiveness.
The two determinants imply unit elasticity; their opposing directions necessarily cancel quantitatively.
items.feedback: Elasticity determinants are tendencies, not mechanical rules.

items.stem: A policymaker compares a steep supply curve and a flat demand curve drawn with different axis scales. What is the proper incidence method?
options: Assign burden to the visually steeper curve
Assign burden to sellers by statute
Compare elasticity estimates, not visual steepness alone
Assume equal burden
items.feedback: Relative percentage responsiveness determines incidence.

items.stem: A market’s supply is inelastic today but highly elastic over five years. A permanent tax is imposed. How should incidence analysis change over time?
options: If demand responsiveness is unchanged, the more elastic long-run supply tends to shift more of the burden to sellers.
If demand responsiveness is unchanged, supply adjustment raises the quantity traded but leaves the burden shares at their short-run values.
If demand responsiveness is unchanged, producers’ ability to adjust makes the statutory taxpayer bear a larger share over time.
If demand responsiveness is unchanged, the more elastic long-run supply tends to shift more of the burden to buyers.
items.feedback: Relative elasticities evolve as producers gain exit and adjustment options.

items.stem: A temporary tax expires before firms can adjust capacity. Compared with a permanent tax, who may bear more of the temporary tax?
options: Producers, because short-run supply is less elastic
Consumers, because temporary taxes make demand vertical
The government
No one because the tax is temporary
items.feedback: Limited short-run producer adjustment makes supply relatively inelastic.

items.stem: A crop quota reduces sales from 1,000 to 900 units and raises price from $10 to $12. Farmers’ variable production cost falls by $300, while administering the quota uses $1,200 of their resources. Which comparison avoids confusing revenue with profit?
options: Revenue rises by $800 and profit must rise by $800 because the demand response is inelastic.
Revenue rises by $800, but net producer profit falls by $100 after cost savings and administration.
Revenue falls by $1,000 and profit falls by $1,900 because fewer units are sold.
Revenue rises by $1,200 and profit rises by $300 because the calculation uses the old quantity at the new price.
items.feedback: Revenue changes from $10,000 to $10,800. Profit changes by +800+300−1,200=−$100. Inelastic response can raise revenue without making an administratively costly policy profitable.

items.stem: A seller estimates elastic demand but still raises price after a cost increase. Why is this not necessarily irrational?
options: Elastic demand predicts a revenue loss from a price rise, so profit must fall by the same amount even if the firm avoids variable costs.
Elastic demand predicts a revenue gain from a price rise, and that gain is sufficient to establish a profit gain after the cost increase.
Elastic demand predicts a revenue loss from a price rise, but reduced unit sales and more revenue left per sale after variable costs may improve profit after the cost increase.
Elastic demand predicts unchanged revenue from a price rise, so the cost increase can be passed on without checking the quantity response.
items.feedback: Revenue and profit are different objectives. A price increase reduces quantity sold when demand is elastic, but whether profit rises also depends on variable costs and the revenue left from the remaining sales.

items.stem: A seller expects a small discount to increase revenue from customers with elastic demand. Those customers can freely resell purchases to customers currently paying the regular price. Which issue must the forecast address before treating the two groups’ sales as separate?
options: Resale guarantees the discount raises profit because every discounted sale is an additional market sale.
Resale makes both groups’ demand perfectly inelastic because the seller names two prices.
Resale affects fixed cost only, so it can be ignored when estimating demand responses.
Resale can shift regular-price purchases into the discounted channel; evaluate that switching as well as each group’s quantity response.
items.feedback: The elastic group may buy partly for resale, replacing rather than adding to regular-price sales. Separate response estimates do not by themselves establish the seller’s overall revenue or profit gain.

items.stem: An importer initially cuts foreign-goods purchases by 2% when their domestic-currency price rises 5%. After close domestic substitutes appear, the same price increase cuts imports 9%. If foreign prices and currency needed per imported unit are unchanged, which implication follows?
options: Import demand becomes more elastic, so the derived quantity demand for foreign currency becomes more responsive to the same domestic-currency price change.
Import demand becomes less elastic because 9% is larger than 2%, so foreign-currency purchases become less responsive.
The foreign-currency quantity must rise when imports fall, because each imported unit now requires more foreign currency.
Derived demand is unchanged because domestic substitutes cannot affect purchases of foreign goods.
items.feedback: The import response ratio rises from 0.4 to 1.8. With unchanged foreign currency required per unit, a larger percentage fall in imports produces a larger fall in currency purchases.

items.stem: A rival cuts its price 10%. Your product’s cross-price elasticity with that rival is +1.5, while your own-price elasticity is −0.5. Holding your price and other determinants fixed, which forecast and interpretation fit?
options: Your sales rise about 15%; positive cross-price elasticity means the goods are complements.
Your sales fall about 15%; the positive cross-price elasticity indicates substitutes.
Your sales rise about 5%; use own-price elasticity with the rival’s price cut.
Your sales fall about 0.15%; multiply by the elasticity as though it were already a percentage.
items.feedback: Use the cross-price coefficient for a rival’s price: 1.5×(−10%)=−15%. The positive relationship between rival price and own sales is the substitute pattern.

items.stem: Income is forecast to rise 5%. Transit demand has income elasticity −0.6; leisure-rail demand has income elasticity +1.4. Prices and other determinants are fixed. Which forecast separates the sign from responsiveness?
options: Transit demand rises about 3%, while leisure-rail demand rises about 7%; discard the minus sign before forecasting.
Transit demand falls about 0.6%, while leisure-rail demand rises about 1.4%; coefficients are percentage changes themselves.
Transit demand falls about 3%, while leisure-rail demand rises about 7%; the estimates classify transit as inferior over this range.
Both demands rise 5% because the income shock is common to the two markets.
items.feedback: Multiply each coefficient by the 5% income rise: −0.6×5%=−3% and 1.4×5%=7%. For income elasticity, the sign identifies the direction and must be retained.

items.stem: A producer’s price rises 8%. Its short-run supply elasticity is 0.25 and its long-run elasticity is 1.5, each applicable near the initial price. Which forecast and explanation fit, with other determinants held constant?
options: Quantity supplied rises 12% in the short run and 2% in the long run because time reduces adjustment options.
Quantity supplied rises 8% in both periods because elasticity measures the direction but not the size of the response.
Quantity supplied falls 2% then 12% because the higher output price raises the firm’s input costs by definition.
Quantity supplied rises about 2% in the short run and 12% in the long run as capacity and inputs can adjust.
items.feedback: Supply response is elasticity times the price change: 0.25×8%=2% and 1.5×8%=12%. Longer adjustment time can allow greater output response.

items.stem: Two reports describe the same demand estimate as −2.3 and 2.3. A manager says they predict opposite sales responses to a 2% price increase. Which diagnosis is appropriate if the second report uses the absolute-value convention?
options: Both imply an approximate 4.6% sales decline; the second reports magnitude rather than an upward-sloping demand response.
One predicts a 4.6% decline and the other a 4.6% rise because absolute values reverse economic behavior.
Both predict a 2.3% sales decline because elasticity should not be multiplied by the price change.
Neither permits a revenue prediction because opposite printed signs prove the data disagree.
items.feedback: The signed estimate gives −2.3×2%=−4.6%. Reporting |Ed|=2.3 retains that downward-demand interpretation; it changes notation, not the estimated behavior.

items.stem: A product has cross-price elasticity −0.9 with a companion service. The service price falls 10%. An analyst discards the minus sign and forecasts a 9% product-sales decline. Which correction is right?
options: Discard the sign: product sales fall about 9%, consistent with the purchases being substitutes.
Keep the sign: product sales fall about 0.9%, because the coefficient already contains the 10% price change.
Keep the sign: product sales rise about 9%, consistent with the two purchases being complements.
Discard both signs: product sales are unchanged because cross-price elasticity cannot predict quantity.
items.feedback: For cross-price elasticity the sign distinguishes complements from substitutes. (−0.9)×(−10%)=+9%, so a cheaper complement raises demand for the product.

items.stem: A binding posted-price ceiling holds the seller’s receipt at $10. Buyers must also pay a $2 per-unit tax, and approved buyers receive a $1 per-unit subsidy. Supply at the ceiling is only 60 units while buyers seek 100. Which analysis correctly distinguishes prices from actual trades?
options: Approved buyers pay $9 and sellers receive $12; all 100 desired units trade because the subsidy removes scarcity.
Approved buyers pay $13 and sellers receive $10; trades are 100 because all policy amounts should be added to demand.
Approved buyers pay $11 and sellers receive $10; trades are necessarily 100 because those prices clear any market.
Approved buyers’ net monetary outlay is $11 and sellers receive $10; trades are limited to 60, so a demand-elasticity calculation alone cannot establish 100 sales.
items.feedback: For approved buyers, $10+$2−$1=$11. Sellers still receive the capped $10, at which only 60 units are supplied. The binding shortage constrains actual trades regardless of desired purchases.

items.stem: A firm has customer-level elasticity estimates, capacity constraints, and rising marginal cost. Why is charging the lowest price to the most elastic customers not automatically optimal?
options: A lower price may attract more units from responsive customers, but those units use scarce capacity and may carry rising marginal cost; compare the extra revenue minus extra cost from using capacity to serve each group.
A lower price attracts more units from responsive customers, so allocate all capacity to them even when the extra revenue minus extra cost from serving them is lower.
Rising marginal cost changes total profit but not the extra revenue minus extra cost from additional units, so allocate capacity using elasticity alone.
A capacity limit makes demand responses irrelevant until capacity expands, so allocate current capacity only by customers’ average spending.
items.feedback: Optimal pricing integrates demand response with costs and capacity.

items.stem: A climate policy raises energy prices, encourages substitution, induces innovation, and changes household location over a decade. What does this imply about short-run versus long-run demand elasticity?
options: Long-run elasticity should be smaller because consumers exhaust their easiest adjustments during the first month
Long-run demand may be more elastic than the first-month estimate.
The policy changes supply responsiveness but leaves household demand responsiveness essentially unchanged over time
The first-month estimate remains the best long-run measure because later innovation and relocation are separate effects
items.feedback: Technology, capital, and location adjustments expand long-run response.

items.stem: At a delivery firm, one worker adds 30 parcels and the next adds 22. The following worker would add 14. Each parcel sells for $6 and each additional worker costs $100, with other costs unchanged. Which hiring conclusion distinguishes diminishing marginal product from profitability?
options: Reject both workers because any decline in marginal product means extra output is unprofitable.
Hire the worker adding 22 parcels; do not hire the one adding 14.
Hire both workers because positive marginal product is sufficient for profit to rise.
Hire only the worker adding 14 parcels because lower marginal product means lower marginal labor cost.
items.feedback: Compare added revenue with the $100 wage. 22×$6=$132 exceeds the wage; 14×$6=$84 does not. Diminishing marginal product need not mean negative marginal product or immediate unprofitability.

items.stem: Two governments each increase purchases by $50. Economy A has an MPC of 0.8, and crowding out reduces its total increase in aggregate demand by $150. Economy B has an MPC of 0.5 and no crowding out. How do the final increases in aggregate demand compare?
options: B has zero effect because a lower MPC eliminates every induced round
A has a negative net effect because the total crowding-out amount must be multiplied by five again
Both net effects are $100; A's larger gross multiplier is offset by greater crowding out
A has the larger net effect $250; a larger MPC always wins
items.feedback: A: 5×50−150=100. B: 2×50=100. A larger increase before crowding out need not mean a larger increase afterward.

items.stem: With MPC 0.75 and fixed prices, government purchases rise $60. Crowding out reduces total AD by $60 after induced effects, leaving a $180 net increase. An analyst instead treats that same $60 as an autonomous investment loss. What changes under the analyst's interpretation?
options: The predicted net effect remains $180 because autonomous and total effects are interchangeable.
Net demand becomes zero: multiplying the autonomous loss by 4 changes the stated total-offset assumption.
The predicted net effect becomes $300 because investment losses must be added to fiscal expansion.
The predicted net effect stays $240 because crowding out cannot affect demand in a fixed-price model.
items.feedback: The original gross increase is 60×4=240 and the total offset is 60, leaving 180. If 60 instead denotes the initial autonomous loss, its total is 240 and the effects cancel. Distinguishing what the number measures prevents multiplying an already-total offset twice.

items.stem: The desired net AD increase is $210. MPC is 0.5, and a total AD crowding-out offset of $70 is expected after induced effects. What purchases increase reaches the target?
options: $420; multiply the target by two, omitting the offset.
$70; subtract the offset before reversing the multiplier.
$280; add the offset without reversing the multiplier.
$140; divide target plus total offset by the multiplier.
items.feedback: 2ΔG−70=210, so ΔG=(210+70)/2=140. Reverse the net-effect equation; the offset is not an autonomous component to multiply again.

items.stem: Two equal-cost fiscal packages provide either a targeted transfer or a broad tax rebate. Recipients of the transfer have the higher MPC, but most transfer payments arrive after a planned stabilization deadline, while the rebates arrive before it. A minister concludes that the transfer must create more AD by the deadline. Which additional comparison is needed?
options: Compare each package’s amount actually received and spent by the deadline, including induced spending completed by then.
Compare only the recipients’ MPCs; the timing of payment cannot affect AD by the deadline.
Count every transfer dollar as purchases immediately, then compare that total with rebate consumption.
Compare the eventual multipliers only; completion of spending rounds before the deadline is irrelevant.
items.feedback: A higher MPC raises consumption from each dollar received, other things equal, but it does not guarantee a larger effect by a date when fewer dollars have been paid. Timely receipts, consumption and induced rounds jointly determine the relevant short-run AD effect.

items.stem: A government wants to reduce aggregate demand while expanding targeted transfers. Under a simple closed-economy expenditure model, MPC = 0.6 for all households, taxes stay fixed, and no crowding-out or price feedback occurs. Transfers rise by $30 billion. What minimum purchases cut produces a $45 billion leftward AD shift rather than merely cancelling the transfer stimulus?
options: $18 billion: cancelling the first-round transfer consumption also provides the full target contraction.
$45 billion: the target AD shift is itself the required purchases cut.
$75 billion: add the full transfer amount to the desired AD reduction.
$36 billion: offset $18 billion of induced first-round consumption and add $18 billion of net autonomous contraction.
items.feedback: Transfers first add 0.6 × 30 = $18 billion of consumption. The spending multiplier is 2.5, so a $45 billion AD reduction requires $18 billion of net autonomous contraction. Purchases must fall by 18 + 18 = $36 billion. The transfer is not itself a government purchase.

items.stem: A $120 billion refundable tax credit can be allocated between two household groups, with MPCs of 0.90 and 0.40. The government wants a first-round consumption increase of $84 billion, before any induced spending. How should the credit be allocated, and why would the same $120 billion of government purchases have a different first-round AD effect?
options: $72 billion to the higher-MPC group and $48 billion to the other; purchases enter AD directly, whereas some credit is saved.
$48 billion to the higher-MPC group and $72 billion to the other; purchases and credits enter AD directly in full.
$60 billion to each group; averaging MPCs guarantees the target regardless of allocation.
$84 billion to the higher-MPC group and $36 billion to the other; each dollar of credit is a dollar of purchases.
items.feedback: Let x go to the higher-MPC group. Then 0.90x + 0.40(120 − x) = 84, giving x = $72 billion and $48 billion to the other group. Their consumption responses are $64.8 billion and $19.2 billion. Government purchases would directly add $120 billion to AD; a credit affects disposable income and only the spent portion enters first-round consumption.

items.stem: Households have an MPC of 0.75. One policy cuts taxes by $60 billion; an alternative raises government purchases by $45 billion. With the same spending multiplier and no crowding out, how do the policies' effects on aggregate demand and their budget costs compare?
options: Both first-round impulses are $60 billion and total shifts $240 billion, because taxes and purchases are identical
The tax cut adds only $45 billion in total, while purchases receive induced spending
Both first-round impulses are $45 billion and total shifts $180 billion, although the budget costs differ
The tax cut first adds $60 billion and ultimately $240 billion, while purchases add only $180 billion
items.feedback: The tax cut initially raises consumption by 0.75 × $60 billion = $45 billion. Purchases also add $45 billion directly. Multiplying each by 4 gives $180 billion in total, but the tax cut costs the budget $60 billion versus $45 billion for purchases.

items.stem: Government raises purchases and lump-sum taxes by $110 each. MPC is 0.8, prices are fixed, resources are idle and there is no other leakage or crowding out. An analyst claims the balanced budget leaves demand unchanged. What mistaken assumption about the initial consumption response underlies this claim?
options: It would require the full tax increase to reduce initial consumption; here consumption falls only $88, leaving a multiplied net increase of $110.
It requires MPC 0.8, because equal dollar tax and purchase changes always have equal initial spending effects.
It requires fixed prices, because fixed prices prevent any induced consumption from a government purchase.
It requires the spending multiplier to be 5, which turns the $110 purchase increase into a zero net effect.
items.feedback: Purchases add $110 directly, while taxes reduce initial consumption by 0.8×110=$88. The $22 initial net impulse times 5 gives $110. Budget balance is not demand balance because some of the tax increase reduces saving rather than consumption.

items.stem: Government pays $120 in transfers instead of buying output. MPC is 0.6 in a fixed-price model with no other changes. A report predicts the same $300 demand increase as a $120 purchases program. Why does replacing purchases with transfers change the result?
options: Transfers enter G just like purchases, so both programs initially add $120 and total $300.
Transfers do not enter G, so they cannot affect consumption or aggregate demand at all.
Transfers initially add $72 to consumption, but applying the spending multiplier again would always double-count it.
Transfers do not enter G; recipients initially spend $72, yielding a $180 total rather than $300.
items.feedback: Purchases directly buy output. Transfers raise disposable income, of which 0.6×120=$72 is initially spent. With multiplier 2.5, the total is $180. The remaining initial $48 is saved, explaining the difference from a purchases program.

items.stem: A lender’s one-year fixed nominal contract pays 12 percent. Expected inflation when written was 5 percent, but actual inflation is 9 percent. Use exact inflation-adjusted returns rather than subtracting inflation from the nominal rate. What are the expected and realized real returns, and what nominal rate on a new loan would preserve the original expected real return if expected inflation is now 9 percent?
options: About 6.67 percent, 2.75 percent, and 16.27 percent.
7 percent, 3 percent, and 16 percent exactly.
About 2.75 percent, 6.67 percent, and 12 percent.
About 6.67 percent, 2.75 percent, and 12 percent.
items.feedback: Expected real return is 1.12/1.05 − 1 = 6.67 percent; realized is 1.12/1.09 − 1 = 2.75 percent. Preserving the original expected real return on a new loan requires (1.12/1.05) × 1.09 − 1 = 16.27 percent nominal.

items.stem: A one-time monetary expansion lowers the value of money today. Credible guidance says the money-growth rate will then return to its previous path. The long-run real interest rate is unchanged. An analyst concludes that nominal interest rates must remain permanently higher. Which evaluation is strongest?
options: A one-time price-level rise does not establish permanently higher expected inflation, so the lasting nominal-rate claim is unsupported.
The higher price level guarantees permanently higher inflation, so the nominal-rate claim follows.
The lower value of money proves the real interest rate falls permanently, so nominal rates must fall.
Monetary neutrality makes expected inflation irrelevant to nominal rates, so the Fisher relationship does not apply.
items.feedback: The Fisher effect relates nominal rates to expected inflation over the loan horizon. A level adjustment alone does not establish a continuing inflation-rate increase. The real-rate assumption therefore does not complete the analyst’s argument.

items.stem: Expected inflation rises 4 points in a credit market of size $160, but the nominal rate rises only 1 point. If the Fisher approximation applies, what happened to the expected real interest rate?
options: The expected real rate fell 3 points.
The expected real rate rose 3 points.
The approximation proves the data impossible.
The actual inflation rate must have fallen 3 points.
items.feedback: Δi=Δr+Δπe implies Δr=1−4=−3 points. A changing real component is compatible with the identity; actual inflation is a separate outcome.

items.stem: For a $180 loan, expected inflation rises from 2% to 5% while the required expected real return falls from 4% to 3%. The nominal rate rises from 6% to 8%. Does its two-point increase refute the Fisher approximation?
options: Yes. Any expectation increase must produce an equal nominal-rate increase even when the required real rate changes.
No. Nominal rates equal expected inflation minus the real return, which gives the observed increase.
Yes. Opposite changes in real returns and expectations must always leave the nominal rate unchanged.
No. The three-point expectation increase is partly offset by the one-point real-return decline; a one-for-one nominal response requires a fixed real rate.
items.feedback: Initially i≈4+2=6; later i≈3+5=8. The two components still sum correctly. Treating the conditional one-for-one expectation response as unconditional would mistakenly hold the supplied changing real return fixed.

items.stem: A country’s nominal loan rate falls from 16 to 9 percent while expected inflation falls from 12 to 4 percent. Using the Fisher approximation, what happens to the expected real rate, and by how much would the new nominal rate have had to fall further to preserve its original expected real rate?
options: The expected real rate rises from 4 to 5 percent; a further 1-point nominal cut was needed.
The expected real rate falls from 4 to 3 percent; a further 1-point nominal cut was needed.
The expected real rate stays at 4 percent; no further nominal change was needed.
The expected real rate rises from 4 to 5 percent; a further 5-point nominal cut was needed.
items.feedback: Subtract expected inflation: 16 − 12 = 4 initially and 9 − 4 = 5 later. Preserving a real rate of 4 with expected inflation of 4 requires a nominal rate of 8, one point below 9.

items.stem: Foreign demand for U.S. exports increases, while a lower U.S. real interest rate raises net capital outflow. In the market for U.S. dollars, demand slopes downward and supply slopes upward. Measuring the exchange rate in foreign currency per dollar, what happens to the exchange rate and the quantity of dollars exchanged?
options: Currency quantity is ambiguous because the rate is fixed
Currency quantity rises, while the exchange-rate direction depends on the relative demand and supply shifts
The exchange rate rises because the export-demand change is stated first
The exchange rate falls because NCO controls both equilibrium variables
items.feedback: Higher NCO shifts supply right, and stronger export demand shifts demand right. Both raise quantity but have opposing effects on the rate.

items.stem: Foreign demand causes the shift from D0 to D1. With domestic and foreign price levels fixed, how does the exchange-rate response shown affect the original export stimulus?
options: The dollar appreciates 20%, making domestic goods dearer abroad and partly restraining the rise in net exports.
The dollar appreciates 50%, making domestic goods dearer abroad and partly restraining the rise in net exports.
The dollar appreciates 20%, making domestic goods cheaper abroad and reinforcing the rise in net exports.
The dollar appreciates 20%, which establishes that the entire initial increase in export demand is canceled.
items.feedback: The rate rises from 1.0 to 1.2 foreign-currency units per dollar, a 20% appreciation. At fixed price levels this also is real appreciation, which restrains net exports along the new relationship. It does not measure the size of the original demand shift or prove a full offset.

items.stem: The dollar market changes from the solid curves to the dashed curve, with price levels fixed. Lower domestic real returns and higher domestic political risk are proposed explanations. What does the figure establish, and what remains unresolved?
options: Dollar supply falls and the dollar appreciates; separate return or risk evidence is needed to distinguish the causes.
Dollar supply rises and the dollar depreciates; the downward rate change rules out a rise in political risk.
Dollar demand rises and the dollar depreciates; depreciation identifies lower domestic returns as the only cause.
Dollar supply rises and the dollar depreciates; separate return or risk evidence is needed to distinguish the causes.
items.feedback: S1 lies right of S0, and B has a lower exchange rate and greater quantity than A. With fixed prices this is also real depreciation. Both lower returns and greater risk can encourage foreign-asset purchases; the figure does not separately identify them.

items.stem: Foreign demand for U.S. goods increases while U.S. purchases of foreign assets decrease. In the market for dollars, demand slopes downward and supply slopes upward, with the exchange rate measured in foreign currency per dollar. Despite the decrease in supply, more dollars are exchanged. What does this imply about the dollar’s value and the relative size of the two shifts?
options: The dollar depreciates; rising quantity shows that the decrease in supply was larger.
The dollar appreciates; rising quantity proves that the supply of dollars actually increased.
The dollar appreciates; at the original quantity, demanders’ willingness to pay rose more than suppliers’ required exchange rate.
The exchange-rate change remains uncertain; quantity information cannot help compare the shifts.
items.feedback: Higher demand and lower supply both raise the foreign-currency price of a dollar. At the original quantity, the increase in demanders’ willingness to pay must exceed the increase in the exchange rate suppliers require for the new equilibrium quantity to be higher.

items.stem: Use the foreign-exchange model in which net capital outflow determines a vertical supply curve for domestic currency. The domestic real interest rate rises, while a separate increase in risk makes investors want to send more funds abroad at each interest rate. The final supply curve for domestic currency lies to the right of its original position. With domestic and foreign price levels fixed and demand for domestic currency unchanged, what does this tell us about the two effects on net capital outflow and the exchange rate?
options: The interest-rate rise caused the supply increase, reversing the usual NCO slope
Risk outweighs higher interest rates; the currency depreciates, but neither effect's size can be determined separately
Vertical supply means NCO is fixed across both equilibria, so the stated curve change is impossible
The effects of risk and the higher interest rate cancel exactly because both supply curves are vertical
items.feedback: A vertical currency-supply curve fixes the quantity supplied for a given level of net capital outflow, not when that level changes. The rightward shift means the increase caused by risk exceeds the decrease caused by the higher interest rate. With currency demand unchanged, the domestic currency depreciates. The final shift alone does not reveal the size of each separate effect.

items.stem: Refer to the numbered graph showing A to B after both dollar-market curves shift right. If demand shifts first and supply second, estimate the intermediate rate to the nearest tenth from the displayed straight lines and compare the intermediate and final outcomes with A. Which statement fits?
options: The intermediate rate rises 20 percent; the final rate returns to its initial value while quantity doubles
The intermediate rate falls 20 percent; the final rate returns to its initial value while quantity doubles
The intermediate rate rises 20 percent; the final quantity rises only 50 percent
The final rate is unchanged, so the intermediate rate must also be unchanged
items.feedback: D1 intersects S0 at approximately 150 units and an exchange rate of 1.2, compared with 100 units and 1.0 at A. At the final equilibrium B, quantity is 200 and the exchange rate is 1.0. The exchange rate first rises about 20 percent and then returns to its initial value, while the final quantity is twice its initial level.

items.stem: Foreign export demand shifts D0 to D1 and residents' foreign-asset purchases shift S0 to S1. Foreign purchases of domestic assets are unchanged. What can be inferred from the diagram and the separate asset-flow information?
options: The exchange rate rises and gross dollar quantity rises; the asset flows imply higher NCO and therefore higher NX.
The exchange rate is unchanged and gross dollar quantity rises; the increase in gross quantity directly measures the increase in NCO.
The exchange rate is unchanged and gross dollar quantity rises; the unchanged rate implies unchanged NCO despite the asset flows.
The exchange rate is unchanged and gross dollar quantity rises; the asset flows imply higher NCO and therefore higher NX.
items.feedback: The final intersection is farther right at the same rate. NCO rises because residents buy more foreign assets with foreign purchases of domestic assets unchanged. In consistent accounts NX equals NCO; gross FX turnover itself is not a measure of that net flow.

items.stem: In the market for U.S. dollars, demand slopes downward and supply slopes upward. At the original exchange rate, stronger export demand increases dollars demanded by 70 units, while greater foreign-asset purchases increase dollars supplied by 45 units. What happens to the equilibrium exchange rate, measured in foreign currency per dollar, and the quantity exchanged? Are these shift amounts enough to calculate the exact changes?
options: Both rise; the exchange rate rises exactly 25 percent
The exchange rate falls and quantity rises; supply determines the rate independently
Both rise; curve slopes are needed for exact changes
The exchange rate is unchanged and quantity rises exactly 115 units
items.feedback: At the original exchange rate, excess demand is 70 − 45 = 25 units, so the exchange rate rises. Both increases raise the equilibrium quantity of dollars exchanged. The exact changes depend on the slopes of demand and supply.

items.stem: The market begins at A, where S0 and D0 intersect, and ends at B on S1 and D1. Compare two paths: demand shifts first, or supply shifts first. Each market clears before the second shift. Approximately how do the intermediate exchange rates differ, and does the order change the final equilibrium?
options: Demand first gives 1.4 and supply first 0.6; both paths end at B once both shifts occur.
Demand first gives 1.2 and supply first 0.8; both paths end at B once both shifts occur.
Demand first gives 1.2 and supply first 0.8; these different temporary rates imply different final equilibria.
Both intermediate rates are 1.0; an unchanged final rate rules out a temporary exchange-rate response.
items.feedback: D1 intersects S0 near 1.2, while D0 intersects S1 near 0.8. The two sequences therefore have different temporary rates but the same final D1-S1 intersection at B. Endpoint evidence cannot establish an unchanged path.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: With constant tradeoffs, Forge can make 36 panels or 12 motors; Harbor can make 20 panels or 10 motors. Forge imports a motor and pays an additional shipping cost of 0.5 panel per motor. Which quoted panel price gives both positive gains?
options: 3 panels per motor
2.25 panels per motor
2 panels per motor
2.75 panels per motor
items.feedback: Forge's domestic cost is 3 panels; Harbor's is 2. Harbor requires a price above 2, while Forge requires price + 0.5 below 3. Only 2.25 is strictly between 2 and 2.5.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Suppose learning-by-doing lowers a nation’s future opportunity cost in a good it does not currently produce. What does this imply?
options: Current comparative advantage may not fully describe future comparative advantage.
Opportunity costs can never change over time.
The nation must already have absolute advantage in that good.
Trade eliminates any reason to consider future productivity.
items.feedback: Investment and learning can alter future relative costs, so dynamic considerations may matter.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: A workshop's cost of a motor is 2 batteries; its trading partner's is 5. The workshop exports motors and pays 1 battery in shipping per motor. Measured in motors per battery, what range of trading prices makes both partners better off after shipping costs?
options: Between 1/5 and 1/3 motor per battery
Between 1/5 and 1/2 motor per battery
Between 3 and 5 motors per battery
Between 1/3 and 1/2 motor per battery
items.feedback: The exporter needs more than 2 + 1 = 3 batteries per motor to cover production and shipping costs. The importer gains when the price is below 5 batteries per motor. Expressing these prices in motors per battery gives a range greater than 1/5 and less than 1/3.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: After specializing, a workshop produces 30 panels and no motors. Before specializing, it consumed 16 panels and 3 motors. It can exchange 3 panels for one motor. Which trade would leave it with more panels and more motors than before?
options: Trade 12 panels for 4 motors
Trade 9 panels for 3 motors
Trade 15 panels for 5 motors
Trade 6 panels for 2 motors
items.feedback: Trading 12 leaves 18 panels and 4 motors, above both former quantities. Nine panels only matches former motors; fifteen leaves too few panels; six leaves fewer motors.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: North specializes at 24 fish and South at 12 nets. North trades 8 fish for 4 nets. Their autarky bundles were North 12 fish and 3 nets, South 6 fish and 6 nets. What are their gains?
options: North gains 4 fish and 1 net; South gains 2 fish and 2 nets
North gains 8 fish and 4 nets; South gains 8 fish and 4 nets
North gains 4 fish and 4 nets; South gains 2 fish and 6 nets
North gains 12 fish and 1 net; South gains 2 fish and 2 nets
items.feedback: Derive both post-trade bundles and compare each with its stated autarky bundle.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: One printer costs Estara 3 scanners and Fenn 7 scanners. Estara exports a printer at a quoted price of 6 scanners but Fenn must also use 2 scanners for shipping. What would make both strictly better off?
options: A quoted price strictly between 3 and 5 scanners
Any quoted price strictly between 3 and 7 scanners
The existing price of 6 because it is below Fenn's domestic cost
A price of 7 because it exactly matches Fenn's production cost
items.feedback: Estara needs a quote above 3. Fenn's full import cost is quote + 2, which must be below 7. Thus 3 < quote < 5; ignoring shipping overstates the mutual-gain range.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: At constant tradeoffs, Oak can make 24 racks or 8 desks; Pine can make 18 racks or 9 desks. Oak adopts a tool that raises its desk maximum to 16 without changing racks. Which conclusion follows?
options: Oak switches to comparative advantage in desks; a 1.75-rack desk price can then benefit both
Pine retains desk advantage because its rack maximum is lower
Oak has comparative advantage in both goods because both maxima exceed Pine's
The old 2.5-rack desk price still gives Oak positive gains when it imports desks
items.feedback: Oak's desk cost falls from 3 to 1.5 racks; Pine's stays 2. Oak becomes the lower-cost desk maker, and 1.75 lies between their costs. At the old import price Oak could now make desks more cheaply.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: With constant opportunity costs, Ridge can produce 24 maps or 12 models. Vale can produce 18 maps or m models. Ridge exports models for 1.5 maps each. Is there a positive value of m that would allow both producers to gain from this trade?
options: No positive m; Ridge loses at the stated export price
m = 6; Vale's higher cost suffices for mutual gains
m = 9; matching costs makes this price mutually beneficial
m = 18; Vale's higher model productivity guarantees mutual gains
items.feedback: Ridge sacrifices 2 maps to make a model but receives only 1.5 maps. Regardless of Vale's productivity, Ridge loses on this export; solving only Vale's inequality misses one side.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Two labs each sacrifice 4 tests for one prototype at constant tradeoffs. One lab doubles its maximum output of both goods. What changes in the pure comparative-advantage model?
options: Its capacity rises, but equal opportunity costs still leave no positive gains for both producers from specialization at any common price
It gains comparative advantage in both goods because both maxima double
A price of 4 tests now gives both a positive gain on each prototype
Doubling capacity halves its opportunity cost of a prototype
items.feedback: Proportional productivity growth leaves the ratio unchanged. At 4 tests both are indifferent; any other price advantages one direction while making the other party worse off.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Specialization creates a gross gain of 24 units of a common consumption good. Shipping uses 5 units and verification uses 7. The proposed division gives one party 15 units of gross gain and assigns it both costs. Does that party gain, and what net gain remains for the other?
options: Yes, it gains 3 units; the other gains 9
Yes, it gains 15 units; the other gains 9
No, it loses 12 units; the other gains 24
Yes, both gain 12 units
items.feedback: Net total gain is 24 - 5 - 7 = 12. The cost-paying party gains 15 - 12 = 3; the other receives the remaining gross 9 and pays no cost.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: An engineer needs 2 hours per design and 1 hour per inspection. A technician needs 6 hours per design and 2 hours per inspection. They move one inspection from the engineer to the technician, who gives up one-third of a design. What net design capacity is freed?
options: One-sixth of a design
One-half of a design
One-third of a design
Five-sixths of a design
items.feedback: The engineer saves an hour, enough for half a design. The technician's two hours cost one-third of a design. Net capacity gain is 1/2 - 1/3 = 1/6; the engineer's absolute inspection advantage does not settle assignment.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Mesa specializes at 30 meals and Bay at 15 repairs, then exchanges 10 meals for 5 repairs. A report says Mesa gains 5 meals and 1 repair, while Bay gains 2 meals and 3 repairs. Which pair of autarky bundles makes all four claims consistent?
options: Mesa: 25 meals, 6 repairs; Bay: 12 meals, 13 repairs.
Mesa: 15 meals, 4 repairs; Bay: 8 meals, 7 repairs.
Mesa: 20 meals, 5 repairs; Bay: 10 meals, 10 repairs.
Mesa: 5 meals, 4 repairs; Bay: 8 meals, 2 repairs.
items.feedback: Post-trade bundles are Mesa (20 meals, 5 repairs) and Bay (10 meals, 10 repairs). Subtracting the claimed gains gives autarky bundles (15, 4) and (8, 7). Adding gains to final bundles or treating the exchange itself as consumption gives the distractors.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Delta can make 24 files or 8 reviews; Echo can make 15 files or 10 reviews at constant tradeoffs. Delta doubles review productivity without changing files. A contract exchanges one review for 2 files. What changes?
options: The cost difference disappears, and the old contract no longer gives both positive gains
Delta gains review advantage because 16 exceeds Echo's 10
Echo retains review advantage because 15 is below Delta's 24 files
Both now receive a positive gain at every price between 1.5 and 3 files
items.feedback: Initially review costs are 3 and 1.5 files, so 2 can benefit both. Delta's new cost is 24/16 = 1.5, equal to Echo's. At 2, a review importer would pay more than domestic cost.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: A lens costs Urban 0.25 sensor and Rural 0.5 sensor. Urban proposes exporting lenses at 3 lenses per sensor, and pays shipping of 0.05 sensor per lens. Which assessment is correct?
options: Both gain: Urban nets more than 0.25 sensor per lens and Rural pays less than 0.5
Urban loses because three is larger than both stated opportunity costs
Rural loses because the reciprocal price is above 0.5 sensor per lens
Both are indifferent because shipping makes the costs equal
items.feedback: The quote is 1/3 sensor per lens. Urban nets 1/3 - 0.05, about 0.283, above 0.25; Rural pays about 0.333, below 0.5. Keep price and cost in the same units.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Lumen specializes at 32 lamps and Shade at 16 rugs. Their autarky bundles were Lumen (16 lamps, 4 rugs) and Shade (8 lamps, 8 rugs). Lumen now sends 18 lamps for 3 rugs, with no exchange costs. A planner says higher combined output proves both receive more of both goods. Which evaluation follows?
options: The claim holds: Lumen gains 2 lamps and 1 rug; Shade gains 10 lamps and 5 rugs.
The claim fails: Lumen gains 2 lamps and 1 rug; Shade loses 10 lamps and 5 rugs.
The claim holds: each receives half of the combined increase of 8 lamps and 4 rugs.
The claim fails: Lumen loses 2 lamps and 1 rug; Shade gains 10 lamps and 5 rugs.
items.feedback: Combined output rises from (24 lamps, 12 rugs) to (32, 16), but the exchange leaves Lumen (14, 3) and Shade (18, 13). Lumen has less of both goods; Shade has more of both. Higher total output does not establish mutually beneficial distribution.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Before specialization, two workshops jointly consume 18 frames and 10 cushions. Specialization produces 23 frames and 13 cushions; transport uses 2 cushions. Which claim follows before the remaining goods are divided?
options: The available bundle rises by 5 frames and 1 cushion, but individual gains depend on the division
Both parties necessarily gain 5 frames and 1 cushion each
Net cushion gain is 3 because transport is separate from production
One party's loss is impossible whenever both aggregate quantities rise
items.feedback: After transport, 23 frames and 11 cushions remain, a net gain of 5 and 1. Aggregate improvement permits beneficial divisions but does not establish the gains of a particular division.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: At constant tradeoffs, A makes 30 filters or 10 pumps; B makes 24 filters or 12 pumps. B exports pumps and pays shipping of 0.4 filter per pump. Which price gives both positive gains and gives B the larger per-pump gain measured in filters?
options: 2.8 filters per pump
2.5 filters per pump
2.4 filters per pump
3 filters per pump
items.feedback: B's net gain is price - 2 - 0.4; A's is 3 - price. At 2.8 the gains are 0.4 and 0.2. At 2.5 A gains more; 2.4 or 3 leaves one party indifferent.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Per hour a manager can make 6 sales or complete 12 accounts; an assistant can make 2 sales or complete 8 accounts. Each sale nets $100. Completing 24 accounts through the assistant also requires one hour of the manager’s supervision. Should the manager delegate the accounts, holding total paid hours fixed?
options: Yes: delegation allows 6 additional sales because the assistant’s forgone sales are the only cost to compare.
Indifferent: delegation sacrifices 12 sales including supervision, the same as completing the accounts personally.
No: delegation sacrifices 18 sales while direct typing sacrifices 8, so direct typing gains 10 sales.
No: the manager’s higher speed at both tasks proves delegation always lowers total sales.
items.feedback: Direct typing takes 24/12=2 manager hours, forgoing 12 sales. Delegation takes 24/8=3 assistant hours, forgoing 6 sales, plus 6 sales forgone during manager supervision: also 12. Delegation does not improve the outcome under the specified measure.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: A trade agreement yields gross national gains of $100 million before $30 million of real adjustment costs. Before adjustment costs, consumers gain $160 million and displaced workers lose $60 million. A $60 million domestic compensation transfer would fully offset that loss but costs $15 million to administer. Which evaluation is correct?
options: Net gain after administration is -$5 million; the compensation payment must be deducted again as a resource loss.
Net gain after administration is $70 million; the transfer automatically occurs when aggregate surplus rises.
Net gain after administration is $55 million; full compensation is feasible under the stated estimates but requires the transfer to be made.
Net gain after administration is $115 million; compensation increases national surplus by the amount workers receive.
items.feedback: Gross gains already net the $60 million worker loss: 160-60=100. National net gain is 100-30-15=55; the domestic transfer is not an additional resource loss. Workers receive compensation only if the policy is implemented.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Arbor specializes at 28 timber and Basin at 14 tools. Their autarky bundles were Arbor (14 timber, 3 tools) and Basin (6 timber, 7 tools). Basin offers 4 tools for t units of timber. With no exchange costs, which range of t gives each party strictly more of BOTH goods than in autarky?
items.feedback: Arbor receives 4 tools and retains 28 - t timber; it needs 28 - t > 14, so t 6. Thus 6 < t < 14. At either endpoint one party only matches, rather than exceeds, its autarky timber quantity.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Quartz can make 10 chips or 20 screens; Sable can make 4 chips or 20 screens. Costs are constant. Quartz exports chips and uses resources worth 0.5 screen per chip to arrange delivery. At 5 screens per chip, who receives a positive gain? If the rate falls to 4, what changes?
options: At 5 only Quartz receives a positive gain; at 4 both gain, with Quartz gaining 1.5 screens and Sable saving 1 screen per chip.
At 5 both receive a positive gain; at 4 only Sable gains, because delivery raises Quartz’s opportunity cost to 4.5 screens per chip.
At 5 only Sable receives a positive gain; at 4 both gain, with Sable gaining 1.5 screens and Quartz saving 1 screen per chip.
At 5 neither receives a positive gain; at 4 Quartz loses 0.5 screen, because delivery costs must be added to Sable’s production cost.
items.feedback: Production costs are 2 and 5 screens per chip. Quartz’s delivered cost is 2.5. At rate 5, Quartz gains 2.5 and Sable is indifferent. At rate 4, Quartz gains 1.5 and Sable saves 1.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Cedar can make 30 boards or 10 doors; Dune can make 16 boards or 8 doors. A tool doubles Dune’s board capacity without changing door capacity. Costs are constant. A proposed contract keeps Dune exporting doors at 2.5 boards per door. Which revision follows?
options: Reverse the specialization: Dune now exports boards, Cedar exports doors, and a rate strictly between 3 and 4 boards per door can benefit both.
Keep Dune exporting doors at 2.5 boards per door, because its door capacity and therefore its door opportunity cost are unchanged.
Reverse the specialization but retain 2.5 boards per door, because any rate above Dune’s original cost benefits both after the tool.
Stop specialization because Dune’s higher board output gives it absolute and comparative advantage in both goods.
items.feedback: Initially door costs are 3 boards in Cedar and 2 in Dune, making 2.5 mutually beneficial. After the tool Dune’s door cost rises to 32/8=4 boards. Cedar now exports doors; the mutual-gain interval is strictly 3 to 4.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Orchid produces 36 flowers and Reed produces 18 baskets after specializing. Before trade, Orchid consumed 18 flowers and 4 baskets; Reed consumed 9 flowers and 9 baskets. They exchange 12 flowers for 6 baskets. Shipping by road uses 1 of Orchid’s received baskets; shipping by air uses 3. No flowers are lost, and Reed pays no shipping cost. Which method leaves each producer with more of both goods than before trade?
options: Both methods; Orchid keeps 5 baskets by road and 7 by air.
Air only; Orchid keeps 3 baskets by road and 5 by air.
Road only; Orchid keeps 5 baskets by road and 3 by air.
Neither method; Orchid keeps 3 baskets by road and 1 by air.
items.feedback: Before shipping costs, Orchid has 24 flowers and 6 baskets, and Reed has 12 flowers and 12 baskets. Road shipping leaves Orchid 5 baskets, above its original 4; air shipping leaves only 3. Reed gains in both goods under either method.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Haven gives up 3 grain per turbine and Isle 7. Haven exports turbines; Isle also uses resources worth 1 grain per imported turbine to transport them. Compare offers of 4 and 6 grain per turbine. Which contract strictly benefits both after transport?
options: Only 4 does: Haven gains 1 and Isle gains 2 grain; at 6 Isle is indifferent after transport.
Both do: Haven gains more at 6, while Isle still gains 1 grain because transport does not enter comparative cost.
Only 6 does: Haven gains 3 and Isle gains 1 grain; at 4 Haven is indifferent after transport.
Neither does: the transport cost makes every rate between production opportunity costs unprofitable for the importer.
items.feedback: At rate r, Haven gains r-3 and Isle gains 7-r-1. At 4 these gains are 1 and 2; at 6 they are 3 and 0. Strict mutual gain now requires 3<r<6.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Peak specializes at 40 services and Glen at 20 devices. Autarky bundles were Peak (20 services, 6 devices) and Glen (10 services, 10 devices). Proposal A exchanges 16 services for 8 devices; B exchanges 22 services for 8 devices. Each party prefers more of either good when the other is unchanged; no other preferences or costs are given. Which assessment is justified?
options: A gives both more of both goods; B gives Peak fewer services but more devices, leaving its welfare change undetermined.
B gives both more of both goods; A gives Glen fewer devices but more services, leaving its welfare change undetermined.
Both give both more of both goods; each party is better off without needing further preference information.
Neither gives either more of both goods; each party’s welfare change under both proposals remains undetermined.
items.feedback: A leaves Peak (24 services, 8 devices) and Glen (16 services, 12 devices), more of both goods for each. B leaves Peak (18, 8) and Glen (22, 12). Glen gains in both, but Peak trades 2 fewer services for 2 more devices relative to autarky. Its welfare comparison requires preferences; total output alone cannot settle it.

items.stem: An economy has consumption of $46 billion, government purchases of $13 billion, exports of $9 billion, imports of $11 billion and GDP of $72 billion. Inventories increase by $4 billion because of newly produced unsold goods. What is total investment, and how are inventories included?
options: I = 15; the 4 of inventories is included within that total
I = 19; add inventories after solving the identity
I = 7; subtract inventories twice to avoid unsold output
I = 37; imports should be added when solving for investment
items.feedback: The expenditure identity gives I = 72 − 46 − 13 − 9 + 11 = 15. Inventory investment is included in this $15 billion total, leaving $11 billion in other investment.

items.stem: A government purchases $18 million of new domestic flood barriers and pays $12 million in household benefits. Recipients spend $7 million on new domestic services and $3 million on imported goods, saving the rest. What GDP contribution and expenditure classification follow?
options: $25 million; G = 18, C = 10, and M = 3
$37 million; benefits and recipient purchases both count
$28 million; imported purchases count only in C
$18 million; spending financed by benefits is excluded
items.feedback: The benefit payment itself is a transfer. Recipient purchases enter C = 7 + 3 = 10; M = 3 removes the imported goods. G = 18, so domestic GDP rises 18 + 10 - 3 = 25 million, without counting the transfer again.

items.stem: At the start of a year, a producer has $8 million of goods made last year. It produces $30 million this year and sells $34 million, leaving $4 million in inventory. With unchanged prices, no imports and all sales to final users, which GDP account is correct?
options: $30 million: final sales 34 plus inventory investment of -4
$34 million: sales determine the production year
$38 million: add beginning inventories to new output
$42 million: add beginning inventories to final sales
items.feedback: Inventory investment is the change in stock: 4 - 8 = -4. Sales of 34 plus inventory investment of -4 equal current production of 30. Selling previously produced goods does not create output again.

items.stem: A revision adds $6 billion of imported household appliances to consumption and records $2 billion of previously omitted current domestic installation services. The same imported appliances were missing from M. How should measured GDP change after all corrections?
options: Rise $2 billion; imported spending cancels while domestic installation remains
Rise $8 billion; all added consumption is domestic output
Fall $4 billion; imports are subtracted without adding their spending
Remain unchanged; every correction associated with imports cancels
items.feedback: C rises by 8 billion and M by 6 billion. The net 2-billion increase is the newly measured domestic service. Subtracting imports removes foreign production, not the associated domestic activity.

items.stem: A domestic firm sells $75 of last year's inventory to households and produces $19 of new goods that remain unsold. No other production occurs. How do the sales and inventory change enter consumption, investment and GDP?
options: C = $0, inventory I = $-56, GDP = $-56
C = $75, inventory I = $56, GDP = $131
C = $75, inventory I = $-56, GDP = $19
C = $75, inventory I = $19, GDP = $94
items.feedback: Consumption records the sale, but inventory investment is new accumulation 19 minus withdrawal 75. C+I = 75+(19−75) = $19, this year's production.

items.stem: Government transfers $80 to households, who buy $20 of imports and $60 of current domestic services. No other spending changes. An expenditure report records G +$80, C +$80 and M +$20, while production records show only $60 of new domestic services. What explains the discrepancy?
options: The transfer was wrongly included in G; removing it gives GDP +$60, matching domestic production.
Imports were wrongly subtracted; removing M gives GDP +$160, matching the services plus imported goods.
Consumption should exclude both transfers and imports, leaving C zero and GDP +$60 from government purchases.
The production records must omit $80 of government output because every cash transfer purchases current output.
items.feedback: The report totals 80+80−20=140, exceeding production by 80. Transfers are not purchases of output. Excluding them from G leaves consumption 80 minus imports 20, or 60, consistent with the domestic services.

items.stem: Households buy $3 million of domestic services and $2 million of imports; firms buy $4 million of domestic machinery and $2 million of stock; government buys $5 million of domestic bridges and pays $1 million in transfers; exports are $2 million. An accountant totals all payments as $19 million of GDP. Which exclusions reconcile that total with production?
options: Exclude $2 million of imports, $2 million of financial assets and $1 million of transfers, leaving $14 million of domestic output.
Exclude only the $2 million of imports, leaving $17 million because shares and transfers are current output.
Exclude the $2 million of stock and $1 million transfer but retain imports as domestic production, leaving $16 million.
Exclude machinery as an intermediate purchase and exports as foreign output, leaving $13 million.
items.feedback: Domestic production is 3+4+5+2=14. The $5 million discrepancy consists of imported production, ownership claims and transfers. These expenditures can move money without adding current domestic output.

items.stem: A domestic assembler sells $420,000 of new equipment, using $150,000 of imported parts and $90,000 of current domestic components. A clerk adds all three values as domestic GDP. What correction reconciles final spending with domestic value added?
options: $270,000 total domestic GDP, including $180,000 at assembly
$420,000 total domestic GDP, including $330,000 at assembly
$510,000 total domestic GDP, including $420,000 at assembly
$180,000 total domestic GDP, excluding the domestic component makers
items.feedback: Final spending of 420,000 less imported inputs of 150,000 yields 270,000 domestic value added. Assembly contributes 420,000 - 150,000 - 90,000 = 180,000; domestic component makers contribute the remaining 90,000. Do not count their output twice.

items.stem: A workshop sells $560 of new furniture after buying $140 of domestic lumber. Its wage bill is $250 and rent plus interest is $90. With no other costs or taxes, which value-added and profit account is consistent?
options: $420 value added, including $80 profit
$560 value added, including $220 profit
$280 value added, including $80 profit
$420 value added, including $420 profit
items.feedback: Value added is final output less intermediate lumber: 560 - 140 = 420. Of that, wages and rent/interest absorb 340, leaving profit of 80. Subtracting wages when computing value added would remove income generated by production.

items.stem: A renovation business bills households $96,000, including $24,000 of imported fixtures. It also brokers an old building for a $6,000 fee; the building sells for $310,000. Ignoring other inputs, what current domestic production and counting rule follow?
options: $78,000; count domestic renovation value and the new brokerage service
$388,000; the old building becomes current output when sold
$102,000; imported fixtures count because households bought them
$72,000; services attached to used assets must also be excluded
items.feedback: Domestic renovation value is 96,000 - 24,000 = 72,000. The current brokerage service adds 6,000, while the old building itself is not new output. Total current domestic production is 78,000.

items.stem: A production audit reports $74 million of final sales and $6 million of new inventories. Domestic production income is $51 million in wages, $9 million in rent and interest, and unreported profit. With no imports, taxes or depreciation adjustments, which result closes both accounts?
options: $80 million GDP and $20 million profit
$74 million GDP and $14 million profit
$86 million GDP and $26 million profit
$60 million GDP and $20 million profit
items.feedback: Current production includes the unsold 6 million, giving expenditure GDP of 80 million. Wages and rent/interest total 60 million, so residual profit is 20 million. Sales alone omit inventory investment.

items.stem: A used machine changes hands for $40,000 through a broker charging $2,000. A new domestic machine worth $28,000 is produced but remains unsold. How much do these activities contribute to this year’s GDP?
options: $30,000: brokerage service plus inventory investment
$42,000: resale plus brokerage service
$70,000: every transaction and unsold machine
$2,000: unsold output cannot count until purchased
items.feedback: The resale transfers an existing asset; the newly produced brokerage service counts. The unsold new machine is inventory investment when produced. Thus current GDP includes 2,000 + 28,000 = 30,000.

items.stem: A producer sells $86 of final output containing a domestic supplier's $46 input. The supplier buys no intermediate inputs. Unrelated domestic services add $61. An accountant reports GDP of $101 after subtracting the input from final output. Which missing entry explains why this is below the expenditure total?
options: The supplier's $46 of gross sales must be added to the full $86 final sale and $61 services, giving $193.
The supplier's $46 of value added; adding it to the producer's $40 and services of $61 gives $147.
The $61 of services should be removed because goods and services cannot appear in the same GDP account.
No entry is missing; subtracting inputs from final expenditure is how GDP avoids double counting.
items.feedback: Subtracting 46 from 86 yields the downstream producer's 40 of value added, not total production. With the supplier's 46 and unrelated services 61 included, value added sums to 147, matching final expenditure 86+61.

items.stem: A domestic farm sells grain for $48 to a mill, which sells flour for $63 to a bakery; bread sells to households for $88. The farm buys no intermediate inputs, and no inventories change. An accountant sums value added but omits the farm, reporting GDP of $40. Would excluding the farm be justified because its grain is intermediate?
options: No. The farm adds $48, bringing total value added to $88.
Yes. Intermediate producers add nothing to GDP, so only downstream value added counts.
No. All three gross sales should be added, making GDP $199.
Yes. The farm's $48 has already been counted in the mill's $15 of value added.
items.feedback: Mill value added is 63−48=15 and bakery value added 88−63=25. Their $40 excludes the farm's $48 contribution. Intermediate sales are not added on top of final expenditure, but each domestic producer's value added belongs in the production account.

items.stem: A household buys a machine produced last year for $90 and pays a dealer a $50 current service fee. Suppose the used-machine price were instead $60 while the fee and service stayed the same. How would that change current GDP from this transaction?
options: GDP would fall $30 because every reduction in the total household payment lowers current output.
GDP would be $110 because both the used machine and dealer fee count as newly produced output.
GDP would be zero because transactions involving used goods exclude even newly provided services.
It would not change the $50 contribution; the lower payment changes the price of an existing asset, not current production.
items.feedback: The original $140 payment contains $90 for an existing asset and $50 for current service. The counterfactual $110 payment still buys the same $50 service. GDP records that service, not the resale price of last year's machine.

items.stem: After a higher hourly minimum wage, a firm raises hourly pay but reduces scheduled hours and employer-paid training. A report calls the higher hourly rate proof that every worker gained. Which review addresses the missing incentive responses?
options: Compare hours, total earnings and training changes for affected workers
Use the hourly rate alone because other employment terms are not wages
Infer that lower hours prove every worker lost despite higher hourly pay
Treat the firm's adjustment as proof it did not respond to the wage rule
items.feedback: The hourly rate is only one margin. Hours and training can change in response, so worker outcomes require the combined compensation and work changes; no additional price-floor mechanics are needed.

items.stem: A subscription service makes cancellation require a phone call but lets upgrades occur with one click. Cancellations fall and complaints rise. What is the strongest inference?
options: Exit friction can reduce cancellation despite dissatisfaction; easier upgrades do not remove the cost of leaving.
Stronger service preference best explains retention; complaints mainly show that retained users demand more service quality.
One-click upgrades best explain retention; the phone requirement mainly reallocates existing demand across service tiers.
The phone call screens out low-value cancellations; fewer cancellations therefore indicate higher consumer welfare.
items.feedback: Retention can rise because leaving now costs more time, even when experience worsens. Neither upgraded service demand nor revealed preference for staying can be inferred without accounting for exit friction.

items.stem: A repair subsidy pays for every completed repair. Claims rise sharply, but most claimants would have repaired anyway; some shops relabel routine servicing. What evidence best identifies the intended response?
options: Additional genuine repairs relative to comparable users without the subsidy
The total number of paid claims, treating each as a newly induced repair
The size of the subsidy budget, treating expenditure as added repair benefit
The stated repair goal, treating relabeling as evidence of no behavioral response
items.feedback: Separate newly induced repairs from payments for existing behavior and changes in reporting. Claims alone mix these margins and overstate the intended response.

items.stem: A software platform ranks creators by daily posting frequency. Posting rises, but creators split one useful guide into many thin updates. What does the response reveal?
options: The ranking rewards posting frequency, so creators can raise measured output while reducing useful content per post.
The ranking reveals stronger reader demand for short posts, so more posts establish an increase in information value.
The ranking lowers the cost of writing, so thinner posts indicate a productivity gain at unchanged information quality.
The ranking rewards guide quality indirectly, so splitting a guide raises both measured output and the original learning benefit.
items.feedback: Creators can substitute toward the measured posting count and away from unmeasured quality. More posts alone do not identify demand, productivity or learning gains.

items.stem: A city reduces bus fares to increase ridership. Ridership rises, but crowding makes some riders switch back to cars. What is the strongest lesson?
options: Lower fares attract riders, but congestion raises time costs and feeds back to reduce part of the initial ridership gain.
The initial fare response proves demand shifted right; riders returning to cars show the fare cut later shifted supply left.
Returning riders reveal more elastic money-price demand; their switch implies the initial ridership increase was measured incorrectly.
Crowding raises the service’s money price implicitly; the resulting ridership decline establishes that the fare policy reduced total welfare.
items.feedback: The fare cut lowers one part of the generalized travel cost while crowding raises another. Feedback can offset some ridership gains without contradicting demand theory or determining the net welfare result.

items.stem: A teacher bonus depends on class-average scores. Teachers provide extra review but also discourage low-performing students from testing. What should an evaluator conclude?
options: Higher scores may reflect both extra instruction and changed test participation; compare learning for the original student group.
Higher scores measure extra instruction if bonuses are uniform; excluding weak students then represents improved classroom efficiency.
Changed participation fully explains higher scores; extra review has no independent effect once selection incentives exist.
Average scores remain comparable across years if the test is unchanged; student participation changes affect only the sample size.
items.feedback: The bonus rewards a measured average. Instruction and selection can both change it, so following the original group is needed to distinguish learning from compositional change.

items.stem: A university receives funding for degrees completed on time. Advising improves, but difficult required courses are weakened. What is the strongest interpretation?
options: Funding rewards completion speed, so advising effort and lower course standards can both improve the metric without equal learning gains.
Funding rewards educational quality, so faster completion and easier courses jointly establish more learning per enrolled student.
Easier courses explain completion gains entirely, so advising improvements cannot contribute to the measured funding outcome.
Faster completion reduces students’ time costs, so course standards have no additional role in evaluating the policy’s net benefit.
items.feedback: A completion metric can reward both useful advising and weakened standards. Evaluating educational success requires learning evidence in addition to completion and time savings.

items.stem: A health insurer waives copays for preventive visits but raises emergency-room copays. Which response is most defensible?
options: Lower preventive prices and higher emergency prices encourage substitution, but access and urgent needs constrain which patients can switch.
The price changes chiefly reduce total visits; patients with limited preventive access can substitute as readily as other patients.
The preventive subsidy raises income rather than relative prices; changes in emergency use therefore identify only the copay increase.
Emergency use should fall most for unavoidable acute cases; elective preventive care is least responsive to the lower copay.
items.feedback: Relative prices favor prevention, but substitution requires access and medical feasibility. Acute emergencies and barriers to preventive care limit the response.

items.stem: A city pays restaurants for each kilogram of food donated. Donations rise, but some restaurants overproduce near closing time. What does this show?
options: The payment rewards donated kilograms, so it can induce both recovery of surplus food and production that would not otherwise occur.
The payment rewards avoided waste, so additional production confirms that previously wasted food has been redirected efficiently.
Overproduction indicates stronger final-consumer demand; donated kilograms are therefore unrelated to the payment’s production incentive.
Donations transfer food between users, so extra production costs cancel from welfare whenever recipients value the donated meals.
items.feedback: A per-kilogram subsidy raises the payoff to donating both existing surplus and newly produced food. The value of donations must be weighed against added production resources and waste.

items.stem: A factory posts team safety rankings without cash prizes. Reporting rises, but some teams relabel minor incidents as near misses. Which conclusion is best?
options: Status rewards can change reporting and relabeling; independently measured injuries are needed to identify real safety improvement.
Higher reporting shows actual injuries increased; relabeling minor cases changes only terminology and not the measured ranking.
Relabeling improves risk classification; higher ranking positions therefore identify better safety even without independent injury data.
Noncash status rewards mainly reveal team preferences; higher reported safety establishes that effort rose equally across teams.
items.feedback: Rankings can motivate reporting and gaming without cash payments. The stem establishes changed records, not improved reporting accuracy or fewer injuries; independent injury evidence is needed.

items.stem: A platform threatens suspension for false listings, but enforcement reviews only complaints from paying users. What response is most plausible?
options: Expected sanctions differ by customer group, so sellers may redirect deception toward users whose complaints do not trigger review.
A uniform suspension penalty creates equal deterrence across users, so different complaint review rules mainly affect paperwork.
Paying users receive more review, so sellers face a stronger incentive to deceive them in order to cover expected sanctions.
The threat discourages entry by dishonest sellers, so surviving sellers’ choices between user groups are unaffected by enforcement.
items.feedback: Expected sanctions combine the penalty with the probability of review. Restricting review to paying-user complaints changes the relative payoff to targeting other users.

items.stem: A government contract pays builders for finishing early and penalizes visible defects, but not hidden maintenance problems. What risk remains?
options: Rewards cover speed and observable defects, so effort can shift from hidden durability toward the measured dimensions.
The defect penalty prices all quality losses, so earlier completion also establishes greater hidden durability.
The speed reward and defect penalty create opposing incentives, so their combined effect on effort must be zero.
Maintenance is paid later, so hidden durability is a sunk cost and should be excluded from evaluating the contract.
items.feedback: When hidden maintenance problems are not penalized, the contract can reward speed and visible quality while encouraging substitution away from durability. Later costs are not thereby sunk.

items.stem: An employer replaces a late-arrival reprimand with a small fee deducted from pay. Some workers become more punctual; others treat lateness as a purchasable option. What does this show?
options: The fee changes both the monetary consequence and its perceived social meaning, allowing deterrence for some and purchased lateness for others.
The fee lowers the monetary cost for every worker, so mixed punctuality must reflect differences in measured arrival times.
The fee strengthens social disapproval for every worker, so treating lateness as purchased shows workers no longer respond to payoffs.
The fee converts lateness into a market transaction, so workers’ prior response to social reprimands is irrelevant to the change.
items.feedback: Replacing a reprimand can alter both financial incentives and social meaning. Responses can differ because workers value money and social sanctions differently.

items.stem: A criminal fine is tripled while the probability of detection falls by two-thirds. Without more information, what can be concluded?
options: Expected monetary penalties are unchanged, while perceived detection and risk attitudes can still alter deterrence.
Expected monetary penalties triple, while lower detection only changes the timing of the payment.
Expected monetary penalties fall by two-thirds, while the larger fine affects only the maximum possible loss.
Expected monetary penalties are unchanged, so deterrence must remain unchanged for every risk attitude.
items.feedback: If detection falls to one-third and the fine triples, probability times fine is unchanged. Equal expected money costs do not establish equal perceived or risk-adjusted deterrence.
