Tariff $7; revenue $196; producer gain $94.5; deadweight loss $49.
Tariff $14; revenue $392; producer gain $94.5; deadweight loss $245.
Tariff $7; revenue $196; producer gain $49; deadweight loss $94.5.
items.feedback: The import contraction of 14 reflects two quantity responses, so the tariff is $7. Receipts are $7 × 28 = $196; each distortion is $24.5. Consumer loss less revenue and the producer transfer leaves $49.

items.stem: In Juno, domestic demand is P = 96 - Qd and domestic supply is P = 28 + Qs. The world price is $38. The government sets a tariff that reduces imports to 24 units. With the world price unchanged, which option correctly gives the tariff per unit, government revenue, and deadweight loss?
options: Tariff $24; revenue $576; deadweight loss $576
Tariff $12; revenue $552; deadweight loss $144
Tariff $12; revenue $288; deadweight loss $144
Tariff $12; revenue $288; deadweight loss $432
items.feedback: Imports equal 124 - 2P, so the target implies P = $50 and tariff $12. Revenue is $12 × 24 = $288. Production expands 12 and consumption contracts 12; their two triangles sum to $144.

items.stem: In Juno, a small-country tariff cuts imports from 48 to 24. For each $1 increase in price, quantity supplied rises by one unit and quantity demanded falls by one unit. A report describes the entire $624 loss of consumer surplus as deadweight loss. Which statement correctly separates transfers from deadweight loss?
options: Tariff $12; revenue $0; producer gain $0; deadweight loss $624.
Tariff $24; revenue $576; producer gain $192; deadweight loss $432.
Tariff $12; revenue $288; producer gain $144; deadweight loss $192.
Tariff $12; revenue $288; producer gain $192; deadweight loss $144.
items.feedback: The import contraction of 24 reflects two quantity responses, so the tariff is $12. Receipts are $12 × 24 = $288; each distortion is $72. Consumer loss less revenue and the producer transfer leaves $144.

items.stem: With Qd = 110 - P, Qs = P - 10 and Pw = $30, a quota is auctioned to allow 40 imports. A $10 tariff is proposed instead. Demand then rises by 20 at every price. With competitive licensing and no administration costs, which post-shift outcome is correct?
options: Quota: price $50 and receipts $800; tariff: price $40 and receipts $600
Both: price $40 and receipts $400
Quota: price $40 and receipts $600; tariff: price $50 and receipts $800
Both: price $50 and receipts $800
items.feedback: After the shift, Qd = 130 - P. A 40-unit cap requires 140 - 2P = 40, so P = 50 and auction rents are 20 × 40 = 800. The tariff keeps P = 40, allows 60 imports and raises 600.

items.stem: An importing market has Qd = 96 - P, Qs = P - 16 and Pw = $28. A voluntary export restraint gives foreign firms free rights to ship 32 units. Compared with free trade, what are the importing-country welfare loss and the part transferred abroad?
options: $144 lost nationally, with no foreign transfer
$528 lost nationally, including $384 in foreign rents
$384 lost nationally, all of it destroyed surplus
$912 lost nationally, including a second deduction for the same rents
items.feedback: The cap implies P = (96 + 16 - 32)/2 = 40, a $12 wedge. Rents are 12 × 32 = 384. Straight curves each change quantity by 12, creating total distortion of 144. National loss is 384 + 144 = 528.

items.stem: An importer initially has Qd = 92 - P, Qs = P - 12 and Pw = $26. A $10 tariff and a 32-unit quota initially match. Demand then falls by 28 at every price. Which outcome follows?
options: Both keep price $36 because initially equivalent restrictions remain equivalent
The quota keeps imports at 32 even when buyers want only 24 at the world price
The quota becomes nonrestrictive at $26 with 24 imports; the tariff still raises price to $36 with 4 imports
The tariff becomes nonrestrictive while the quota raises price above $36
items.feedback: New demand is 64 - P. At Pw = 26 the desired import gap is 38 - 14 = 24, below the cap. Under the tariff P = 36 and imports are 28 - 24 = 4. A cap is a maximum, not a required shipment.

items.stem: A quota causes a $520 consumer loss, a $170 domestic producer gain and $280 of rents. Domestic firms hold the rights and spend $60 of real resources competing for them. A competitive auction would yield the same rents and use $15 of real resources. How much would switching to the auction improve national welfare?
options: $280; all auction proceeds are newly created surplus
$325; add auction proceeds to the resource saving
$60; auctions have no resource cost regardless of the stated data
$45; it saves resources while changing who receives an existing transfer
items.feedback: Distortion before rent-seeking is 520 - 170 - 280 = 70. The present system loses 70 + 60 = 130; the auction loses 70 + 15 = 85. National welfare improves by 45, not by the rent amount.

items.stem: Demand is P = 86 - Qd, supply is P = 14 + Qs and Pw is $30. A ministry compares tariffs of $6 and $14. Which comparison correctly distinguishes government revenue from national welfare?
options: Both raise $168, but the $14 tariff destroys $160 more surplus
Both raise $168 and therefore have equal national welfare
The $14 tariff raises more revenue because its rate is larger
The $6 tariff destroys more surplus because it permits more imports
items.feedback: Imports are 40 - 2t. At t = 6, revenue is 6 × 28 = 168 and DWL = 36. At t = 14, revenue is 14 × 12 = 168 and DWL = 196. The difference is 160.

items.stem: Officials propose a tariff on emergency valves because a foreign supply outage could halt hospitals. Domestic firms cannot expand within five years; audited reserves and two independent allied suppliers could cover an outage sooner at lower resource cost. Which assessment is best?
options: The security label alone establishes that any tariff improves resilience
The security concern can be real, but the evidence favors reserves and diversified supply over this tariff
The tariff must solve the outage risk because it raises domestic producer surplus
All resilience spending is wasteful because the small-country trade model has gains from trade
items.feedback: Evaluate whether the instrument actually reduces the stated risk and whether another instrument does so at lower cost. A legitimate objective does not make an ineffective tariff the preferred response.

items.stem: A new sensor industry predicts learning gains worth $18 million in present value. Protection would cost $24 million in present-value consumer surplus, transfer $9 million to domestic producers and yield $5 million of tariff revenue. Suppose learning is additional and there are no other effects. Which evaluation is correct?
options: The modeled net loss is $6 million because all consumer loss is destroyed
The modeled net gain is $32 million because producer gains and revenue are additional to learning
The modeled net gain is $8 million, but the case depends on the learning forecast being credible
The policy is proven desirable regardless of whether learning occurs
items.feedback: Static national loss is 24 - 9 - 5 = 10 million. Additional learning of 18 gives a modeled gain of 8. If the learning is not caused by protection or does not materialize, the conclusion can reverse.

items.stem: A tariff preserves 240 jobs in an input industry but eliminates 160 downstream jobs. Retaliation would eliminate another 120 export jobs if it occurs; its probability is one-half. What follows from these employment estimates alone?
options: Expected employment rises by 80, so the tariff necessarily raises welfare
Expected employment falls by 40 because retaliation is certain
Expected employment rises by 240 because losses outside the protected industry are irrelevant
Expected employment rises by 20, but this alone does not establish a national welfare gain
items.feedback: Expected job change is 240 - 160 - 0.5 × 120 = 20. Employment counts alone do not measure consumer surplus, resource costs or other welfare effects.

items.stem: A minister defends a tariff by citing $12 million of domestic producer gains. It also raises $8 million in revenue and costs consumers $17 million. Retaliation causes a separate $7 million net loss to domestic exporters. Ignoring other effects, which conclusion follows?
options: National surplus falls $4 million; the protected industry does not capture the whole policy effect
National surplus rises $3 million because retaliation affects only foreigners
National surplus rises $12 million because the protected producers are the relevant group
National surplus falls $24 million because producer gains and revenue cannot offset consumer losses
items.feedback: Include all the stated domestic effects once: 12 + 8 - 17 - 7 = -4 million. Retaliation transmits costs beyond the original protected industry; producer gains alone do not establish a national gain.

items.stem: Opening trade gives consumers $720 and costs producers $420. A plan transfers $420 from consumers to producers but uses $75 of real resources delivering assistance. Compared with autarky, which statement is correct?
options: Consumers retain $300 because assistance resources are just transfers
Producers can be restored and consumers retain $225; compensation and efficiency must both be evaluated
National surplus rises $720 because producer compensation cancels the original loss without cost
National surplus falls $195 because compensation must be subtracted twice
items.feedback: The initial national gain is 720 - 420 = 300. The transfer restores producers but changes no total; resource use reduces the gain to 225. The result presumes the assistance is actually delivered.

items.stem: Use the displayed avocado import graph. Suppose a policy raises domestic price $1 above the shown world price, with world price and both straight curves unchanged. What tariff revenue and remaining national gain relative to autarky follow? Quantities are in thousands.

$100 thousand revenue and $100 thousand remaining gain

items.stem: From the displayed avocado import graph, a program would restore the domestic producers' autarky surplus using a lump-sum transfer from consumers. Administration uses $30 thousand of real resources. How much of the opening-to-trade gain would consumers retain after both payments?
options: $100 thousand
$300 thousand
$70 thousand
$370 thousand

items.stem: In the displayed avocado export graph, suppose Pw falls by $1 while both straight domestic curves stay fixed. What are the new exports and the decrease in gains from trade relative to the displayed free-trade outcome? Quantities are in thousands.

100 thousand exports; gains from trade fall $125 thousand

100 thousand imports; gains from trade rise $125 thousand
items.feedback: Price falls from 10 to 9. The graph's slopes give Qs = 225 and Qd = 125, hence 100 exports. Gains over autarky fall from 0.5 × 3 × 150 = 225 to 0.5 × 2 × 100 = 100 thousand: a 125-thousand decline.

items.stem: Read the displayed avocado export graph. A producer-funded lump-sum transfer exactly compensates domestic consumers for opening to trade, with no resource costs. Which pair gives the required transfer and the producers' remaining gain?

items.feedback: The price rise is $3. Consumer loss is 0.5 × 3 × (175 + 100) = 412.5 thousand; producer gain is 0.5 × 3 × (175 + 250) = 637.5 thousand. Their difference, 225 thousand, remains after compensation.

items.stem: Compared with free trade, how does the tariff in the graph change consumer surplus, producer surplus, government revenue, and total welfare?

Consumer surplus falls by $2 x (250 + 200) / 2 = $450k; producer surplus rises by $2 x (50 + 100) / 2 = $150k. Post-tariff imports are 200 - 100 = 100 thousand, so revenue is $2 x 100 = $200k. Net welfare changes by -$450k + $150k + $200k = -$100k, the sum of the two $50k distortion triangles.

items.stem: Use the phone-case tariff graph. If the tariff is reduced halfway from its displayed level to zero, with linear demand and supply curves and an unchanged world price, what happens to tariff revenue and total distortion loss?

items.stem: Use the phone-case tariff graph. A minister proposes keeping the tariff but returning all its revenue to consumers as lump-sum payments, with no administrative cost. Relative to free trade, what happens to consumers and total national surplus?

Consumers lose $825k; producers gain $337.5k; quota rents are $150k; net welfare falls $337.5k

Domestic license holders receive those rents, making the net welfare change -$712.5k + $337.5k + $150k = -$225k, the sum of the two $112.5k distortion triangles.

items.stem: Using the phone-case quota graph, replace free domestic import licenses with a voluntary export restraint that gives foreign firms the same rights free. items.stem: In one period, consumption rises $96 billion, including $72 billion of imports. Measured investment rises $35 billion, including $11 billion of imported equipment. Exports rise $18 billion, while government purchases and other imports are unchanged. How do GDP and national saving change?
options: GDP rises $149 billion and national saving rises $53 billion
GDP rises $66 billion and national saving rises $30 billion
GDP rises $83 billion and national saving falls $13 billion
GDP rises $66 billion and national saving falls $30 billion

items.stem: Two countries initially have S = $700 billion and I = $750 billion. In Alder, saving rises $65 billion while investment rises an unknown amount. In Brin, saving rises $40 billion and investment rises $25 billion. What condition makes Alder end with a smaller trade deficit than Brin but still a deficit?
options: Alder investment rises by less than $15 billion
Alder investment rises by more than $50 billion but less than $65 billion
Alder investment rises by more than $15 billion but less than $50 billion
Alder investment rises by exactly $65 billion
items.feedback: Brin ends with NX = −50 + 40 − 25 = −35. Alder ends at NX = −50 + 65 − ΔI = 15 − ΔI. Requiring −35 < 15 − ΔI < 0 gives 15 < ΔI < 50, in billions.

items.stem: Initially NX and NCO are zero. Residents increase foreign-asset purchases by $126 billion. Exports then rise $54 billion and imports rise $18 billion. What change in foreign purchases of domestic assets reconciles both accounts, and what does it establish about the causal sequence?
options: They rise $162 billion; capital inflow necessarily causes the export increase
They rise $90 billion; the identities do not establish which flow caused the trade change
They fall $90 billion; the identities establish that trade moved first
They rise $36 billion; the asset and trade balances need not match
items.feedback: ΔNX = 54 − 18 = 36, so ΔNCO = 36 = 126 − Δinflow. Therefore inflow rises 90. Period accounting reconciles the totals but does not identify the behavioral timing.

items.stem: Imports increased, national saving fell, and domestic investment also fell. A commentator says these observations prove that the trade deficit widened. What additional comparisons would let us check this claim using both saving and investment and the export and import figures?
options: Compare the saving decline with the investment decline, and compare the import rise with the export change
Compare the saving decline with the import rise; exports are unnecessary
Compare the investment decline with the import rise; saving is unnecessary
Compare the levels of saving and exports; their changes are unnecessary
items.feedback: ΔNX = ΔS − ΔI, so falling saving and investment alone do not sign the change. Independently, ΔNX = ΔX − ΔM; exports must be compared with imports. Either complete accounting comparison should produce the same answer.

items.stem: A deficit lowers public saving $74 billion. Private saving rises by an unknown amount, domestic investment falls $22 billion, and net exports fall $31 billion. How much does private saving rise, and why is the decline in net exports smaller than the increase in the deficit?
options: Private saving rises $43 billion; NX must fall by the full deficit increase
Private saving falls $21 billion; investment crowding out enlarges the NX decline
Private saving rises $105 billion; the deficit necessarily produces a trade surplus
Private saving rises $21 billion; the NX decline is smaller than the deficit increase
items.feedback: Let p be the private-saving rise. ΔNX = (p − 74) − (−22) = p − 52 = −31, so p = 21. Offsetting private saving and lower investment both cushion the external-balance effect.

items.stem: For the same period, a data release reports S = $480 billion, I = $525 billion, X = $210 billion, M = $240 billion, foreign-asset purchases by residents of $70 billion, and domestic-asset purchases by foreigners of $115 billion. If exactly one trade figure is wrong and all other figures are correct, how could the trade figures be corrected, and can we tell which figure is wrong?
options: Raise X to $225 billion or lower M to $225 billion; the identity does not select between them
Raise M to $255 billion; the identity proves that imports alone are wrong
Raise M to $255 billion or lower X to $195 billion; the identity does not select between them
Lower X to $195 billion; the identity proves that exports alone are wrong
items.feedback: S − I = −45 and asset NCO = 70 − 115 = −45, but reported NX is −30. Trade must fall another 15: either M rises from 240 to 255 or X falls from 210 to 195. The stated data do not identify which trade entry is erroneous.

items.stem: Output is $5.0 trillion, consumption $3.1 trillion, government purchases $0.9 trillion, and investment $1.2 trillion. Domestic purchases of foreign assets are $260 billion. How much must foreigners purchase in domestic assets?
options: $660 billion
$460 billion
$60 billion
$260 billion
items.feedback: NX = 5.0 − 3.1 − 0.9 − 1.2 = −$0.2 trillion, so NCO is −$200 billion. With NCO = $260 billion − foreign purchases, foreign purchases equal $460 billion.

items.stem: A $100 billion rise in exports accompanies a $130 billion rise in imports. National saving rises by $50 billion. What change in domestic investment preserves all identities?
options: An increase of $80 billion
An increase of $20 billion
A decrease of $20 billion
An increase of $180 billion
items.feedback: NX falls $30 billion, so NCO falls $30 billion. Since ΔNCO = ΔS − ΔI, −30 = 50 − ΔI, making ΔI = $80 billion.

items.stem: A firm buys imported equipment for $44 million. Measured consumption rises $31 million, of which $19 million is imported. Government purchases are unchanged, and GDP rises $27 million. With no other expenditure changes, reconstruct exports and NX changes.
options: Exports rise $27 million and NX falls $36 million
Exports rise $71 million and NX rises $8 million
Exports fall $17 million and NX falls $80 million
Exports rise $15 million and NX falls $48 million
items.feedback: Imports rise 44 + 19 = 63. Solve 27 = 31 + 44 + ΔX − 63, giving ΔX = 15. Then ΔNX = 15 − 63 = −48 million.

items.stem: In a competitive labor market, employment is 100 at the clearing wage. A binding wage floor produces labor supply of 140 and demand of 95. Assuming everyone seeking work is available and active, which comparison is correct?
options: Employment falls by 5, while the labor surplus is 45; these are different quantities
Employment falls by 45 because every person in the surplus previously had a job
Employment falls by 40, matching the increase in labor supply
There is no surplus because 95 people remain employed
items.feedback: Employment changes from 100 to 95, a loss of 5. The new excess of labor supplied over labor demanded is 140 - 95 = 45, including the effect of increased job seeking as well as reduced hiring. The surplus is not the number of pre-existing jobs lost.

items.stem: A benefit extension lowers the cost of continued search. A simultaneous placement program improves matching. Average unemployment duration then falls. Which conclusion is warranted from these facts alone?
options: Duration fell, but the benefit extension’s separate effect is unknown
The fall proves benefit extensions always shorten search
The extension must have been ineffective at protecting income because duration fell
The placement program cannot matter because benefits determine every search decision
items.feedback: Income support can reduce search urgency while better matching shortens search. Their combined result does not isolate either effect; a credible separate comparison would be needed. The duration result also does not measure the value of income protection.

items.stem: A negotiated wage rises from $20 to $24 while employment falls from 100 to 90, with hours per worker fixed. What happens to the total wage bill, and what distributional claim is justified?
options: The wage bill rises 8%; retained workers gain hourly pay while some workers lose jobs
The wage bill falls 10%; no workers gain from the contract
The wage bill rises 20%; the employment change is irrelevant
The wage bill rises 8%; this proves every original worker is better off
items.feedback: The wage bill changes from 20 × 100 = 2,000 to 24 × 90 = 2,160 per common unit of hours, an 8% rise. The aggregate increase does not erase the job losses; gains to retained workers and losses to displaced workers differ.

items.stem: A firm considers raising wages from $18 to $21 per hour. Output per hour is expected to rise from 6 to 7 units through better retention and effort, with other unit costs unchanged. Which cost calculation and caution are correct?
options: Wage cost stays $3 per unit if the productivity forecast holds; the forecast still needs evidence
$3.50 per unit is certain because productivity cannot respond to wages
$2.57 per unit is certain because the old wage applies to the new output
$3 per unit proves the wage policy eliminates unemployment throughout the economy
items.feedback: The old wage cost is 18/6 = 3 per unit; the proposed cost is 21/7 = 3 if the effort/retention forecast occurs. This makes an efficiency-wage rationale possible, but does not prove the forecast or settle economy-wide unemployment.

items.stem: Job-search assistance speeds matching for 230 applicants, while reduced search pressure permits others to wait longer for suitable offers. Which unemployment prediction requires more evidence?
options: The net frictional-unemployment change, because faster matching and longer chosen searches oppose
Whether either channel concerns frictional unemployment; all search is structural by definition
Whether faster matching reduces a spell, because matching can affect only wages
Whether weaker search pressure raises the natural rate permanently regardless of matching gains
items.feedback: Faster matching shortens spells; waiting longer can lengthen them. Both involve the search component, so relative magnitudes are needed for the net rate.

items.stem: Above-market wages improve effort among 240 retained employees. A proposal predicts that productivity gains must exactly offset reduced hiring. Which missing comparison is essential?
options: Whether retained employees are classified as unemployed when the wage is above equilibrium
Whether the statutory unemployment denominator should exclude workers receiving higher wages
Whether every firm uses identical technology, which alone guarantees an exact offset
The size of the productivity/turnover benefit relative to the higher labor cost and hiring response
items.feedback: The efficiency mechanism can benefit the employer, but it does not algebraically guarantee a particular employment or cost offset. Relative magnitudes determine the net result.

items.stem: Job-search assistance speeds matching for 280 applicants, while reduced search pressure permits others to wait longer for suitable offers. Which unemployment prediction requires more evidence?
options: Whether either channel concerns frictional unemployment; all search is structural by definition
Whether faster matching reduces a spell, because matching can affect only wages
Whether weaker search pressure raises the natural rate permanently regardless of matching gains
The net frictional-unemployment change, because faster matching and longer chosen searches oppose
items.feedback: Faster matching shortens spells; waiting longer can lengthen them. Both involve the search component, so relative magnitudes are needed for the net rate.

items.stem: Two regions report real GDP per person of $44,000 and $40,000. In the first, output per hour is $40 and annual hours per resident are 1,100; in the second they are $50 and 800. Which comparison is supported without assigning a value to leisure?
options: The first has higher output per person; the second has higher hourly productivity, so welfare is not ranked
The first is more productive per hour because its GDP per person is higher
The second has higher GDP per person because it is more productive per hour
The first has higher overall welfare by exactly 10%
items.feedback: The products 40 × 1,100 = 44,000 and 50 × 800 = 40,000 reconcile the figures. More hours explain the first region’s higher average output despite lower hourly productivity. Neither GDP nor these hours alone values all welfare differences.

items.stem: After a storm, rebuilding adds $12 million of current production while lost business activity reduces other current production by $5 million. Destroyed existing buildings were worth $30 million. Which GDP and welfare statement is defensible?
options: GDP is $7 million higher than otherwise; this does not establish a welfare improvement
GDP is $23 million lower because destroyed wealth is subtracted from current production
GDP is $12 million higher; lost current production is irrelevant
GDP is $37 million higher because rebuilding replaces the destroyed stock
items.feedback: The change in current production is 12 - 5 = 7 million. Destruction of existing wealth is a separate loss, not a negative item of current production. Higher measured GDP therefore does not establish higher well-being.

items.stem: A free translation tool replaces $9 million of paid translation services. Users report more completed translations and less effort; domestic firms produce $2 million of new paid implementation services. No other output changes. Which claim is supported?
options: Measured GDP falls $9 million; the implementation services do not count
Measured GDP rises because the number of translations rose
Measured GDP falls $7 million; the value of users’ net welfare gain is not determined
Measured GDP falls $7 million, proving welfare fell by $7 million
items.feedback: The measured output change is -9 + 2 = -7 million. Greater use and convenience can improve welfare despite reduced market spending, but the stated information does not price the total welfare change.

items.stem: Households begin paying $15 million for domestic childcare they formerly provided unpaid, with the same hours and quality of care. GDP rises by that fee. Which conclusion and limitation follow?
options: Measured market production falls; payment replaces household income rather than creating output
Measured market production rises; unchanged care services mean that rise alone does not establish a welfare gain
Measured market production rises; the full fee therefore measures an equal increase in welfare
Measured market production is unchanged; shifting an unpaid service into markets cannot affect GDP
items.feedback: Paid current childcare enters measured production; the same unpaid care was largely outside GDP. Marketization can raise GDP without an equal increase in services or welfare.

items.stem: A formerly paid domestic information service worth $19 million becomes freely available at the same quality. Its paid output disappears from measured GDP, with no replacement market sales. Which inference is supported?
options: Measured output rises by the former fees because zero price is recorded as additional consumption
Measured market output can fall while users retain the service; welfare need not fall with the measured amount
Measured output must be unchanged because useful free services always receive an imputed market price
Measured output falls, so users necessarily lose services worth exactly the former fees
items.feedback: The market transaction disappears, while usefulness need not. GDP and access to valuable services can diverge when a service becomes free.

items.stem: Households begin paying $20 million for domestic childcare they formerly provided unpaid, with the same hours and quality of care. GDP rises by that fee. Which conclusion and limitation follow?
options: Measured market production rises; unchanged care services mean that rise alone does not establish a welfare gain
Measured market production rises; the full fee therefore measures an equal increase in welfare
Measured market production is unchanged; shifting an unpaid service into markets cannot affect GDP
Measured market production falls; payment replaces household income rather than creating output
items.feedback: Paid current childcare enters measured production; the same unpaid care was largely outside GDP. Marketization can raise GDP without an equal increase in services or welfare.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: Refer to the graph. The economy starts at B with MD0 and MS0. Money demand changes to MD1. The central bank increases money supply to MS1, but wants to restore B’s original nominal interest rate. If the straight MD1 line continues as drawn, approximately how much additional money beyond MS1 is needed?
options: 25 units; a total money quantity of 125.
No additional money; C already restores the original rate.
75 units; a total money quantity of 175.
12.5 units; a total money quantity of 112.5.
items.feedback: B’s rate is 3. MD1 passes through A at (75,6) and C at (100,4), a fall of 2 rate points per 25 money units. A further 1-point fall requires 12.5 additional units, beyond MS1 at 100.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: The money market moves from e to d as money demand and supply both increase. What can be inferred about their competing effects on the interest rate?
options: The demand increase more than offsets the rate-reducing supply effect, so the rate rises.
The supply increase more than offsets the rate-raising demand effect, so the rate falls.
The effects offset exactly, so the rate stays at its original level.
The rate rises because increasing the money supply reinforces the upward pressure from demand.
items.feedback: e is at r 2 and d at the higher r 3. Increased demand pushes the rate up and increased supply pushes it down. The rise shown identifies a larger demand effect; it does not change the usual separate effects.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: Real income rises while the overall price level falls. With money supply fixed, what can be concluded about the equilibrium interest rate from liquidity-preference theory alone?
options: Higher income reduces money demand and lower prices reduce it; the unchanged supply yields a lower rate
Higher income raises money demand and lower prices reduce it; opposing directions ensure an unchanged rate
Higher income raises money demand and lower prices reduce it; their relative effects determine the rate change
Higher income raises money demand and lower prices raise it; the unchanged supply yields a higher rate
items.feedback: Higher real income increases transactions demand for money; a lower price level reduces the nominal money needed for those transactions. Money supply is fixed. The net demand shift, and therefore the equilibrium interest-rate direction, depends on the relative magnitudes of those opposing effects.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: Starting at e, money demand changes to MD2 and the central bank chooses MS2. Has that choice kept the interest rate at its original value? What adjustment would be needed if not?
options: No; d is below the original rate, so holding that rate requires less money than MS2 supplies.
Yes; increasing money supply always offsets any increase in money demand exactly.
No; d is above the original rate, so the central bank must reduce supply further to lower it.
No; d is above the original rate, so holding that rate requires more money than MS2 supplies.
items.feedback: The original rate is r 2 at e; d has r 3, above r 2. On MD2, the quantity demanded at r 2 exceeds Qm2, so a larger money supply would be required. The direction follows from the actual under-offset shown.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: Real income rises, shifting money demand right, yet the observed equilibrium interest rate falls. Which inference is most consistent with the liquidity-preference model?
options: Money demand could not have risen because income never affects transaction demand.
The central bank must have held money supply fixed because a fixed supply guarantees a lower rate.
Money supply must have increased enough to more than offset the upward interest-rate pressure from higher money demand.
Money supply must have fallen because lower supply always lowers interest rates.
items.feedback: If money demand rises but the equilibrium interest rate falls, money supply must have risen by enough to more than offset the upward interest-rate pressure from money demand.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: Transaction demand for money increases at every rate in an economy with money supply 60. The central bank wants to hold the interest rate fixed in the standard liquidity-preference model. Which response and curve distinction are correct?
options: Leave supply fixed because higher demand is only movement along the original curve
Shift money demand back by redefining the unchanged nominal supply as a demand curve
Raise money supply enough to meet the added demand at that rate; the demand curve still shifted
Reduce money supply to match the higher demand; the interest rate then stays fixed
items.feedback: At the old rate, higher money demand creates excess demand. Increasing supply to meet it can keep the rate unchanged; a fixed observed rate does not prove no demand shift.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: The interest rate stays fixed while both money demand and supply contract. A report describes unchanged monetary conditions because the rate did not move. Which observation challenges that conclusion?
options: The equilibrium quantity of money can fall even though opposing rate effects balance.
The equilibrium quantity must be unchanged whenever the observed interest rate is unchanged.
The money-supply contraction raises the equilibrium quantity while demand contraction lowers rates.
The money-demand contraction raises rates while the supply contraction lowers rates.
items.feedback: Inward supply and demand shifts exert opposing rate pressures. If they offset at the observed rate, the quantity can still fall; the unchanged price of liquidity does not establish an unchanged money-market allocation.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: At the interest rate marked by b, money supply is MS2 and demand is MD2. Compare the initial portfolio adjustment with a central-bank sale that reduces supply to MS1 before the rate changes.
options: Excess balances prompt bond purchases and downward rate pressure; the sale instead makes e the new equilibrium.
Excess balances prompt bond sales and upward rate pressure; the sale makes a the new equilibrium.
A shortage of balances prompts bond sales; reducing supply leaves d as the equilibrium.
Excess balances prompt bond purchases and downward rate pressure; the sale instead makes a the new equilibrium.
items.feedback: At b's r 4, desired balances on MD2 are Qm1 while supply is Qm2. Attempts to buy bonds with excess money push rates downward. Reducing supply to MS1 before that adjustment makes MD2 intersect it at a, not e on MD1.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: A commentator says the move from e to d proves that expanding money supply raises interest rates. How does the diagram bear on this claim?
options: The rate falls from r 3 to r 2, with the supply expansion's downward pressure exceeding the demand increase.
The rate rises from r 2 to r 3, confirming that supply expansion by itself pushes rates upward.
The rate stays at r 2 because simultaneous increases in supply and demand must offset exactly.
The rate rises from r 2 to r 3, but money demand also rises; its upward pressure exceeds the supply expansion's downward pressure.
items.feedback: The observed increase is from r 2 to r 3 with both curves shifting right. Holding demand fixed, more money supply lowers the rate. The joint outcome therefore cannot be attributed to that supply effect alone.

items.stem: At the start, real GDP per person is $32,000 in Alder and $8,000 in Birch. Their persistent growth rates are 1.75% and 7%. Using the Rule of 70, which comparison follows after 40 years?
options: After 40 years, Alder is near $64,000 and Birch near $128,000.
Both are near $64,000 because Birch began at one-quarter of Alder’s level
Alder is near $64,000 and Birch near $32,000; count only one doubling for Birch
Birch stays poorer because a lower starting level cannot be overcome
items.feedback: Approximate doubling times are 40 years for Alder and 10 for Birch. Over 40 years Alder doubles once to 64,000, while Birch doubles four times to 128,000. Reaching a rival’s initial level is distinct from catching a rival that also grows.

items.stem: Over a decade, real GDP rises 12%, population rises 5%, and total labor hours rise 20%. How do real GDP per person and output per hour change, to one decimal place?
options: Real GDP per person rises 6.7%; output per hour falls 6.7%
Both rise 12% because total real GDP rose
Real GDP per person rises 7%; output per hour falls exactly 8%
Real GDP per person falls 6.7%; output per hour rises 6.7%
items.feedback: Per-person output changes by 1.12/1.05 - 1 ≈ 6.7%; hourly output changes by 1.12/1.20 - 1 ≈ -6.7%. More total hours can raise average output even while productivity per hour falls.

items.stem: At comparable base prices, Cedar has nominal GDP $960 billion, deflator 120 and 32 million residents; Delta has $1,320 billion, deflator 150 and 44 million residents. Does the real-GDP-per-person comparison establish that every Cedar resident has a higher living standard than every Delta resident?
options: No. Cedar averages $25,000 and Delta $20,000; neither average describes every resident.
Yes. Once the average is deflated, it gives the real income of each individual resident.
No. Both averages are $30,000 because comparable base prices make deflation unnecessary.
Yes. Delta's larger nominal GDP necessarily means every Cedar resident is poorer regardless of population.
items.feedback: Real totals are 960/1.2=800 and 1320/1.5=880 billion. Dividing by populations gives $25,000 and $20,000 per person. Those are averages of measured production, not individual income observations or complete welfare measures.

items.stem: Real output per hour rises 10%, annual hours per employed person fall 5%, and the employed share of the population falls from 60% to 58%. Which conclusion about real GDP per person follows, assuming these cover all production?
options: It rises about 1.0%; the other two factors offset much of the productivity gain
It rises 10%; hourly productivity alone determines the exact change
It falls 7%; add the percentage and percentage-point declines
It rises 5%; the employed share does not enter output per person
items.feedback: Output per person equals output/hour × hours/worker × workers/person. Its factor is 1.10 × 0.95 × (58/60) ≈ 1.01017. Average output rises about 1.0%, much less than the hourly-productivity increase.

items.stem: Real GDP per person rises from $130 to $143, but gains accrue mainly to a small group. Which inference distinguishes an average from individual outcomes?
options: Every person's real income rises 10% because the average rises 10%
No real output grew because not everyone gained equally
Average real output falls if the largest gains go to high-income people
Average real output rises 10%; the typical person's gain requires distributional evidence
items.feedback: The aggregate per-capita ratio rises 10%, but that does not identify every person's income or the median. Distribution is additional evidence, not part of the arithmetic average.

items.stem: A country with initial real GDP per person $140 sustains 4% growth instead of 2%. Another policy raises the level once by 4% but leaves later growth at 2%. Which comparison recognizes the long-run distinction?
options: Sustained growth changes only the level; the level increase shortens subsequent doubling time.
Both shorten subsequent doubling time equally; each policy specifies the same 4% figure.
Sustained growth compounds faster; the level increase leaves subsequent doubling time unchanged.
Neither changes the future path; percentage changes affect nominal measures rather than output.
items.feedback: A growth-rate change repeatedly changes the path, whereas a one-time level gain shifts the starting point. Under Rule of 70, sustained 4% growth implies roughly 17.5-year doubling versus 35 at 2%.

items.stem: Country A starts at $48,000 real GDP per person and grows 2 percent annually. Country B starts at $24,000 and grows 4 percent. Using the Rule of 70, what is the strongest implication after about 35 years?
options: A remains twice as rich because starting income determines the permanent ranking.
B reaches only $48,000 because a 4 percent rate doubles once in 35 years.
A reaches $192,000 while B remains at $24,000.
Both are near $96,000 per person because A doubles once and B doubles twice.
items.feedback: At 2 percent A doubles in about 35 years. At 4 percent B doubles in about 17.5 years, so it doubles twice in roughly 35 years.

items.stem: Country A begins at $40110 real GDP per person and grows 2% annually; B begins at half that level and grows 7%. Using the Rule of 70, which warning corrects the claim that B catches A in ten years?
options: B doubles in ten years; A's starting level establishes catch-up then.
A doubles in ten years; B doubles in thirty-five, preventing catch-up.
B doubles in five years; doubling its growth rate halves catch-up time.
B doubles in ten years; A also grows, delaying catch-up.
items.feedback: 70/7≈10 years doubles B's starting level; 70/2≈35 years doubles A's. A is a moving target, so B reaching A's initial level is not the same as reaching A's contemporaneous level.

items.stem: Refer to the graph above. Treat the lines as straight. Starting at A, a technology change shifts D0 horizontally right while S0 stays fixed. The new equilibrium real rate is 10 percent, although the new demand curve is not drawn. What can be inferred about the shift and the quantity response?
options: Demand shifted right by 40 units; equilibrium investment rose by 40 through a rightward shift of S0
Demand shifted right by 80 units; equilibrium investment rose by 80 because saving must match the shift
Demand shifted right by 40 units; equilibrium investment rose by 80 through movement along D0
Demand shifted right by 80 units; equilibrium investment rose by 40 through movement along S0
items.feedback: On S0, a 10 percent rate corresponds to 180 units. Old D0 demands 100 units at that rate, so the new demand schedule must be 80 units to the right. Equilibrium investment rises from 140 to 180, or 40 units. The unchanged saving schedule accommodates that quantity through a rate-induced movement; an accounting identity does not force a shift in the supply of loanable funds.

items.stem: At a real interest rate below equilibrium, desired investment exceeds desired saving. A student claims this disproves S = I in a closed economy. Which response correctly separates the accounting statement from the market adjustment?
options: Realized saving exceeds realized investment until the rate rises; inventory changes are excluded from investment
Realized investment equals desired investment at every rate; the saving identity applies only after the rate adjusts
Realized saving includes the financing gap as foreign saving; the rate rises until that gap disappears
Realized investment, including unplanned inventories, equals realized saving; excess demand for funds puts upward pressure on the rate
items.feedback: S = I is an ex-post closed-economy accounting identity, including inventory investment. Planned quantities can disagree at a posted rate; that behavioral imbalance creates upward pressure on the real rate. Market clearing explains compatible plans, not the validity of the identity.

items.stem: Initially, desired investment is I = 300 − 10r, with I in billions of dollars and r measured in percentage points. Technology changes only the intercept. The real rate rises from 4 to 7 percent, and equilibrium investment rises by $20 billion. What happened to investment demand, and what would investment have been at the original rate after the technology change?
options: Demand shifted right by $20 billion; investment at 4 percent would be $280 billion
Demand shifted right by $50 billion; investment at 4 percent would be $310 billion
Demand shifted right by $30 billion; investment at 4 percent would be $290 billion
Demand shifted right by $50 billion; investment at 4 percent would be $280 billion
items.feedback: Initial investment is 300 − 10(4) = $260 billion, so the new equilibrium quantity is $280 billion. The 3-point rate increase reduces quantity demanded by $30 billion along the new schedule. Technology therefore raises demand by $50 billion at every rate, making investment $310 billion at 4 percent.

items.stem: Refer to the graph above. Each quantity unit represents $1 billion. The straight S0 and S1 curves capture a fiscal change, with the private-saving schedule unchanged and D0 fixed. Starting from B, a second policy raises planned private saving by $15 billion at every real rate. How much must public saving rise from its level at B to restore A?
options: $45 billion; together with the $15 billion private-saving increase, this restores a 60-unit supply shortfall.
$5 billion; adding the $15 billion private increase to the 20-unit equilibrium gap restores the original supply schedule.
$55 billion; the private-saving increase must be added to, rather than deducted from, the 40-unit shortfall.
$25 billion; together with the $15 billion private-saving increase, this restores the 40-unit supply shortfall.
items.feedback: At any given rate, S1 lies 40 units left of S0. Restoring S0 therefore requires $40 billion of additional planned national saving, not merely the 20-unit difference in equilibrium quantity. Private saving supplies $15 billion of that shift, leaving $25 billion of public saving. With D0 fixed, restoring S0 restores A.

items.stem: The graph shows the investment-demand response to new technology. Suppose a deficit also reduces the supply of loanable funds by an unknown amount. Which statement separates the plotted result from that added scenario?
options: The graph alone raises quantity from 80 to 140; with the added saving decline, the net quantity change from 80 is uncertain.
The graph alone raises quantity from 80 to 120; with the added saving decline, the net quantity change from 80 is uncertain.
The graph alone raises quantity from 80 to 120; the extra deficit leaves that final quantity unchanged because both shocks raise the rate.
The graph alone raises quantity from 80 to 120; the extra deficit must reduce quantity below 80 regardless of its size.
items.feedback: A/B give the demand-only quantity response 80 to 120 on fixed supply. A saving decline shifts supply left, adding upward rate pressure but opposing the demand-driven quantity increase. Its unknown size prevents determining the combined quantity relative to 80.

items.stem: Refer to the graph above. Each quantity unit represents $1 billion, and the straight-line shifts summarize all changes in saving and investment behavior. Public saving falls by $10 billion at every real rate, while technology raises investment demand. What private-saving shift is required to reconcile the graph with that fiscal change?
options: Private saving must rise $70 billion: together with public saving falling $10 billion, this gives a $60 billion supply increase.
Private saving must rise $50 billion: together with public saving falling $10 billion, this gives the plotted $40 billion supply increase.
Private saving must rise $30 billion: subtract the $10 billion public-saving loss from the plotted $40 billion increase.
Private saving must rise $10 billion: an unchanged equilibrium rate implies no national-saving change.
items.feedback: At 6 percent, S0 and D0 each have quantity 40, while S1 and D1 each have quantity 80. Each schedule shifts right by $40 billion. Since national saving combines private and public saving, the private shift must satisfy private change − 10 = 40, giving +$50 billion. The two shifts leave the depicted equilibrium rate at 6 percent.

items.topic: Long-Run Aggregate Supply and Potential Output
items.stem: For this capacity calculation only, potential output equals usable capital multiplied by output per unit of usable capital; other inputs are sufficient and unchanged. Usable capital falls by 5 percent while output per unit rises by 8 percent. A planner claims that any productivity gain above 5 percent would restore the original LRAS position. Which assessment is correct?
options: Potential output rises by 2.6 percent, but exactly restoring it would require a productivity gain of about 5.26 percent.
Potential output rises by 3 percent, and a 5 percent productivity gain would exactly restore it.
Potential output falls by 2.6 percent, and an 8 percent productivity gain cannot offset the capital loss.
Potential output is unchanged because the two percentage changes cancel exactly.
items.feedback: Capacity becomes 0.95 × 1.08 = 1.026 times its original value, a 2.6 percent increase and a rightward LRAS shift. The break-even productivity factor is 1/0.95, or a gain of approximately 5.26 percent. Percentages with different bases cannot simply be subtracted.

items.topic: Long-Run Aggregate Supply and Potential Output
items.stem: A permanent improvement in education raises worker productivity, but a new regulation raises current compliance costs. Which statement is most complete?
options: LRAS shifts right; opposing SRAS effects make its net shift uncertain
LRAS shifts left; both changes move SRAS to the left
LRAS is unchanged; both changes move SRAS to the right
LRAS shifts right; compliance costs necessarily outweigh productivity gains
items.feedback: Education raises capacity; compliance costs can reduce short-run supply.

items.topic: Long-Run Aggregate Supply and Potential Output
items.stem: Capital is destroyed while a new technology raises productivity. Which LRAS conclusion is valid?
options: Capital loss reduces capacity and technology raises it; net LRAS direction requires relative effects
Capital loss reduces capacity and technology raises it; opposite effects establish unchanged LRAS
Capital loss reduces capacity and technology affects only current costs; LRAS shifts left
Technology raises capacity and capital loss affects only current costs; LRAS shifts right
items.feedback: Lost capital and better technology push potential output in opposite directions.

items.stem: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS2, a lasting demand expansion moves AD to AD2. Wage adjustment then moves SRAS all the way to AS1. Only after this adjustment does a delayed fiscal contraction return AD to AD1. With wages slow to change again, why does this delayed action fail to restore the original equilibrium immediately?
options: It ends at Y3/P2; returning to Y1/P1 now requires wage and cost adjustment toward AS2.
It ends at Y2/P2; returning to Y1/P1 now requires wage and cost adjustment toward AS2.
It ends at Y3/P2; that is the new potential output because the earlier wage adjustment shifted LRAS.
It ends at Y1/P1; restoring the old demand curve is sufficient even though supply has changed.
items.feedback: The sequence is AD1-AS2 at Y1/P1, AD2-AS2 at Y2/P2, AD2-AS1 at Y1/P3, then AD1-AS1 at Y3/P2. After wages adjusted to the demand expansion, simply restoring old demand creates a new recessionary gap. Subsequent lower wage and expected-price pressures can return SRAS toward AS2.

items.stem: The economy starts at AD1-AS1. Officials choose between allowing wage adjustment to AS2 and expanding demand to AD2. What happens if the full demand expansion takes effect after wage adjustment has already reached AS2?
options: It reaches Y2/P2, above potential; a stimulus sized for the original gap is excessive after self-correction.
It reaches Y3/P3, above potential; a stimulus sized for the original gap is excessive after self-correction.
It reaches Y2/P2, the new potential; combining the policies permanently raises productive capacity.
It reaches Y1/P3; prior wage adjustment has no effect on the endpoint of a fixed demand expansion.
items.feedback: Either change alone can reach Y1 from the initial gap. Together AD2 and AS2 intersect at Y2/P2, above LRAS. The demand intervention should be reassessed after the supply adjustment.

items.stem: After a negative aggregate-demand shock, real output begins recovering toward potential even though policymakers make no fiscal or monetary change. Nominal wage growth has slowed and firms report easing unit labor costs. What is the strongest interpretation?
options: The evidence requires LRAS to have shifted left until it met current output, converting the recessionary gap into long-run equilibrium.
The recovery shows wage adjustment is irrelevant because only changes in aggregate demand can move real output back toward potential.
The evidence is consistent with self-correction through a rightward SRAS shift, not necessarily an active stabilization policy.
The recovery proves aggregate demand was shifted right by discretionary policy even though no fiscal or monetary action is observed.
items.feedback: Self-correction is the endogenous SRAS response to an output gap; stabilization policy is a separate deliberate intervention.

items.stem: An economy has a recessionary gap of 50. Wage adjustment is slow, and a stimulus would arrive only after forecasts predict recovery. Which evaluation recognizes both adjustment and policy timing?
options: Delayed stimulus remains beneficial at arrival solely because the initial diagnosis was valid.
Delayed stimulus can overshoot after recovery despite the valid initial diagnosis.
Forecast recovery invalidates the initial diagnosis and proves no output gap existed.
Slow wage adjustment rules out eventual recovery and makes arrival timing irrelevant.
items.feedback: A policy can be correctly motivated when chosen and poorly timed when implemented. Compare the arrival date with expected adjustment instead of treating a current gap as permanent.

items.stem: An economy is below potential, and falling wages begin to increase short-run aggregate supply. Before adjustment is complete, aggregate demand falls further. Without knowing the sizes of these changes, what can be predicted about output?
options: The wage adjustment supports recovery, but the additional demand loss makes the net output change uncertain.
Falling wages guarantee a return to potential before the demand decline can affect output.
The demand decline guarantees falling output even if the supply response is larger.
Both changes reduce potential output because both shift long-run aggregate supply.
items.feedback: Lower wage costs support output, while the new demand decline reduces it. Their relative sizes determine the net movement. Neither change by itself establishes a loss of productive capacity.

items.stem: Policy holds unemployment below natural with successive demand expansions. Expected inflation rises each round. The repeated expansions then stop and actual inflation stabilizes at its higher rate. Which subsequent path is consistent with the natural-rate model?
options: A sequence of upward-shifting SRPCs ending back at natural unemployment with higher inflation
One unchanged SRPC delivering permanently lower unemployment after every contract renewal
A leftward LRPC shift caused solely by faster inflation with unchanged labor structure
A downward SRPC shift ending in deflation and a lower natural unemployment rate
items.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate. Return to natural is conditional on ending the repeated effort to maintain a surprise.

items.stem: Unemployment is below the original natural rate during a demand boom. Later it stays low after expectations adjust, but matching institutions have improved. Which comparison prevents misattributing the persistent gain?
options: Infer permanently lower inflation; improved matching forces all nominal prices to fall.
A lower natural rate can sustain gains that surprise demand alone cannot.
Use the original natural rate forever; reforms cannot affect a long-run unemployment benchmark.
Credit demand alone; expectations adjustment preserves any original surprise unemployment gain.
items.feedback: If real labor-market structure changes, the natural benchmark can change. Persistence of lower unemployment then need not refute the expectations-adjusted Phillips model; the reform's effect must be separated from the temporary demand surprise.

items.stem: A labor-market reform lowers the natural rate while a demand expansion temporarily lowers unemployment even further. Which distinction is essential?
options: Demand shifts LRPC permanently while reform only changes the current inflation rate
Neither change can alter a Phillips curve once expectations are specified
The reform shifts LRPC; the demand expansion creates temporary movement relative to it
Both changes are movements along one unchanged SRPC despite different mechanisms
items.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

items.stem: Two economies finish disinflation with identical inflation and natural unemployment rates. Their records show different cumulative output losses. Is that combination inconsistent with a vertical LRPC?
options: No; identical long-run endpoints can be reached through different costly transition paths.
Yes; a vertical LRPC requires identical output losses at every point in both transitions.
No; different losses prove their final natural unemployment rates were actually different.
Yes; positive output losses imply that the long-run curve slopes downward.
items.feedback: LRPC describes the fully adjusted unemployment-inflation relation, not a unique transition path. Credibility, contracts and policy timing can produce different cumulative losses even when both economies reach the same endpoint.

items.stem: A project's next three stages have benefits of 14, 8 and 19 points and costs of 9, 12 and 10 points. Stages must occur in order. A manager would stop after stage one because stage two loses points. What is the best decision?
options: Complete all three; their total net benefit is 10 points
Stop after one; any negative increment rules out later stages
Complete only stage three; it has the largest net benefit
Complete two; positive total benefits justify the second stage
items.feedback: Feasible cumulative net benefits are 0, 5, 1 and 10. Stages two and three together add 5 points. The last stage cannot be taken alone.

items.stem: A firm spent $12 million on a prototype. Completing it costs $7 million. Selling the finished product yields $6 million, while selling the unfinished prototype now yields $1.5 million. How much better is the best current choice than completing it?
options: $4.5 million better by completing
$10.5 million better by selling now
$2.5 million better by selling now
$1 million better by selling now
items.feedback: Completion yields $6m - $7m = -$1m from now; selling now yields $1.5m. Selling is better by $2.5m. The $12m already spent is common and sunk.

items.stem: A producer earns a positive total profit. The next indivisible batch adds $320 in revenue and $350 in cost, but is required for a second batch adding $410 in revenue and $340 in cost. Which choice maximizes additional profit?
options: Produce both batches for a $40 gain
Produce neither because the first batch loses $30
Produce the second batch alone for a $70 gain
Produce the first alone to spread fixed cost
items.feedback: The feasible additions yield $0, -$30 and +$40. Although the first batch loses money, the required pair gains $40. The second batch is not independently feasible.

items.stem: A policy has already spent $2 billion. Continuing for one year costs $600 million and produces expected benefits of $520 million; ending it costs $30 million in transition expenses. Should the policy continue for another year or end now?
options: End the policy: ending costs $30 million, while continuing would cost $80 million more than it provides in benefits.
End because total cost since the program began exceeds total benefit
Continue so the $2 billion already spent is not wasted
Continue because the $520 million in benefits exceeds the $30 million transition cost.
items.feedback: The decision should compare future alternatives: continue loses $80 million; ending costs $30 million.

items.stem: A hospital evaluates all benefits and costs using the same points scale. One treatment provides 88 benefit points and has a 42-point supply cost. The staff could instead remain available for emergencies, an alternative valued at 35 points. A different treatment method reduces the supply cost by 8 points but also reduces the benefit by 12 points. Which treatment method provides the greater net benefit compared with keeping the staff available for emergencies?
options: The original treatment, with an 11-point net gain
The cheaper method, with a 15-point net gain
Neither, because readiness must be added to benefit
Both versions give the same gain because both save supplies
items.feedback: Original net gain is 88 - 42 - 35 = 11. The cheaper method gives 76 - 34 - 35 = 7. Both beat the alternative, but cost saving alone does not make the revised method better.

items.stem: A software team’s next round of development work has a 50% chance of creating $180,000 in value and costs $70,000. It also delays maintenance worth $25,000. What should it do?
options: Do not run it because expected benefit $90,000 is below relevant cost $95,000
Run it because possible benefit is $180,000
Run it because development cost alone is below expected benefit
Do not run it because uncertainty makes expected benefit zero
items.feedback: Expected benefit is $90,000; direct plus opportunity cost is $95,000.

items.stem: The next two maintenance zones add benefits of 18 and 13 points and operating costs of 10 and 11 points. Opening either requires a one-time setup cost of 9 points. Zones must be opened in order. Which option has the greatest net benefit?
options: Open both zones, gaining 1 point
Open neither, because the first zone alone loses 1 point
Open only the first, gaining 8 points
Open both, gaining 10 points
items.feedback: Including setup once, one zone gives 18 - 10 - 9 = -1; both give 31 - 21 - 9 = 1. The second zone covers the remaining setup loss and adds a net gain.

items.stem: Total benefit at five inspection stations is $900,000 and total cost is $610,000. At six they are $970,000 and $688,000. Station six also displaces a separate activity worth $9,000. How much added benefit would make station six break even?
items.feedback: Station six adds $70,000 in benefit and $78,000 in direct cost plus $9,000 forgone value. It is short by $17,000; the positive total surplus does not settle the incremental choice.

items.stem: Sequential grants have expected net benefits of $2.0m, $0.7m, -$0.4m and $0.6m. Each later grant requires all earlier grants. How many maximize total expected net benefit?
options: Four grants, yielding $2.9m
Two grants, yielding $2.7m
Three grants, yielding $2.3m
One grant, yielding $2.0m
items.feedback: Feasible totals for zero through four grants are 0, 2.0, 2.7, 2.3 and 2.9 million. Grants three and four jointly add $0.2m, so stopping at the first negative increment misses the best feasible package.

items.stem: A program's average benefit is 16 points per participant. The next participant adds 9 benefit points and 7 cost points; accommodating that participant also lowers benefits to existing participants by 3 points. What is the correct marginal decision?
options: Reject; the overall incremental net benefit is -1 point
Accept; 9 exceeds the direct cost of 7
Reject solely because 9 is below the average of 16
Accept; a positive average establishes a positive marginal gain
items.feedback: Count the 3-point loss to existing participants as an added consequence: 9 - 7 - 3 = -1. The existing average is not the relevant comparison.

items.stem: A plant's prepaid lease is unchanged. An extra order earns $760 and needs $490 in materials and $140 in overtime. It also occupies capacity that could earn $160 net on another order. What minimum price increase makes accepting it break even?
items.feedback: Relevant cost is $490 + $140 + $160 = $790, against $760 in revenue. Another $30 reaches break-even; the unchanged lease does not enter.

items.stem: A campaign has already spent $400,000. A final placement costs $60,000 and yields additional revenue of $100,000 if it succeeds, otherwise zero. With no other effects, which success probability makes the placement break even?
options: A probability above 100% because past spending must be recovered
items.feedback: Set expected incremental revenue equal to avoidable cost: p times $100,000 = $60,000, so p = 0.60. Past campaign expenditure is sunk.

items.stem: At 12 trips a route has total benefits of 840 points and costs of 610. At 13 trips these become 892 and 655. At 14 they become 930 and 699. With no later trips available, which expansion from 12 is best?
options: Add one trip; the two increments net +7 and -6 points
Add two trips because total benefit still exceeds total cost
Add neither because both trips raise total cost
Add two trips because 14 trips has the highest total benefit
items.feedback: Trip 13 adds 52 - 45 = 7 points. Trip 14 adds 38 - 44 = -6. Relative to 12 trips, the feasible gains are 0, 7 and 1; add only trip 13.

items.stem: A university pilot has spent $6 million. Extending it costs $900,000 and yields $1.1 million in expected benefit, while ending now requires $250,000 in transition cost. What is best?
options: Extend because its future net gain exceeds the cost of ending
End because total spending is already too high
Extend only to avoid wasting the $6 million
End because transition cost is less than extension cost
items.feedback: Extending gains $200,000, while ending loses $250,000.

items.stem: A city adds park lighting in blocks. Marginal benefits are 100, 82, 61, and 40; private costs are 55 each, but marginal light-pollution costs are 10, 18, 25, and 32. How many blocks should be lit?
options: Two blocks
One block
Three blocks
Four blocks
items.feedback: Social MC is 65, 73, 80, and 87; only the first two pass.

items.stem: An inspection costs $70,000 and prevents $500,000 in repairs if it finds a defect in time, otherwise saving nothing. It displaces work worth $20,000. What detection probability makes the inspection break even?
items.feedback: Expected benefit is p times $500,000. Direct plus opportunity cost is $90,000, so break-even requires p = 90,000 / 500,000 = 18%.

items.stem: A warehouse has packed 900 orders; that work is irreversible. The last 100 avoid $2,100 of penalties if completed tonight. Overtime costs $1,600 and displaces training worth $700. An outside packer can finish them for $1,900 without using warehouse staff. Which decision maximizes incremental value?
options: Use the outside packer: its $200 gain exceeds overtime’s $200 loss and leaving the orders unfinished.
Use overtime: its $500 gain exceeds the outside packer’s $200 gain because training is not a cash payment.
Leave them unfinished: both methods cost more than zero, and previous packing costs must be recovered first.
Use overtime: the 900 completed orders make finishing the final 100 worthwhile regardless of displaced training.
items.feedback: Relative to leaving the orders unfinished, overtime yields 2100-1600-700=-200; outsourcing yields 2100-1900=200. The prior 900 orders are sunk. The relevant choice compares complete incremental costs across feasible methods.

items.stem: A software firm has spent $2 million irreversibly. Updating costs $90,000 and adds $70,000 in revenue. Canceling avoids the update but triggers a $35,000 support-termination payment. Selling the unfinished code yields $15,000 and requires $10,000 of handover work, with no termination payment. Which option is best from today?
options: Sell: its $5,000 net receipt exceeds updating’s $20,000 loss and cancellation’s $35,000 loss.
Update: its $70,000 revenue exceeds the sale receipt, so the remaining $90,000 cost should be ignored.
Cancel: avoiding the $90,000 update cost is sufficient even though selling has a positive net receipt.
Update: the $2 million already spent makes the smallest additional cash outlay the relevant criterion.
items.feedback: Future net values are 70-90=-20 thousand for updating, -35 thousand for canceling and 15-10=5 thousand for selling. The historical $2 million is common to every alternative and cannot justify continuation.

items.stem: A transit line can add up to three buses in order. Their direct marginal benefits are $140k, $105k and $78k; each costs $100k. Adding any buses requires $30k of dispatch setup. Only a three-bus plan also enables transfers worth $60k. Which plan has the highest net benefit?
options: Three buses: net benefit is $53k, exceeding $15k for two and $10k for one.
Two buses: stop before the third because its direct $78k benefit is below its $100k cost.
One bus: its $40k direct surplus exceeds the second bus’s $5k direct surplus.
No buses: dispatch setup makes every positive-size plan have negative net benefit.
items.feedback: One bus nets 140-100-30=10. Two net 140+105-200-30=15. Three net 140+105+78+60-300-30=53. The third enables a complementary benefit, so its relevant incremental benefit is 78+60.

items.stem: A city can buy sensors sequentially. Direct MBs are 90, 72, 50 and 31; MCs are 40, 60, 55 and 48. A linked alert system worth 25 becomes feasible only with at least three sensors and costs no more. Which number maximizes total net benefit?
options: Three: totals are 50, 62, 82 and 65 for one through four sensors.
Two: the third direct MB is below MC, so any linked benefit must be excluded.
Four: four sensors have the largest total direct benefit regardless of incremental cost.
One: its individual net benefit is largest, so later positive gains should be ignored.
items.feedback: Cumulative direct net gains are 50, 62, 57 and 40. Add 25 for plans with at least three sensors: 82 and 65. Three is optimal because the third unlocks an additional benefit while the fourth does not.

items.stem: A project has spent $5 million irreversibly. Finishing costs $900,000 and yields $1 million. Canceling costs $180,000. Selling the project as-is brings $350,000 but requires $120,000 of transfer work and avoids cancellation fees. Which choice is best?
options: Sell: its $230,000 future net value exceeds finishing’s $100,000 and canceling’s -$180,000.
Finish: the $1 million receipt is the largest, and the sunk investment should be recovered before considering a sale.
Cancel: its $180,000 outlay is below finishing cost, so the sale receipt should not affect the comparison.
Finish: the relevant sale alternative is $350,000 minus the entire $5 million already spent.
items.feedback: Compare future net values: 1,000,000-900,000=100,000; -180,000; 350,000-120,000=230,000. Selling wins. The historical $5 million is unchanged by the decision.

items.stem: A hospital can add a mobile unit with expected benefits of $700,000 and direct costs of $520,000. Its team would abandon prevention work worth $210,000. Hiring temporary prevention staff costs $140,000 and preserves all that work; no other constraints change. Which plan maximizes incremental benefit?
options: Add the unit and hire temporary staff: net gain is $40,000, versus a $30,000 loss if prevention is displaced.
Do not add the unit: the $210,000 prevention value must be lost under every plan.
Add the unit without replacement: its $180,000 cash surplus establishes the largest social gain.
Add the unit and hire staff: net gain is $250,000 because preserved prevention is an extra benefit above the baseline.
items.feedback: Without replacement the incremental gain is 700-520-210=-30 thousand. With replacement it is 700-520-140=40 thousand; the preserved prevention service is already in the baseline, not an extra 210 gain.

items.stem: A manufacturer can hire a worker for one job that adds $1,400 in output. Wages are $980 and equipment costs $260 but can be resold for $100 after the job. The worker’s workstation could instead be rented out for $190 during the job. Which net contribution is relevant?
options: $70: subtract wages, net equipment cost and forgone workstation rent.
$260: subtract wages and net equipment cost but ignore the owned workstation.
$160: subtract wages and the full equipment purchase but ignore resale and rent.
-$30: subtract wages, the full equipment purchase and rent, ignoring resale.
items.feedback: Net equipment use costs 260-100=160. Relevant contribution is 1400-980-160-190=70. Ownership does not remove forgone rental income, and recoverable resale value reduces the equipment cost.

items.stem: A cleanup method yields $500 in health benefits, costs the operator $370 and damages habitat by $150. A gentler method gives the same health benefit, costs $430 and causes $20 of habitat damage. Which method is socially preferable, and what would an operator ignoring habitat costs choose?
options: Society prefers the gentler method ($50 net); the operator prefers the original ($130 private net versus $70).
Society prefers the original ($130 net); the operator prefers the gentler method because its habitat damage is lower.
Both prefer the original because its cash cost is lower and habitat losses are transfers between users.
Both reject cleanup because the original method’s $520 social cost proves every available method has negative net benefit.
items.feedback: Original social net benefit is 500-370-150=-20; gentler net benefit is 500-430-20=50. Ignoring habitat, private nets are 130 and 70, so private and social rankings differ.

items.stem: A preventable failure has a 25% probability and would cost $800,000. Prevention costs $170,000 and eliminates the loss. A perfect test costs $20,000 and permits prevention only when failure would otherwise occur. For a risk-neutral decision maker, which strategy has the lowest expected cost?
options: Test then prevent if needed: $62,500, versus $170,000 for unconditional prevention and $200,000 for no action.
Prevent unconditionally: $170,000, versus $220,000 for testing because testing cannot change the failure probability.
Take no action: $0, because a 25% possible loss is not a current cash outlay.
Test then prevent if needed: $190,000, because prevention must be paid even after a negative test.
items.feedback: No action costs 0.25×800000=200000 in expectation. Unconditional prevention costs 170000. Testing allows conditional prevention, costing 20000+0.25×170000=62500. Information has value because it changes action in the no-failure state.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. The market moves from D1/S1 to D2/S2. An analyst claims that simultaneous demand and supply increases must leave price unchanged. Then part of the supply increase is reversed: supply lies strictly between S1 and S2 at every shown price, while demand stays D2. Which assessment is correct?
options: The original offset is specific to the graph; afterward price is between P2 and P3 and quantity between Q2 and Q3.
The original offset is a general rule; afterward price stays P2 and quantity stays Q3.
The original offset is specific to the graph; afterward price is between P1 and P2 and quantity exceeds Q3.
The original offset is a general rule; afterward price reaches P3 and quantity falls below Q1.
items.feedback: Both initial increases raise quantity, but their opposing price effects need not cancel in general. They happen to cancel at P2 in this drawing. With D2 fixed, partially reversing S2 toward S1 places the new intersection between (P2,Q3) and (P3,Q2). Price rises above P2, and quantity falls from Q3 but remains above Q2 and the original Q1.

items.stem: A disease reduces berry supply while a nutrition trend raises berry demand. The final quantity is above its original level. Which conclusion follows with ordinary downward demand and upward supply?
options: Price is higher; the demand increase more than offsets the supply reduction’s effect on quantity.
Price is lower; greater final quantity proves that supply increased.
Price is unchanged; the higher quantity shows that the two shifts offset completely.
Price is higher; the observed quantity proves that the supply reduction dominated demand.
items.feedback: Both shifts raise price. Supply reduction alone lowers equilibrium quantity, so the observed quantity increase requires the demand effect to outweigh that reduction in the final outcome.

items.stem: Two initially identical device markets face the same increase in demand. Only Market Y also loses a component supplier. Compared with Market X’s final equilibrium, what must be true in Market Y?
options: Y has a higher price and lower quantity, although its quantity relative to the original equilibrium is uncertain.
Y has a lower price and higher quantity, although its quantity relative to the original equilibrium is uncertain.
Y has a higher price and quantity, because both changes increase demand.
Y has the same price and quantity, because both markets face the same demand change.
items.feedback: Starting from X’s final equilibrium, the additional supply reduction in Y raises price and lowers quantity. Compared with the common original equilibrium, Y’s demand increase and supply decrease have opposing quantity effects.

items.stem: Lunch-delivery demand falls while improved routing lowers delivery costs. Final price is lower and the number of deliveries is unchanged. Which explanation is consistent?
options: Demand fell and supply rose; their quantity effects offset at the final equilibrium.
Demand and supply both fell; their quantity effects offset at the final equilibrium.
Demand and supply both rose; unchanged deliveries reflect offsetting quantity effects.
Only demand fell; a fixed upward-sloping supply curve kept deliveries unchanged.
items.feedback: Lower demand and higher supply both reduce price but have opposite quantity effects. The observed unchanged quantity reflects an offset in this case; it is not a general prediction of those shifts.

items.stem: Bicycles are a normal good. Income and production-input costs rise, yet equilibrium bicycle sales fall. A manager concludes that bicycle demand must have fallen. Evaluate the conclusion.
options: Incorrect: demand rose, but the supply reduction more than offset its effect on quantity; price rose.
Correct: lower equilibrium sales establish a demand decrease even when income rises.
