Incorrect: supply rose, but demand fell enough to reduce both price and quantity.
Correct: higher input costs reduce bicycle demand directly while supply stays fixed.
items.feedback: Higher income increases demand for a normal good; higher input costs reduce supply. Both raise price. Lower sales can result when the supply effect dominates quantity, so sales alone do not identify a demand shift.

items.stem: A production improvement increases supply while tastes shift away from the product. An analyst predicts that price and quantity must both fall. What is the precise correction?
options: Price must fall, but quantity falls only if the demand reduction outweighs the supply increase’s quantity effect.
Quantity must fall, but price falls only if the production improvement outweighs the taste change.
Price must rise, but quantity can rise or fall depending on the relative shifts.
Neither direction can be inferred because simultaneous shifts make both variables indeterminate.
items.feedback: Both changes lower equilibrium price. Lower demand reduces quantity while higher supply increases it, so the analyst needs relative effects to assert a quantity decline.

items.stem: A coffee shop sees more customers after a celebrity endorsement. At the same time, wages for baristas rise. If the relative sizes of the two shifts are unknown, which equilibrium outcome can be predicted with certainty?
options: Price rises; quantity is ambiguous
Quantity rises; price is ambiguous
Both price and quantity fall
Price falls; quantity rises
items.feedback: Demand increases and supply decreases. Both raise price, but quantity depends on which shift is larger.

items.stem: A new production method makes shoes cheaper to produce. At the same time, a fashion shift makes shoes less popular. What is certain?
options: Price falls; quantity is ambiguous
Quantity falls; price is ambiguous
Both price and quantity rise
Price rises; quantity falls
items.feedback: Supply increases and demand decreases. Both lower price, but quantity is ambiguous.

items.stem: A hurricane disrupts production and reduces supply while households expect prices to rise tomorrow and rush to buy today. What is the strongest prediction for today’s market?
options: Price rises; quantity is ambiguous
Quantity rises; price is ambiguous
Both price and quantity fall
Price falls; quantity rises
items.feedback: Expected future price increases raise current demand, while the hurricane lowers supply. Price rises; quantity is ambiguous.

items.stem: Fewer buyers want a product and several producers exit. Final price is above the starting price. Which interpretation is consistent with both shifts and that observation?
options: Quantity falls; the supply reduction’s upward price effect outweighs the demand reduction’s downward effect.
Quantity rises; the demand reduction’s downward price effect outweighs the supply reduction’s upward effect.
Quantity stays fixed; an increase in price prevents either curve from shifting.
Quantity falls; the higher price proves that demand increased rather than decreased.
items.feedback: Both lower demand and lower supply reduce equilibrium quantity. Their price effects oppose each other; the observed price increase identifies the dominant price effect in this case.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. The market starts at D1/S1 and ends at D0/S0. Demand changes first while supply is initially fixed. Which sequence and explanation fit the graph?
options: First $4 and 200 thousand, then $3 and 150 thousand; demand falls before supply rises.
First $4 and 100 thousand, then $5 and 150 thousand; demand falls before supply falls.
First $3 and 150 thousand, then $4 and 100 thousand; supply rises before demand falls.
First $4 and 100 thousand, then $3 and 150 thousand; demand falls before supply rises.
items.feedback: The initial D1/S1 intersection is $5 and 150 thousand. Holding S1 fixed, lower demand takes the market to D0/S1 at $4 and 100 thousand. Higher supply then takes it to D0/S0 at $3 and 150 thousand.

items.stem: An analyst attributes the move from B back to A to cheaper streaming substitutes and lower theater operating costs. Which evaluation correctly connects these events to the changes shown in the movie-ticket graph?
options: Consistent: demand falls and supply rises; price falls $2 while quantity remains 200 thousand.
Consistent: demand and supply both fall; price falls $4 while quantity remains 200 thousand.
Consistent: demand falls and supply rises; price falls $4 while quantity remains 200 thousand.
Consistent: demand and supply both fall; price falls $2 while quantity remains 200 thousand.
items.feedback: Cheaper streaming substitutes reduce demand for theater tickets, while lower operating costs increase supply. B is at $14 and 200 thousand tickets; A is at $10 and 200 thousand. Both shifts lower price, producing the $4 fall. Their opposite effects on quantity offset in this graph.

items.stem: A widely reported health study increases consumers’ willingness to buy fresh berries. At the same time, frost destroys part of the berry crop. With ordinary downward-sloping demand and upward-sloping supply, and unknown effect sizes, which equilibrium conclusion is certain?
options: Quantity rises; price may rise or fall because the two changes push price in opposite directions.
Price falls; quantity may rise or fall because lower crop output reduces sellers’ willingness to sell.
Price rises; quantity may rise or fall because the two changes push quantity in opposite directions.
Quantity falls; price may rise or fall because stronger willingness to buy offsets the crop loss.
items.feedback: The health information shifts demand right; crop loss shifts supply left. Both raise price, but demand growth raises quantity while the supply contraction lowers it. Their relative sizes determine the quantity change.

items.stem: A market has Qd = 180 - 2P and Qs = 20 + 2P. At every price, demand then falls by 24 units and supply falls by 8 units. Which final change and explanation are correct?
options: Price rises $4 and quantity falls 16 units; demand’s larger reduction raises price.
Price falls $4 and quantity falls 16 units; demand’s larger horizontal reduction dominates the price effect.
Price falls $4 and quantity rises 16 units; both curve reductions expand sales.
Price is unchanged and quantity falls 32 units; the horizontal reductions simply add.
items.feedback: Initially 180 - 2P = 20 + 2P gives P = 40 and Q = 100. After the changes, 156 - 2P = 12 + 2P gives P = 36 and Q = 84. Stating horizontal units makes the comparison of shift sizes well defined.

items.stem: Unchanged linear schedules give Qd=900 and Qs=1,150 at $10, and Qd=1,100 and Qs=950 at $8. Sellers currently charge $10. An analyst calls the resulting surplus evidence of a supply shift and predicts it will persist even without a price control. Which correction is complete?
options: The surplus is 250 at $10; price must rise to $11.25 and quantity 1,025, while a $10 ceiling would preserve the gap.
The surplus is 250 at $10; price can fall to $8.75 and quantity 1,025 along unchanged curves, while a $10 floor would preserve the gap.
The shortage is 250 at $10; price can fall to $8.75 and quantity 1,025 only if supply shifts left.
The surplus is 150 at $10; price can fall to $8 and quantity 950, while unchanged curves prevent further adjustment.
items.feedback: The schedules imply Qd=1900-100P and Qs=150+100P. Equating them gives P=8.75 and Q=1025. At 10, excess supply is 250. Price adjustment moves along existing curves; a binding floor at 10 could block the fall and sustain surplus.

items.stem: Vaccination creates an external benefit, but a fixed number of appointments is already fully used. A subsidy is introduced without expanding capacity or changing how appointments are allocated. Which assessment best separates the externality diagnosis from this policy’s current effect?
options: Private demand rises, but vaccinations cannot rise yet; additional spillover benefits require more capacity or a better allocation.
The subsidy necessarily raises vaccinations to the efficient quantity despite the fixed appointment limit.
Fixed capacity means the external benefit disappears and the original externality diagnosis is false.
Subsidy spending itself equals new transmission benefits even when the vaccinated group is unchanged.
items.feedback: The external benefit can justify stronger private incentives, but supply is constrained here. With both quantity and recipients fixed, subsidizing existing appointments changes payments rather than the transmission benefit. Capacity and allocation matter for the feasible remedy.

items.stem: A fishery is open to many boats, and each boat ignores how its catch reduces future stocks for others. Which policy logic fits?
options: Subsidize every additional catch.
Limit or price access so users face more of the depletion cost.
Remove all information about stocks.
Set a price ceiling on fish without limiting harvest.
items.feedback: Access rules, quotas, or charges can internalize the shared depletion cost.

items.stem: A broadband network has high fixed cost and low marginal cost. Marginal-cost pricing would expand valuable access but leave a financing deficit. Average-cost pricing can cover costs but excludes some users whose value exceeds marginal cost. Public support has a real collection cost. What information is needed to choose between the two rules?
options: Only whether marginal-cost pricing creates an accounting loss, because loss proves social inefficiency.
Only whether average-cost pricing breaks even, because break-even proves maximum social surplus.
The extra access benefits net of resource cost, compared with the real cost of financing the deficit.
Only the subsidy payment, because every transferred dollar is a destroyed social resource.
items.feedback: The financing problem and the access distortion are distinct. Compare additional gains from valuable access with financing’s real costs under feasible support arrangements. Accounting losses and transfer amounts do not alone rank the rules.

items.stem: A festival can run late, end early, or run late with sound insulation. Relative to ending early, running late adds $1,000 of gains to attendees and organizers and $1,400 of resident harm. Insulation costs $600 and reduces that harm to $200. Ignore bargaining costs. Which arrangement maximizes net gains, and what remains to be negotiated?
options: End early; all late operation has negative social value even with insulation.
Run late without insulation; the $1,000 private gain establishes efficiency.
Run late with insulation; divide its $200 net gain through compensation.
Run late with insulation; resident compensation itself adds another $200 of social benefit.
items.feedback: Late without insulation yields 1000 - 1400 = -$400. Late with insulation yields 1000 - 600 - 200 = $200 relative to ending early. Compensation can distribute gains but is not an additional resource benefit.

items.stem: An exclusive right lets an innovator charge above marginal cost. Removing it would expand current access but could reduce future investment in similar products. Which evidence is needed before claiming removal raises welfare?
options: Only the current markup, because all markups equal net profit and total social loss.
Only the innovator’s revenue, because consumer gains are transfers that cannot affect welfare.
Only the number of new buyers, because future incentives are unrelated to exclusive rights.
Gains from additional current trades and the size of any resulting loss of valuable future innovation.
items.feedback: Market power can exclude mutually beneficial current purchases, while expected returns can affect investment. A welfare comparison needs both margins and cannot be settled by the markup or seller revenue alone. This asks about incentives, not a legal test.

items.stem: A health agency observes that a vaccine subsidy increases vaccinations but an unrelated change also reduces exposure to infection. Which additional evidence is needed to judge whether the subsidy improves efficiency?
options: Only the subsidy budget, because larger transfers imply larger social gains.
The marginal spillover benefit at the new quantity, the real cost of extra doses, and policy implementation costs.
Only the number of new doses, because each added dose must be efficient.
Only recipients’ private willingness to pay, because the outside benefit is already in every purchase.
items.feedback: A quantity increase is consistent with correcting underconsumption but does not prove optimal scale. Changed exposure can alter marginal external benefits. Evaluate incremental social benefits and real resource/implementation costs; the payment budget alone is not welfare.

items.stem: Use the graph. A $2 rider subsidy implements the socially efficient quantity at a real administration cost of $12 thousand per day. A private agreement achieves the same quantity but costs $18 thousand to arrange and enforce. Ignore financing distortions. Compared with the private outcome shown in the graph, what is the net gain from each approach, and why do those gains differ?
options: $28 thousand for the subsidy and $22 thousand for bargaining; real implementation costs determine this ranking.
$38 thousand for the subsidy and $32 thousand for bargaining; subsidy payments themselves create additional resource benefits.
$28 thousand for the subsidy and $22 thousand for bargaining; subsidy payments themselves create additional resource benefits.
$38 thousand for the subsidy and $32 thousand for bargaining; real implementation costs determine this ranking.
items.feedback: Expansion from 150 to 200 thousand rides closes a $2 marginal gap, giving gross gains 0.5 × 50 × 2 = $50 thousand. Subtracting the respective real costs gives $38 thousand and $32 thousand. Transfers are not resource gains, and this ranking depends on the stated costs.

items.stem: Refer to the imperfect-correction graph. The city raises the vaping tax from $2 to the full $4 correction. Ignoring administration and financing costs, what additional welfare gain is obtained, and how does tax revenue change?
options: Welfare rises $20 thousand; revenue rises $240 thousand.
Welfare rises $240 thousand; revenue rises $20 thousand.
Welfare rises $80 thousand; revenue rises $320 thousand.
Welfare rises $40 thousand; revenue falls $240 thousand.
items.feedback: At $2, quantity is 160 thousand and residual loss is 0.5 x (160 - 140) x 2 = $20 thousand. Full correction removes it. Revenue changes from 2 x 160 = $320 thousand to 4 x 140 = $560 thousand, an increase of $240 thousand.

items.stem: Two pollution-permit systems impose the same cap, meaning the same total limit on emissions. One gives firms equal numbers of permits; the other auctions them. Permits can be traded in both systems. Which comparison separates the cost of cutting emissions from who receives the permits’ value?
options: Trading changes the emissions limit; the initial allocation leaves permit income unchanged.
Trading can lower cleanup costs in both; giving away or auctioning permits distributes their value differently.
Auctioning alone guarantees lower cleanup costs; trading cannot affect those costs.
Equal permit allocations guarantee equal cleanup costs; auctioning makes permit revenue disappear.
items.feedback: With the same cap and functioning permit trading, firms can trade toward the least-cost allocation of emissions reductions. Giving permits away transfers their value to recipients; auctioning them raises revenue for the seller. Those distributional effects differ from the cost of achieving the cap.

items.stem: Plants would emit 500 tons without abatement. A binding cap is reduced to 420 tons. The first 50 tons can be abated for $10 each; the next 50 for $30 each, with no other abatement or trading costs. What allocation and total cost meet the new cap most cheaply?
options: Abate 80 low-cost tons for $800, even though only 50 are available.
Abate 40 tons in each cost group for $1,600.
Abate 420 tons because the new cap is the required reduction.
Abate all 50 low-cost tons and 30 higher-cost tons, for $1,400.
items.feedback: Required abatement is 500 - 420 = 80 tons. Exhaust the 50 tons at $10, then use 30 at $30: 500 + 900 = $1,400. The cap limits remaining emissions, while trading can allocate reductions to the cheaper opportunities.

items.stem: A landlord can insulate a noisy building for $700. The improvement raises the present value of rents by $500 and gives neighboring properties $400 of additional benefits. There are no other effects. Neighbors could organize a payment at a real cost of $250. Which diagnosis is correct?
options: The landlord installs without a payment because all $900 of benefits become its rent.
The proposed bargain creates $200 of net gains because coordination costs are transfers.
Insulation is socially wasteful because benefits outside the building do not count.
Insulation yields a $200 social gain before coordination; the $250 coordination cost makes the bargain unprofitable.
items.feedback: Total benefit is 500 + 400 = $900, above the $700 cost by $200. The landlord captures only $500. Coordinating neighbors consumes $250, more than the available $200 joint gain, so that arrangement does not close the incentive gap profitably.

items.stem: A polluter has the right to continue operating. Option A prevents $900 of damage, costs $500 to install and $100 to contract. Option B prevents $1,200 of damage, costs $650 to install and $300 to contract. Victims pay all contract costs; transfers have no resource cost. Which option offers the larger bargaining surplus, and what payment interval supports it?
options: Option B: more than $650 but less than $900, because it prevents more damage.
Option A: more than $500 but less than $800 paid to the polluter.
Option A: more than $500 but less than $900, because contracting uses no resources.
Option B: exactly $1,200, because all avoided damage must become compensation.
items.feedback: A yields 900 - 500 - 100 = $300; B yields 1200 - 650 - 300 = $250. Under A, a payment above $500 covers the polluter’s cost, while one below $800 leaves victims better off after their $100 contracting cost.

items.stem: Noise reduction costs $700 and benefits neighbors $1,000. Agreement costs $400. Is bargaining worthwhile?
options: Yes; every external benefit guarantees bargaining
Yes; net gain is $700
No; initial rights prevent efficiency
No; the $300 gross gain is below the $400 transaction cost
items.feedback: Gross gain is $300, below transaction cost. The action creates only $300 of gross joint surplus, so spending $400 to reach and enforce an agreement would make the bargain inefficient.

items.stem: Preventing a spillover avoids $2 million of harm and uses $1.2 million of resources. A bargain adds $1 million in real transaction costs. An enforceable regulation can achieve the same prevention with $0.3 million of administration and compliance costs beyond prevention. With no other effects, which ranking follows?
options: The bargain gains $0.8 million and ranks first because transfers are voluntary.
No prevention ranks first because failed bargaining proves prevention is inefficient.
Regulation loses $0.7 million because avoided harm should be excluded from policy evaluation.
Regulation gains $0.5 million; no prevention ranks next; the bargain loses $0.2 million.
items.feedback: Gross prevention gains are 2 - 1.2 = $0.8 million. Net gains are 0.8 - 1 = -$0.2 million for this bargain and 0.8 - 0.3 = $0.5 million for regulation. Bargaining failure does not establish that every feasible remedy fails.

items.stem: A town hires private contractors to provide three services. Each packed meal can be consumed only once, so the town proposes charging per meal. Its archive requires a login and is not crowded; the town proposes opening access after a sponsor covers the full cost. Anyone can receive its warning broadcast without reducing others’ ability to listen; the town proposes a binding community agreement to fund it. Which statement correctly explains these funding choices?
options: Private contractors make all three goods rival, so each additional user must be rationed through an individual charge.
Opening the archive turns it into a depleted common resource, while collecting warning contributions makes warning reception excludable.
Meals still require allocation among rival users; sponsorship can finance open nonrival access; the agreement can address warning-service free riding.
Meal fees solve the warning’s free-rider problem automatically, so the community agreement cannot change provision.
items.feedback: Meal consumption uses up a rival unit. Archive exclusion can change without creating rivalry, and sponsorship can replace login revenue. The warning remains nonexcludable, but a binding funding agreement can coordinate contributions. Consumption characteristics and financing institutions must be evaluated separately.

items.stem: A digital hazard map is initially open, nonrival and free to copy. Verified accounts can enforce a paywall at a real cost. A paywall would finance updates but exclude some users whose benefit exceeds the near-zero cost of serving them. Which evaluation is complete?
options: Adopt the paywall whenever revenue increases, because all lost access represents wasted consumption.
Reject account verification because nonrival information cannot be made excludable.
Treat account enforcement as a change in rivalry rather than a change in feasible exclusion.
Compare the benefit of financed updates with exclusion losses and enforcement costs; better revenue does not alone prove higher welfare.
items.feedback: Technology can make a nonrival service excludable and improve revenue capture. That can support useful updates while also blocking valuable low-cost access and consuming enforcement resources. Net welfare depends on all three effects.

items.stem: A nonexcludable siren project is worth $300 to each of five households and costs $1,000. One household cannot finance it alone. A binding agreement would collect $200 from each household only if all five sign, with no contracting costs. Which comparison follows?
options: The project is inefficient because no single household values it at its full $1,000 cost.
Uncoordinated funding can fail despite $500 of total gains; the conditional agreement can make every household $100 better off.
The agreement makes the siren rival because every household now pays a fee.
The agreement creates $1,000 of new social benefit solely by collecting contributions.
items.feedback: Total value is 5 x 300 = $1,500, leaving $500 after resource cost. Each household gains 300 - 200 = $100 under the binding agreement. It coordinates contributions without changing the warning’s rivalry or excludability.

items.stem: A nonrival safety bulletin yields $1,500 of total user benefit when open and costs $900 to produce. Donations provide $500. A sponsor would pay $1,000 to keep it open; alternatively, a paywall yields $1,100 of receipts, retains $1,200 of user benefit and costs $100 to enforce. Treat payments as transfers and assume no other effects. Which financing plan is viable and gives larger net social benefit?
options: The paywall: its $1,100 receipts prove greater welfare than the sponsor’s $1,000 payment.
Donations: $1,500 of benefit means the producer can cover costs with $500 of receipts.
Sponsorship: it covers production and preserves $600 of net social benefit, versus $200 under the paywall.
Both paid plans yield identical welfare because information remains nonrival.
items.feedback: Sponsorship receipts cover $900 of cost and leave net social benefit 1500 - 900 = $600. Paywall receipts cover production plus enforcement, but net social benefit is 1200 - 900 - 100 = $200. Revenue feasibility and welfare are separate comparisons.

items.stem: A village’s open fishery is depleted while its nonexcludable flood-warning system receives too few contributions. Leaders propose a catch fee and a collective warning-service fund. Why do these two services need different funding or pricing policies?
options: Both remedies should discourage consumption because fish and warnings are depleted by each user.
The fee discourages rival extraction that harms other users; the fund coordinates payment for a shared nonrival benefit.
Both remedies should subsidize individual use because nonexcludability always causes too little consumption.
The fishery needs only voluntary donations, while the warning requires a catch-style quantity quota.
items.feedback: The fishery combines difficult exclusion with rival use, encouraging excessive extraction. The warning is nonrival and nonexcludable, encouraging underpayment and underprovision. Similar access problems need different incentives because rivalry differs.

items.stem: A platform has market power and users create privacy spillovers. What is the best diagnosis?
options: Separate the output distortion from third-party privacy costs
A high price by itself establishes market failure
The outcome is disliked but no incentive wedge is identified
Inequality alone proves productive inefficiency
items.feedback: Market failure requires a specific reason private incentives diverge from efficient social outcomes.

items.stem: A nonrival, nonexcludable water-quality alert system would generate $12,000 in total benefits and cost $8,000 to operate. Individual fee collection would cost $5,000; a binding cooperative funding agreement would cost $1,000. Both could fund the same service. Which evaluation is correct if there are no other effects?
options: Individual collection creates $4,000 of net gains because collection uses no resources.
The cooperative creates $3,000 of net gains; individual collection costs exceed the $4,000 operating surplus.
Both methods create $12,000 of net gains because users benefit whether or not they pay.
Neither can work because a private agreement cannot finance a nonexcludable service.
items.feedback: Before funding costs the gain is 12,000 - 8,000 = $4,000. Net gains are -$1,000 with individual collection and $3,000 with the agreement. Nonexcludability complicates funding but does not rule out every institution.

items.stem: A disclosure rule is forecast to prevent $90 of harm at $20 resource cost. A pilot finds that confusion causes $35 of additional harm and that only $50 of the original harm is actually prevented. A simpler label prevents $40 at $10 cost with no added confusion. Which comparison uses the observed performance?
options: The original rule has +$70 net benefit because forecasts should replace contradictory pilot evidence.
The original rule has +$30 net benefit because confusion is only a transfer, making it equivalent to the simpler label.
The original rule has net benefit −$5, while the simpler label has +$30; revise the policy despite its initially plausible mechanism.
Neither can be compared because any information rule guarantees an efficient outcome.
items.feedback: Use the pilot’s actual effects: 50−35−20=−5. The alternative yields 40−10=30. The intended mechanism is relevant, but implementation evidence determines the net result.

items.stem: A fishery’s paper quota is strict, but hidden catches make actual harvest high. A feasible alternative combines verified landing reports with transferable catch rights. What evidence would establish that this alternative improves net social benefit?
options: The new quota is numerically smaller, regardless of hidden catches or enforcement costs.
Quota holders receive valuable rights, so their transfer income equals the total welfare gain.
Trading occurs frequently, so actual harvest must equal the legally allowed total.
Reduced depletion losses exceed added monitoring and adjustment costs, while transfers permit lower-cost compliance.
items.feedback: Evaluate actual behavior, not just the announced cap. Verification can reduce hidden harvest; transfers can lower compliance costs. Net improvement requires avoided resource losses to exceed real implementation and adjustment costs.

items.stem: A market maximizes measured total surplus but distributes it unequally; no externality, information gap, market power or public-good problem is identified. Policy A transfers $30 between participants without resource cost or changed behavior. Policy B makes the same transfer but destroys $8 of gains through changed allocation. Which assessment is correct?
options: Inequality motivates a separate equity judgment; A preserves measured surplus while B trades $8 of it for the same intended redistribution.
Both policies correct a demonstrated efficiency failure because any unequal outcome is inefficient.
B must be more efficient because changing allocation proves it addresses a market failure.
A raises total surplus by $30 while B raises it by $22 because transfers are new resources.
items.feedback: An unequal split does not by itself demonstrate a missing efficiency condition. The costless transfer changes distribution; B additionally sacrifices $8 of gains. Whether that tradeoff is acceptable requires an equity judgment.

items.stem: Refer to the sirens graph, treating provision as continuous. A proposal installs 60 rather than the quantity that maximizes net social benefit. What excess provision and loss follow, and can positive total benefits alone justify the proposal?
options: 20 excess sirens and $400,000 of lost net benefit; every dollar spent on them is a net loss.
20 excess sirens and $100,000 of lost net benefit; positive total benefits do not establish that the extra sirens are worthwhile.
40 excess sirens and $200,000 of lost net benefit; the marginal-cost value is the target quantity.
No excess provision; any quantity with positive MSB maximizes net social benefit.
items.feedback: MSB = MC at 40. From 40 to 60, the gap MC - MSB rises from 0 to $10,000 per siren. The excess-loss triangle is 0.5 x 20 x 10,000 = $100,000. Extra sirens may have positive benefit while costing even more.

items.stem: Refer to the fireworks graph and treat displays as continuous. Suppose a proposal uses only North’s willingness to pay to decide provision. What quantity and welfare loss result compared with using both neighborhoods’ benefits, ignoring funding costs?
options: Four displays and no welfare loss, because the larger neighborhood represents everyone.
Zero displays and $200,000 of forgone net benefits, equal to the full cost of four displays.
Eight displays and $20,000 of forgone benefits, because neighborhood quantities should be added.
Zero displays and $80,000 of forgone net benefits.
items.feedback: North MB equals MC only at Q = 0 and is below MC for positive quantities. Summed MSB starts $40,000 above MC and meets MC at Q = 4. Omitting all four displays loses the triangle 0.5 x 4 x 40,000 = $80,000.

items.stem: Household purchases fall after an economy-wide income decline. A chain then closes stores, causing further household income losses. Which research plan covers the stated feedback?
options: Link household and firm responses to aggregate income and spending changes
Classify each store closure as macro solely because the chain is nationwide
Study aggregate income alone and infer every household responds equally
Study store choices alone and treat national income as unaffected
items.feedback: The mechanism crosses levels: aggregate income affects individual choices, and firm choices feed back into aggregate income. Neither level alone covers the full sequence.

items.stem: Wages rise at every sampled technology firm. The sample excludes shrinking industries and tracks only workers who kept jobs. What is needed before inferring an economy-wide wage change?
options: Confirmation that each sampled firm operates nationally
The largest observed wage increase as an aggregate estimate
Representative coverage and treatment of changes in which workers are observed
A larger sample of the same surviving technology workers
items.feedback: Both industry selection and changing worker composition can distort aggregation. More observations from the same selected group do not repair those omissions.

items.stem: A restaurant chain loses customers to other restaurants and cuts jobs. A report calls this evidence of a national downturn. Which finding would most directly undermine that inference?
options: The chain closes outlets in several regions
The chain's managers report lower profits
Some customers reduce visits to that chain
Other restaurants absorb the spending and workers, leaving national totals unchanged
items.feedback: A shift among firms can produce substantial micro effects without changing economy-wide totals. The relevant test is whether activity was lost nationally or reallocated.

items.stem: A researcher measures how a nationwide credential rule changes nurses' job choices. A colleague says nationwide rules can only be macro topics. Which extension actually changes the level of the question?
options: Estimate how the rule changes total employment across all occupations
Include nurses from more hospitals in the same choice study
Compare nurse responses in public and private hospitals
Increase the sample to include every licensed nurse
items.feedback: National reach does not make an occupational choice question macro. The extension asks about economy-wide employment, including effects beyond the occupation.

items.stem: An equipment rebate shifts purchases toward one technology. A report totals emissions from that technology and labels the study macro because the estimate is national. What is the best correction?
options: A subsidy question is micro even when it studies aggregate output
National sector totals alone do not establish a macro question; examine economy-wide outcomes to make that link
Environmental questions are macro regardless of the unit studied
A national total rules out any microeconomic interpretation
items.feedback: Geographic reach and environmental relevance do not define macroeconomics. A sector study can be micro; a separate economy-wide output or employment question would establish the macro link.

items.stem: One bank raises loan rates and loses borrowers to rivals. At the same time, national lending declines. What separates a micro finding from an unsupported macro explanation?
options: Rivals gaining customers refutes the reported national decline
The bank's large size makes its pricing decision purely macro
Borrower switching explains the bank's share; economy-wide evidence is needed to explain the total decline
The bank's lost borrowers necessarily equal the national lending decline
items.feedback: Market-share shifts concern individual institutions. Explaining the aggregate decline requires counting lending across banks and identifying broader mechanisms.

items.stem: Workers relocate from rural districts to a city. City rents and employment rise. Which claim needs additional economy-wide evidence?
options: National employment rose rather than being redistributed across locations
The city's housing market experienced a local change
The move changed some households' location choices
Employers in the city gained access to more workers
items.feedback: Local gains can reflect transfers from other locations. National employment must account for origin districts and other responses; city outcomes alone cannot settle it.

items.stem: An industry's average wage rises after its lowest-paid jobs disappear, although every continuing worker's wage stays fixed. What should an analyst conclude before generalizing nationally?
options: Unchanged individual wages prove the reported industry average cannot rise
Composition changed the industry average; neither individual raises nor national wage growth follows
The higher average proves continuing workers received raises
An industry average is automatically the national average when many workers are sampled
items.feedback: Removing low-paid jobs changes the mix being averaged. Distinguish composition from individual wage changes, then assess representative national evidence.

items.stem: A national staffing rule raises hospital employment 20% in cities containing three-quarters of the country’s initial hospital jobs and lowers it 10% in the remaining cities. Other employment is not measured. Which analysis correctly connects micro evidence and the aggregate claim?
options: Hospital jobs rise 12.5% overall; the city responses are micro evidence, but total national employment cannot be inferred without other sectors.
Hospital jobs rise 5% overall; averaging the two city growth rates establishes the change in total national employment.
Hospital jobs rise 20% overall; the majority-city response is the macro result and the smaller group can be ignored.
Hospital jobs rise 12.5% overall; that sectoral percentage must also be the percentage change in economy-wide employment.
items.feedback: Weight by initial hospital jobs: 0.75×20%+0.25×(-10%)=12.5%. Aggregation of one sector does not establish the effect on total employment; other sectors and reallocation matter.

items.stem: A fuel tax raises one fuel price by 10%. Fuel has a 5% fixed weight in a national consumer-price index; all other prices are unchanged for this exercise. A household spends 20% of its budget on that fuel. Which statement correctly links the levels of analysis?
options: The index and household basket both rise 10%; a nationwide tax makes each individual effect identical to the macro effect.
The index rises 0.5%, while that household’s fixed-basket cost rises 2%; the fuel-market, household and aggregate questions are linked but distinct.
The index rises 2%, while the household basket rises 0.5%; national aggregation uses each household’s own expenditure weight.
The index cannot change because the tax affects one product; only a tax on every product can have a macroeconomic effect.
items.feedback: Under the fixed-basket assumptions, national impact is 0.05×10%=0.5%, and household impact is 0.20×10%=2%. A micro market shock can contribute to an aggregate price measure without having the same effect on each household.

items.stem: A wealthy region accounts for 25% of initial national real consumption. Its consumption rises 12%, while the rest of the country falls 4%. A large survey covers only the wealthy region. Which conclusion is warranted?
options: National real consumption rises 12%; a large sample makes the observed region representative by itself.
National real consumption rises 4%; equally averaging the two regional rates gives the national result.
National real consumption is unchanged; survey size does not fix its unrepresentative coverage.
National real consumption falls 4%; the larger population outside the region makes the wealthy-region change irrelevant.
items.feedback: Weight by initial consumption: 0.25×12%+0.75×(-4%)=0%. A precise estimate for one region is not a representative national estimate. Large sample size reduces sampling noise within coverage, not coverage bias.

items.stem: After a national policy-rate cut, banks serving 60% of initial business lending lower loan rates and lending there rises 10%. Capital-constrained banks serving the rest do not change lending. A commentator predicts every firm invests 10% more. Which correction is strongest?
options: Measured aggregate lending rises 10%; a national rate cut ensures all firms face the same financing change.
Measured aggregate lending rises 5%; equal bank-group averaging identifies both national lending and each firm’s investment.
Measured aggregate lending is unchanged; unchanged lending at constrained banks cancels growth at unconstrained banks.
Measured aggregate lending rises 6%; heterogeneous bank constraints matter, and lending growth alone does not identify every firm’s investment response.
items.feedback: Weighted lending growth is 0.60×10%+0.40×0%=6%. The macro policy transmits through heterogeneous micro constraints; borrowing changes also need not translate one-for-one into each firm’s investment.

items.stem: A model omitting banks explains routine household-firm payments well. It misses a collapse in purchases when lending stops. Which revision preserves its useful result while addressing the failure?
options: Retain the payment framework and add a credit constraint for the disrupted setting
Use the old fit to treat lending as irrelevant during the disruption
Add banks and treat the expanded model as valid for every question
Discard the payment relationships because an omitted institution mattered once
items.feedback: The original abstraction can explain routine flows. When credit becomes a binding constraint, the application needs that mechanism; adding it does not establish universal validity.

items.stem: A repair-shop model omits imported parts because local labor usually determines completion time. During a parts embargo it overpredicts repairs, but performs well again after deliveries resume. What does this pattern support?
options: Labor had no explanatory role because the embargo forecast failed
Resumed accuracy proves the embargo observations were measurement errors
Adding parts availability would make all remaining assumptions unnecessary
The omission is useful conditionally; parts availability matters when it constrains repairs
items.feedback: Failure during a parts constraint and recovery afterward support a conditional explanation: labor can govern normal operations while parts govern disrupted operations.

items.stem: A model predicts that a training program expands output if trained workers can use available machines. Output stays flat: trainees return to workplaces with no spare machine time. Which conclusion and test fit the evidence?
options: The capacity condition failed; compare similarly trained workplaces with spare machines
Training has no possible effect; repeat the same constrained program
The prediction is normative; ask whether managers approve of training
The model is confirmed; count certificates rather than output
items.feedback: The prediction requires access to machine time. Testing otherwise comparable workplaces with spare capacity checks that condition without treating certificate counts as output gains.

items.stem: A commuting model assumes five workplace days and forecasts trips accurately. Offices then permit two home days; trips fall only among eligible workers. Which explanation best fits both observations?
options: The attendance condition changed; the old relationship may still fit ineligible workers
The old fit proves attendance rules are irrelevant to travel
The failure means trip counts cannot test commuting models
Eligibility differences show the forecast error must be random
items.feedback: The concentrated decline links forecast failure to a changed attendance condition. Workers whose conditions did not change provide a useful comparison.

items.stem: An ordering model fits stores before app alerts. Later it underpredicts purchases by alert subscribers but fits nonsubscribers. Subscribers also receive discounts. What would best diagnose the missing mechanism?
options: Attribute the full subscriber difference to alerts because the old model omitted them
Treat unchanged nonsubscriber purchases as proof discounts have no effect
Re-estimate one average and assume the subscriber gap disappears
Compare alerts on and off among otherwise comparable buyers facing the same discounts
items.feedback: Alerts and discounts change together for subscribers. Holding discounts comparable while varying alerts separates the proposed information mechanism from the price difference.

items.stem: A model assumes producers can add capacity within a month. It overpredicts first-month output in districts with permit delays, but predicts annual output well. What scope is best supported?
options: Reject annual predictions because the monthly abstraction failed
Treat permit delays as a change in society's preferences
Use it for the annual question; model permit delays before using its monthly prediction
Use annual accuracy to validate the first-month prediction
items.feedback: The same abstraction can fit one horizon and fail at another. The observed delay matters for the monthly adjustment even when annual capacity catches up.

items.stem: Two delivery models fit ordinary weeks. Only one includes warehouse capacity. After a warehouse closure, delays rise where spare storage is scarce but not where spare storage is ample. Which further observation would most weaken that mechanism?
options: Both models previously fitted ordinary delivery volumes
Restoring storage leaves the excess delays unchanged under otherwise comparable conditions
The models continue to agree during weeks without closures
Districts with spare storage avoid the initial delay increase
items.feedback: If restoring the alleged binding resource leaves delays unchanged, the capacity mechanism needs reassessment. Ordinary-week fit cannot discriminate between the models.

items.stem: A classroom exchange model predicts quick switching when a better offer appears. Real customers face long contracts. Switching rises only when contracts expire. What follows for applying the model?
options: The choice mechanism may apply at renewal; contract timing limits short-run transfer
Delayed switching refutes the possibility that customers compare offers
The classroom result establishes that contracts carry no switching cost
Observed switching proves the model predicts the timing without modification
items.feedback: Customers may compare offers as modeled but act only when contractual constraints relax. Application must distinguish the renewal margin from immediate switching.

items.stem: A model predicts equipment failures using machine age and claims age itself causes failure. It fits old data, but after maintenance is randomized, equally old machines fail at different rates. What can be concluded?
options: The original fit proves maintenance cannot affect failure
The new evidence makes age useless for every forecasting purpose
Randomized maintenance turns a factual prediction into a value judgment
Age can remain predictive while the causal claim needs maintenance evidence
items.feedback: Age can proxy for maintenance history. A maintenance effect at a fixed age challenges the proposed causal explanation without automatically erasing age's predictive usefulness.

items.stem: A model favors plan A over B if participation exceeds 60%. Credible estimates range from 45% to 75%; both plans fit past data. What finding would resolve the model's ranking most directly?
options: A statement that A has the larger possible benefit
Selecting 75% because it yields a definite recommendation
Reliable local evidence placing participation on one side of 60%
More past observations both plans already explain
items.feedback: The ranking reverses at the participation threshold. Evidence narrowing participation to one side addresses the decision; preferred endpoints and shared past fit do not.

items.stem: A detailed scheduling model cuts average forecast error but often reverses the recommended shift when uncertain inputs change. A simpler model consistently chooses the shift that performs well in trials. Which evaluation fits this decision?
options: Average the recommended shifts without checking feasibility
Compare decision performance and robustness, rather than forecast error alone
Choose the detailed model because lower average error guarantees better choices
Choose the simpler model solely because fewer variables guarantee validity
items.feedback: A forecast metric and a scheduling decision are different objectives. Trial performance and stability under plausible inputs matter when selecting a model for the actual decision.

items.stem: A reimbursement model assumes firms keep cost-saving effort unchanged. After payments become more generous, effort falls and actual costs exceed forecasts. Which update addresses both the failure and a future rule change?
options: Model how the payment rule affects effort, then test costs under the new rule
Raise the old cost estimate by a fixed amount for every future rule
Keep effort fixed because that assumption once fitted the data
Call the forecast normative because firms responded strategically
items.feedback: Payment rules can change behavior. Modeling and testing that response is more transferable than applying a fixed correction that assumes behavior never changes again.

items.stem: A housing model predicts lower purchases when price rises, holding neighborhood quality fixed. In the data, renovated neighborhoods have both higher prices and more purchases. A critic calls this a refutation. Which evaluation and test are most informative?
options: Higher purchases prove demand slopes upward; controlling for quality would remove economically relevant evidence and invalidate the test.
Quality changes may confound the comparison; compare price changes within similar-quality neighborhoods before rejecting the conditional prediction.
The prediction is immune to data because holding quality fixed is an assumption; no observed comparison can challenge it.
Renovation proves quality causes all purchases; the model’s price mechanism is established even without a conditional comparison.
items.feedback: The model makes a ceteris-paribus prediction. Varying quality may shift demand while price changes, so the raw correlation does not isolate the price effect. Comparable-quality evidence can test the relevant conditional prediction.

items.stem: Two models predict different effects of a tax because one assumes fixed supply and the other allows firms to enter. What should economists do first?
options: Average both tax predictions without examining their assumptions
Choose the model containing the greater number of equations
Match assumptions to the relevant time horizon and evidence
Reject both models simply because their predictions disagree
items.feedback: Whether firms can enter depends on the horizon and evidence, so the assumptions determine applicability.

items.stem: A model predicts that a price ceiling causes a shortage, but observed quantity sold does not fall. Which finding would most strongly preserve the model rather than refute it?
options: The ceiling was above the market-clearing price
Consumers preferred other products during the policy
The market included many buyers and sellers
Officials described the ceiling as a fair policy
items.feedback: A ceiling above equilibrium is nonbinding, so the shortage prediction does not apply.

items.stem: A labor model predicts a payroll subsidy lowers hiring costs and expands employment at flexible wages. In a new region, bargaining agreements guarantee workers the entire subsidy as higher wages while firms’ net hiring costs stay unchanged. Which transfer of the model is defensible?
options: Keep the original employment forecast; a subsidy of the same statutory size must have the same effect under any bargaining rule.
Reject the original model in its own region; failure to transfer proves flexible wages never mattered for employment.
Rework the wage-setting mechanism; the unchanged net hiring cost removes the model’s stated employment-expansion channel.
Predict an equal employment contraction; workers receiving the subsidy necessarily shifts firms’ labor demand left by the same amount.
items.feedback: The original mechanism depends on a reduction in firms’ net labor cost. If wage bargaining absorbs the subsidy completely, that channel is absent. The model may still describe its original institutions, but needs revision for the new setting.

items.stem: Two models fit past recessions equally well. One says reduced credit supply cuts investment; the other says weak expected sales reduce both borrowing and investment. A new policy randomly expands credit access for some otherwise comparable firms. Which observation best distinguishes the proposed mechanisms?
options: Borrowing and investment remain correlated in the historical sample after adding more recession years.
Investment rises among newly credit-eligible firms relative to controls without a prior relative improvement in expected sales.
Both models continue to predict the same national investment total during the experiment.
Firms with the strongest expected sales borrow most before the randomized eligibility change.
items.feedback: Randomized credit access creates variation separate from firms’ preexisting sales outlook. A relative investment response supports the credit-supply channel; historical co-movement alone is compatible with both mechanisms.

items.stem: A simple model forecasts regional employment with a 5% error on data that were not used to build it. It recommends policy A across a plausible range of numerical assumptions. A more complex model reduces that error to 4.8%, but small, plausible changes in its assumptions reverse whether it recommends A or B. The policy would be costly and difficult to reverse. What should policymakers do before choosing a policy?
options: Report the modest prediction gain and unstable ranking, test the assumptions that change the recommendation, and assess whether the policy choice is reliable enough for this decision.
Choose the complex model because any lower forecast error establishes a more reliable policy ranking.
Choose A solely because the simple model is stable, treating stability as proof that its mechanism and recommendation are correct.
Average the two point recommendations without examining the assumptions, because averaging eliminates uncertainty about how the models represent the economy.
items.feedback: Forecast accuracy and the reliability of a policy recommendation are different concerns. A small improvement in forecast accuracy may not justify a costly, hard-to-reverse decision when reasonable changes in assumptions reverse the recommendation. Policymakers should test those assumptions and explain the uncertainty.

items.stem: In a hypothetical fully loaned-up system with a fixed 10 percent reserve ratio and no excess reserves, the public permanently switches $36 million from deposits to currency. The monetary base stays fixed. Banks restore their reserve ratios through loan repayments that destroy deposits; there are no defaults or other changes. What are the final changes in deposits and in currency plus deposits?
options: Deposits fall $360 million; money falls $324 million.
Deposits fall $36 million; money is unchanged.
Deposits fall $360 million; money falls $396 million.
Deposits fall $324 million; money falls $360 million.
items.feedback: Currency rises $36 million and reserves fall $36 million. At reserves/deposits = 0.10, deposits must fall $360 million in total. Money changes by +$36 million − $360 million = −$324 million.

items.stem: Two otherwise comparable banking systems receive $160 in reserves. In A, banks lend available funds and payments are redeposited. In B, banks hold additional reserves and customers retain more currency. Which comparison is supported?
options: B must support a larger expansion because holding reserves is itself lending
Both expansions must be equal because the required reserve ratio alone determines actual lending
A's expansion must be zero because redepositing cancels every loan
A can support a larger deposit expansion; the simple multiplier is less descriptive of B's behavior
items.feedback: Extra reserve holdings and currency retention reduce successive lending/redepositing rounds. The same reserve injection and formal required ratio need not produce the same actual multiplier.

items.stem: A simple deposit-expansion model with a 10% required reserve ratio predicts a $1800 deposit maximum from $180 in new reserves. Actual deposits rise only $720. Which diagnosis and inference are justified?
options: The banks must have created negative reserves because every prediction is an accounting identity
The shortfall proves the central bank cannot create reserves in the first place
Reserve hoarding or currency leakage can lower the expansion; the effective multiplier here is 4
The required ratio must be 25%; behavior can never lower expansion below the reciprocal rule
items.feedback: Observed deposit growth divided by new reserves is 720/180=4. The 1/rr rule is a maximum under restrictive assumptions, not a behavioral guarantee; the data alone do not uniquely identify which leakage caused the shortfall.

items.stem: In a hypothetical banking system initially without excess reserves, the public deposits $56,000 of existing currency. The required-reserve ratio stays at 20 percent. Each bank lends all excess reserves; after every loan, 25 percent stays as currency and 75 percent reaches the next bank. No other constraint binds. Including the initial deposit, what is the eventual deposit increase, and what is the net increase in currency plus deposits?
options: Deposits rise $140,000; net money rises $112,000.
Deposits rise $280,000; net money rises $224,000.
Deposits rise $140,000; net money rises $140,000.
Deposits rise $112,000; net money rises $84,000.
items.feedback: Successive deposits have ratio 0.80 × 0.75 = 0.60, so their sum is $56,000/(1 − 0.60) = $140,000. Total loans are 0.80 × $140,000 = $112,000; $28,000 returns to public currency. Currency changes by −$56,000 + $28,000, so net money rises $112,000.

items.stem: Banks receive $200 in reserves but face few creditworthy loan applications. A proposal assumes more reserves alone will create a fixed proportional lending boom. Which missing link matters?
options: Reserve creation requires prior loan applications; weak demand prevents the injection.
Reserves already represent loan applications; the injection establishes adequate credit demand.
Loans require equal reductions in existing deposits; weak demand preserves deposits.
Banks need willing, qualified borrowers as well as reserve capacity.
items.feedback: Having liquidity is different from finding loans acceptable to both lender and borrower. Reserve supply alone does not establish demand, risk-adjusted profitability or capital headroom.

items.stem: Refer to the value-of-money graph. A worker earns $24 at point a and $30 at point b. Treat each point’s price level as the reciprocal of its displayed value of money. What happens to the worker’s real wage, and what nominal wage at b would instead preserve the original purchasing power?
options: Real wage falls from 48 to 45 output units; $32 would preserve it.
Real wage rises from 12 to 20 output units; $18 would preserve it.
Real wage rises from 48 to 60 output units; $24 would preserve it.
Real wage falls from 48 to 45 output units; $36 would preserve it.
items.feedback: P is 1/2 at a and 2/3 at b. Real wages are 24/(1/2) = 48 and 30/(2/3) = 45. To retain 48 units at b requires 48 × 2/3 = $32.

items.stem: Assume stable velocity, long-run monetary neutrality, and the approximation that inflation equals money growth minus real output growth. Money grows 8% and real output grows 2% annually. A two-year wage contract raises nominal wages 5% in year 1. Before year 2, money growth permanently rises to 11%, while real output growth stays 2%. The year-2 nominal raise equals year-1 inflation plus 1 percentage point. Using the approximate real-wage growth rate in each year, what happens to purchasing power, and what year-2 raise would preserve it?
options: Real wages fall 1% in year 1 and rise 1% in year 2; a 6% year-2 raise would preserve purchasing power.
Real wages rise 5% in year 1 and 7% in year 2; any positive raise would preserve purchasing power.
Real wages fall 3% in year 1 and 4% in year 2; an 11% year-2 raise would preserve purchasing power.
Real wages fall 1% in year 1 and 2% in year 2; a 9% year-2 raise would preserve purchasing power.
items.feedback: Inflation is initially 8−2=6%, then 11−2=9%. The nominal raises are 5% and 6+1=7%. Approximate real-wage growth is therefore −1% and −2%. The backward-looking contract misses the inflation increase; matching year-2 inflation requires a 9% nominal raise.

items.stem: Compare two economies after identical one-time money increases. A resets wages immediately; B has fixed contracts for a year. Productive resources and technology are unchanged in both. Which counterfactual separates short-run adjustment from long-run neutrality?
options: Temporary output paths coincide; neutrality rules out the effects of contract lags.
Only B's prices change; flexible wages prevent nominal adjustment in A.
Temporary output paths differ; both ultimately return to unchanged potential.
Long-run potentials differ; temporary rigidity permanently alters B's productive technology.
items.feedback: Different nominal rigidities can produce different transition paths. With unchanged real productive conditions, those paths need not imply different long-run real output endpoints.

items.stem: In a hypothetical steady-state banking model, the required-reserve ratio is 10 percent, banks hold excess reserves equal to 5 percent of deposits, and the public holds currency equal to 25 percent of deposits. These ratios remain fixed. Money is currency plus deposits; the monetary base is currency plus total reserves. What base increase is needed for a $250 million money increase, and why is the simple 1/required-ratio estimate too small?
options: $80 million; both currency holdings and excess reserves absorb base money.
$25 million; every base dollar supports ten dollars of money.
$100 million; currency is excluded from the money measure.
$62.5 million; retaining a fixed fraction once describes every lending round.
items.feedback: With deposits D, money is 1.25D and the base is (0.25 + 0.10 + 0.05)D = 0.40D. The money/base ratio is 3.125, so the base must rise $250/3.125 = $80 million. The simple multiplier ignores both leakages.

items.stem: A policy package supplies $160 of reserves but also increases the return banks can earn by holding reserves. What can be concluded about bank lending?
options: Reserve capacity increases, holding reserves becomes more attractive; the net lending response remains uncertain.
Reserve capacity increases, holding reserves becomes more attractive; both changes encourage additional lending equally.
Reserve capacity decreases, holding reserves becomes more attractive; both changes discourage additional lending equally.
Reserve capacity increases, the return on reserves is irrelevant; a fixed multiplier determines lending.
items.feedback: Reserve availability and the incentive to hold reserves are different margins. Their combination does not determine lending without the relevant behavior, risk, demand and magnitudes.

items.stem: In an explicitly simplified scarce-reserves model, a central bank buys $180 of securities from banks while the required ratio is unchanged. Which balance-sheet change begins the expansionary transmission?
options: Government tax liabilities fall by the purchase amount; reserves are unaffected
Bank securities fall and reserves rise; easier reserve conditions can support lower short-term rates and lending
Bank securities rise and reserves fall; tighter reserve conditions support lower short-term rates
Bank capital rises by the purchase amount; no reserve or securities asset changes
items.feedback: The purchase exchanges securities for reserve balances on bank balance sheets. Under the stated scarce-reserves model, greater reserve availability eases money-market conditions; it is not a fiscal tax cut or automatic equity gain.

items.stem: In a hypothetical scarce-reserves system, deposits are $1,000 and reserves are $150. The required reserve ratio is 10%, and banks hold no desired excess reserves. The central bank sells $30 of bonds to banks, lowering their reserves without initially changing deposits, and cuts the required ratio to 8%. It also raises interest paid on reserves relative to unchanged loan yields. Which assessment separates the reserve constraint from the lending incentive?
options: Excess reserves fall from $50 to $40; the ratio cut partly offsets the sale, while higher reserve interest encourages more lending.
Excess reserves fall from $50 to $40; the ratio cut partly offsets the sale, while higher reserve interest further discourages lending.
Excess reserves rise from $50 to $70; the ratio cut more than offsets the sale, while higher reserve interest discourages lending.
Excess reserves fall from $50 to $20; the ratio cut has no effect, while higher reserve interest encourages more lending.
items.feedback: Initially, excess reserves are 150−0.10×1,000=50. After the sale and ratio cut, they are 120−0.08×1,000=40. The ratio cut frees $20 and only partly offsets the $30 reserve drain. Higher reserve interest makes alternative lending less attractive; it does not itself remove reserve balances.

items.stem: In a simplified reserve-ratio exercise, a bank has deposits of $2,200 and reserves of $440. The requirement rises from 10% to 15%, with balances unchanged. The bank was already unwilling to lend because no applicant met its credit standards. Does the reserve change establish a $110 reduction in actual lending?
options: No. Excess reserves fall from $220 to $110, but lending was already constrained by credit standards.
Yes. Every dollar decline in excess reserves must remove a dollar of loans regardless of borrower quality.
No. Excess reserves rise to $330 because the larger requirement increases lending capacity.
Yes. The requirement writes down bank capital by $110, forcing the same loan reduction.
items.feedback: Required reserves rise from 220 to 330, leaving 110 excess. That accounting change does not reveal an actual loan reduction when the bank already rejects applicants. Reserve availability, capital and creditworthiness are distinct constraints.

items.stem: Policymakers want to reduce aggregate demand by $300 billion. MPC is 0.5, and each one-percentage-point increase in the interest rate reduces investment by $50 billion. Under this spending model, how much must the rate rise?
options: 3 percentage points
6 percentage points
1.5 percentage points
2 percentage points
items.feedback: The multiplier is 2. A $300 billion total demand reduction requires investment to fall $150 billion. At $50 billion per percentage point, that requires a 3-percentage-point rate increase.

items.stem: Refer to the two-panel graph. Between A and B, the central bank expands money supply while SRAS stays fixed. A commentator says output and prices rose by the same percentage because they both rose. Which numerical comparison and inference are supported?
options: Output rises 12.5 percent and the price level 25 percent; their responses must be proportional.
Both rise 25 percent; equal directions establish equal percentage changes.
Both rise 6.25 percent; a common point label establishes a common percentage change.
Output rises 25 percent and the price level 12.5 percent; their responses need not be proportional.
items.feedback: Read output 100 to 125 and P 50 to 56.25. Their percentage changes are 25/100 = 25 percent and 6.25/50 = 12.5 percent. The diagram supplies distinct responses along fixed SRAS.

items.stem: Initially, money demand is Md=500−20r and money supply is 300, with r measured in percentage points. The central bank cuts supply to 260, while a payment innovation lowers demand to Md=440−20r. Investment changes by −$10 billion for each percentage-point change in r. MPC is 0.5. With fixed prices and no other spending changes, which net result follows?
options: The rate falls from 10% to 9%, investment rises $10 billion, and total spending rises $20 billion.
The rate rises from 10% to 12%, investment falls $20 billion, and total spending falls $40 billion.
The rate falls from 10% to 9%, investment rises $10 billion, and total spending rises only $10 billion.
The rate stays 10%, investment is unchanged, and the two money-market shifts cancel exactly.
items.feedback: Initially 500−20r=300 gives r=10. After both shifts, 440−20r=260 gives r=9. Lower money demand more than offsets the supply cut. The one-point rate decline raises investment $10 billion and, with multiplier 2, spending $20 billion.

items.stem: In a fixed-price spending model, monetary tightening reduces investment by $90 billion while improved business expectations independently raise autonomous investment by $30 billion. MPC is 0.6, with no taxes, imports or further interest-rate feedbacks. What is the net AD change, and what independent investment recovery would exactly offset the monetary effect?
options: AD shifts left $150 billion; a $90 billion recovery would cancel it.
AD shifts left $225 billion; a $30 billion recovery would cancel it.
AD shifts left $60 billion; a $150 billion recovery would cancel it.
AD shifts right $150 billion; a $90 billion recovery would cancel it.
items.feedback: Net autonomous investment changes by −90 + 30 = −$60 billion. The multiplier is 2.5, so AD falls $150 billion. An independent $90 billion recovery would cancel the autonomous monetary loss before any multiplication.

items.stem: The Fed wants to reduce aggregate demand by $300 billion. MPC is 0.75, and each one-percentage-point rise in the interest rate lowers investment by $25 billion. Under these assumptions, how much must the rate rise?
options: 3 percentage points
4 percentage points
12 percentage points
1 percentage point
items.feedback: A multiplier of 4 means investment must fall $75 billion to lower total demand by $300 billion. Dividing by $25 billion per percentage point gives a 3-percentage-point rate increase.

items.stem: Money supply falls from MS1 to MS2 in the displayed diagram. Compare that change with a counterfactual in which interest rates respond but firms no longer change investment. Which link would fail, and what does the original money-market panel establish?
options: The rate-to-investment link fails; the original rate stays at r 1, consistent with a flat-rate liquidity-trap segment.
The rate-to-investment link fails; the original rate changes from r 1 to r 2, so that panel does not show a liquidity trap.
The supply-to-rate link fails; the original rate changes from r 1 to r 2 despite the assumed investment insensitivity.
The rate-to-investment link fails; the original rate change proves policy has the same output effect even when investment stops responding.
items.feedback: The figure shows the rate moving from r 1 to r 2 as supply contracts. The hypothetical failure is farther along the chain: the rate no longer changes investment. A rate-responsive money market is different from the flat near-zero-rate case used to illustrate a liquidity trap.

items.stem: Suppose monetary easing lowers the interest rate and increases investment by $110. At the same time, fiscal tightening reduces aggregate demand by a total of $220 after induced effects. If the spending multiplier on the investment increase is 3, what is the net effect on aggregate demand?
options: AD rises by $110.
AD falls by $110.
AD falls by $330.
AD rises by $550.
items.feedback: The $110 increase in investment raises AD by 3 × $110 = $330. The $220 fiscal contraction is already stated as a total effect, so subtract it once. Net AD rises by $110.

items.stem: Use current U.S. definitions, in which savings deposits are part of M1. A household shifts $75,000 from checking to savings at the same bank. Later the bank originates a $12,000 loan by crediting another customer’s checking account; no loan is repaid and no other balance changes. Relative to the starting totals, how do M1 and M2 change?
options: Both rise by $12,000.
M1 falls by $63,000; M2 rises by $12,000.
Both rise by $87,000.
Both remain unchanged.
items.feedback: The checking-to-savings transfer changes neither aggregate and does not release reserves. The new loan adds a $12,000 deposit, raising both M1 and M2 by that amount.

items.stem: A customer deposits $260 of currency into checking. A bank later makes a separate loan by crediting a borrower's checking account. Which comparison correctly separates the two events?
options: Neither event can change M1 because every bank deposit merely replaces currency
The currency deposit creates new M1; lending changes only the ownership of existing currency
The currency deposit changes M1 composition; the later loan can create a new deposit and raise M1
Both events create new M1 equal to the amounts credited because checking balances rise
items.feedback: In the first event, public currency falls as checking rises; in the second, a loan asset and deposit liability are created together. The initial transfer and subsequent credit creation must not be conflated.

items.stem: A household has $280 in checking, $560 in savings and $280 in a small time deposit. Under current U.S. definitions, it moves the time deposit into savings. A report records M1 up $280 and M2 up $280, attributing both to this transfer. Can that account be reconciled without another transaction?
options: Yes. Entering savings creates $280 of new broad money even though the funds were already in a time deposit.
No. M1 rises $280, but M2 is unchanged; the reported M2 increase requires another source or a reporting error.
No. M1 must fall $280 because savings is excluded while small time deposits are included.
Yes. Moving any deposit between accounts increases both aggregates by the amount transferred.
items.feedback: Under the stated current convention, savings belongs to M1 and small time deposits do not; both belong to M2. The transfer changes the narrower classification while leaving broad money unchanged. It cannot alone explain both reported increases.

Shut down and incur the fixed-cost loss of $520.00
Produce about 21.33 units and count $1,024.00 as economic profit
Produce about 21.33 units and count revenue of $1,561.60 as economic profit
items.feedback: MR = MC gives Q = 21.333333; demand gives P = 73.200000. Revenue minus the stated total cost is 504.000000, so the rounded economic profit is $504.00. Revenue covers variable cost; operating contributes $1,024.00 toward fixed cost. With free entry, positive economic profit attracts rivals; it is not a long-run guarantee.

items.stem: Verdant Spa faces demand P=73−0.625Q and total cost TC=882+10Q+0.5Q². Its initial long-run optimum is Q=28, where P=ATC=$55.5; minimum ATC occurs at Q=42. A licensing reform reduces fixed cost to $220.5 and leaves MC unchanged. Entry then shifts each firm’s demand intercept until tangency restores zero profit; its demand slope stays 0.625. The new tangency is Q=14, P=ATC=$32.75, with minimum ATC at 21. Which interpretation reconciles the initial and final outcomes?
options: The lower fixed cost immediately shifts MC left, so the smaller final output must be a movement along the original demand curve.
Output need not fall immediately when fixed cost falls; the later entry-driven demand shift supports the smaller tangency output, while positive markup and excess capacity remain.
Zero long-run profit means price equals MC at 14, so the stated positive excess capacity proves the new outcome is impossible.
The new output must be 21 because entry makes every differentiated firm minimize ATC at its chosen output.
items.feedback: A fixed-cost reduction initially leaves MR=MC output unchanged and creates profit. Subsequent entry changes demand. At the new Q=14, MC=10+14=$24, below price $32.75; actual Q is also below 21. Thus zero profit can coexist with both markup and excess capacity after adjustment.

options: Unregulated profit is $1,600; MC pricing needs no subsidy; AC pricing achieves the efficient output
Unregulated profit is $800; MC pricing needs an $800 subsidy; AC pricing leaves the same output as monopoly
Unregulated profit is $800; MC pricing needs an $800 subsidy; AC pricing covers cost but leaves P above MC
Unregulated profit is zero; MC pricing needs an $800 subsidy; AC pricing produces more than the efficient quantity
items.feedback: MR = MC gives Q = 40 and P = $50: profit is (50 - 10) × 40 - 800 = $800. MC pricing gives Q = 80 and covers only variable cost, leaving an $800 financing gap. Higher-output AC pricing gives Q about 68.28 and P about $21.72: zero profit, but P > MC and fewer trades than under MC pricing.

items.stem: A district-heating network is regulated at P = ATC and earns zero economic profit. Its ATC is declining over the relevant range and exceeds MC. Officials propose P = MC with a subsidy equal to the resulting shortfall in revenue relative to total economic cost. Which appraisal best addresses the regulatory dilemma?
options: The rule necessarily covers all total costs because MC includes the average fixed infrastructure cost
The rule can expand mutually beneficial service, but public financing and weak cost-control incentives under automatic cost reimbursement must be assessed
The rule must reduce service because lowering price moves buyers up the demand curve
The rule is unnecessary because zero economic profit proves the original allocation maximizes total surplus
items.feedback: Cost-covering P = ATC leaves price above MC, excluding some positive-surplus uses. Setting P = MC can recover those uses but, with ATC > MC, leaves a cost-recovery gap. Funding that gap and designing incentives to control cost are part of the policy comparison; zero profit alone is not an efficiency test.

items.stem: A natural monopolist has demand P=120−1.5Q, MC=$15, and total cost TC=1200+15Q. The two outputs where demand price equals ATC are approximately 14.38 and 55.62. options: Choose Q≈55.62, P≈$36.58; P=MC would raise output to 70.00 with no loss.
Choose Q≈55.62, P≈$36.58; P=MC would raise output to 70.00 but leave a $1200 loss.
Choose Q≈14.38, P≈$98.42; the smaller break-even output serves the greatest number of buyers.
Choose Q≈70.00, P=$15; equality of price and MC also covers the $1200 fixed cost.
items.feedback: Both listed intersections break even, but the larger one serves more buyers. Demand gives P≈$36.58 there. P=MC instead implies Q=(120−15)/1.5≈70.00 and leaves the fixed cost $1200 uncovered. The two break-even roots are supplied so the task requires interpretation rather than quadratic solving.
