Output rises to 7; this necessarily recovers the fixed fee regardless of marginal cost.
Output remains 4; profit changes from $10 to −$5.
Output remains 4; profit stays $10 because fixed costs affect neither output nor profit.
items.feedback: Before the fee the largest amount of revenue left after variable cost is $50 at Q=4. Every output’s profit is reduced by the same $15, so the maximizing quantity is unchanged and profit becomes $-5.

items.stem: A competitive firm faces price $31. Fixed cost is $58, unavoidable this period but avoidable by exiting before next period. Marginal costs of units 1–7 are [8, 13, 19, 26, 34, 43, 53] dollars; variable cost at zero output is zero. Choose the largest output if two quantities tie for maximum profit. Next period the price is expected to be $7, with marginal costs unchanged. Which comparison separates current operation from the response to that price?
options: Currently Q=4 and profit is $0; at $7, keep output 4 to spread fixed cost.
Currently Q=7 and profit is maximized; at $7, add units because their sales cover some fixed cost.
Currently Q=0 because fixed cost is positive; at $7, enter because a lower price means lower cost.
Currently Q=4 and profit is $0; at $7, every marginal unit costs more than its price, so choose zero output.
items.feedback: The current largest maximizing output is 4, giving contribution $58 and profit $0. At the future price 7, even the first unit’s MC=8 exceeds price and later marginal costs are higher, so no positive output improves profit.

items.stem: A competitive firm faces a price of $34. Fixed cost is $86, unavoidable this period but avoidable by exiting before next period. Marginal costs of units 1–7 are [9, 14, 20, 27, 35, 44, 54] dollars; variable cost at zero output is zero. Choose the largest output if two quantities tie for maximum profit. An accountant recommends immediate shutdown because profit is negative. Another adviser recommends operating now but exiting before the fixed cost can recur. Which comparison supports the better proposal?
options: Produce 4 now: lose $20 instead of $86; exit before the fixed cost recurs if conditions persist.
Shut down now: lose $0 instead of $20; remain next period because shutdown avoids all fixed costs.
Produce 4 now: earn $66 of economic profit; remain next period because contribution equals profit.
Produce 7 now: higher revenue eliminates the loss; remain next period because more output always raises profit.
items.feedback: At Q=4, contribution is $66, so the loss is $86−$66=$20. Shutdown still loses all $86 now. Next period the cost is avoidable through exit, changing the relevant alternative.

items.stem: A competitive firm faces price $9. Fixed cost is $30, unavoidable this period but avoidable by exiting before next period. Marginal costs of units 1–7 are [10, 15, 21, 28, 36, 45, 55] dollars; variable cost at zero output is zero. Choose the largest output if two quantities tie for maximum profit. A verified process improvement lowers every marginal unit cost by $2, with fixed cost and price unchanged. Which counterfactual is correct?
options: Output stays at 0; only fixed-cost changes can affect an operating decision.
Output changes from 0 to 1; profit changes from −$30 to −$29.
Output changes to 7 and profit becomes positive because every cost-saving innovation guarantees profit.
Output changes to 1; profit is $1 because the improvement eliminates the original fixed cost.
items.feedback: After the improvement, contributions at outputs 0–7 are [0, 1, -3, -13, -30, -55, -89, -133]. The largest maximum is Q=1 with contribution $1. Subtract unchanged F=$30 for profit $-29, compared with the original $-30.

items.stem: A competitive firm faces price $40. Fixed cost is $115, unavoidable this period but avoidable by exiting before next period. Marginal costs of units 1–7 are [11, 16, 22, 29, 37, 46, 56] dollars; variable cost at zero output is zero. Choose the largest output if two quantities tie for maximum profit. A new unconditional license fee adds $15 to this period’s fixed cost. A manager proposes reducing output because the fee “raises MC.” Which correction is right?
options: Output falls to 4; profit rises because spreading fewer units over the fee lowers MC.
Output rises to 7; this necessarily recovers the fixed fee regardless of marginal cost.
Output remains 5; profit changes from −$30 to −$45.
Output remains 5; profit stays $-30 because fixed costs affect neither output nor profit.
items.feedback: Before the fee the largest amount of revenue left after variable cost is $85 at Q=5. Every output’s profit is reduced by the same $15, so the maximizing quantity is unchanged and profit becomes $-45.

items.stem: A competitive firm faces price $43. Fixed cost is $85, unavoidable this period but avoidable by exiting before next period. Marginal costs of units 1–7 are [12, 17, 23, 30, 38, 47, 57] dollars; variable cost at zero output is zero. Choose the largest output if two quantities tie for maximum profit. Next period the price is expected to be $11, with marginal costs unchanged. Which comparison separates current operation from the response to that price?
options: Currently Q=5 and profit is $10; at $11, keep output 5 to spread fixed cost.
Currently Q=7 and profit is maximized; at $11, add units because their sales cover some fixed cost.
Currently Q=0 because fixed cost is positive; at $11, enter because a lower price means lower cost.
Currently Q=5 and profit is $10; at $11, every marginal unit costs more than its price, so choose zero output.
items.feedback: The current largest maximizing output is 5, giving contribution $95 and profit $10. At the future price 11, even the first unit’s MC=12 exceeds price and later marginal costs are higher, so no positive output improves profit.

items.stem: A competitive firm has P = $42, ATC = $34, AVC = $22, Q = 70, and TFC = $840. Q is the output where price equals rising marginal cost. Which answer correctly covers the short-run outcome and long-run pressure?
options: Produce 70; profit $560; entry pressure
Produce 70; profit $840; entry pressure
Shut down; loss $840; exit pressure
Produce 70; profit $560; exit pressure
items.feedback: Separate output, operating status, profit or loss, and long-run entry or exit pressure.

items.stem: A competitive firm has P = $31, ATC = $37, AVC = $21, Q = 65, and TFC = $1,040. Q is the output where price equals rising marginal cost. Which answer correctly covers the short-run outcome and long-run pressure?
options: Shut down; loss $1,040; exit pressure
Produce 65; loss $390; exit pressure
Produce 65; profit $650; entry pressure
Produce 65; loss $390; entry pressure
items.feedback: Separate output, operating status, profit or loss, and long-run entry or exit pressure.

items.stem: A competitive firm has P = $26, ATC = $26, AVC = $18, Q = 80, and TFC = $640. Q is the output where price equals rising marginal cost. Which answer correctly covers the short-run outcome and long-run pressure?
options: Shut down; loss $640; exit pressure
Produce 80; profit $640; entry pressure
Produce 80; zero economic profit; no entry or exit pressure
Produce 80; zero economic profit; entry pressure
items.feedback: Separate output, operating status, profit or loss, and long-run entry or exit pressure.

items.stem: A competitive firm has P = $20, ATC = $29, AVC = $16, Q = 75, and TFC = $975. Q is the output where price equals rising marginal cost. Which answer correctly covers the short-run outcome and long-run pressure?
options: Shut down; loss $975; exit pressure
Produce 75; profit $300; entry pressure
Produce 75; loss $675; entry pressure
Produce 75; loss $675; exit pressure
items.feedback: Separate output, operating status, profit or loss, and long-run entry or exit pressure.

items.stem: A competitive firm has P = $15, ATC = $28, AVC = $19, Q = 60, and TFC = $540. Q is the output where price equals rising marginal cost. Which answer correctly covers the short-run outcome and long-run pressure?
options: Shut down; loss $540; exit pressure
Produce 60; loss $780; exit pressure
Shut down; zero economic loss; no exit pressure
Produce 60; loss $240; entry pressure
items.feedback: TFC = (28 − 19) × 60 = $540. Price is below AVC, so shutdown minimizes the short-run loss to fixed cost. Persistent losses create exit pressure.

items.stem: A competitive firm has P = $24, ATC = $32, AVC = $24, Q = 55, and TFC = $440. Q is the output where price equals rising marginal cost. Which answer correctly covers the short-run outcome and long-run pressure?
options: Produce only; zero economic profit; no exit pressure
Produce or shut down; loss $440 either way; exit pressure
Shut down only; zero economic loss; exit pressure
Produce or shut down; loss $770 either way; entry pressure
items.feedback: TFC = (32 − 24) × 55 = $440. Price equals minimum AVC at the candidate output, so producing and shutting down both lose fixed cost. Persistent losses create exit pressure.

items.stem: Use the two-panel graph. A permanent demand increase raises market price before entry can occur. Assume a constant-cost industry with free entry. Which sequence correctly separates an incumbent’s immediate response from the final industry outcome?
options: Incumbents keep output fixed until entry occurs; the additional firms permanently maintain the initial price increase.
Incumbents expand by shifting their MC curves right solely because market price rises; entry then raises price further.
Incumbents choose a higher individual selling price than the market; entry later forces every firm to minimum AVC.
Incumbents expand along rising MC and may earn profit; entry then expands market supply until price returns to the original long-run level.
items.feedback: The initial higher market price raises each price taker’s MR, changing its output on the existing MC curve. Profit induces entry. With industry expansion leaving firm costs unchanged, long-run price returns to the original zero-profit level.

items.stem: Demand rises permanently in a constant-cost competitive industry. Which full adjustment statement is correct?
options: Price rises; profit attracts entry; long-run price returns to its original level
Price rises; profit attracts entry; the short-run price persists with ongoing economic profit
Price falls; losses induce exit; long-run price returns to its original level
Price rises; profit attracts entry; long-run price ends above its original level
items.feedback: Trace the demand shock, profit or loss, entry or exit, and the cost condition.

items.stem: Demand rises permanently in an increasing-cost competitive industry. Which full adjustment statement is correct?
options: Price rises; profit attracts entry; the short-run price persists with ongoing economic profit
Price rises; profit attracts entry; long-run price ends above its original level
Price falls; losses induce exit; long-run price ends above its original level
Price rises; profit attracts entry; long-run price ends below its original level
items.feedback: Trace the demand shock, profit or loss, entry or exit, and the cost condition.

items.stem: Demand rises permanently in a decreasing-cost competitive industry. Which full adjustment statement is correct?
options: Price rises; profit attracts entry; the short-run price persists with ongoing economic profit
Price falls; losses induce exit; long-run price ends below its original level
Price rises; profit attracts entry; long-run price ends below its original level
Price rises; profit attracts entry; long-run price ends above its original level
items.feedback: Trace the demand shock, profit or loss, entry or exit, and the cost condition.

items.stem: Demand falls permanently in a constant-cost competitive industry. Which full adjustment statement is correct?
options: Price falls; losses induce exit; the short-run price persists with ongoing economic profit
Price rises; profit attracts entry; long-run price returns to its original level
Price falls; losses induce exit; long-run price ends above its original level
Price falls; losses induce exit; long-run price returns to its original level
items.feedback: Trace the demand shock, profit or loss, entry or exit, and the cost condition.

items.stem: Demand falls permanently in an increasing-cost competitive industry. Which full adjustment statement is correct?
options: Price falls; losses induce exit; long-run price ends below its original level
Price falls; losses induce exit; the short-run price persists with ongoing economic profit
Price rises; profit attracts entry; long-run price ends below its original level
Price falls; losses induce exit; long-run price ends above its original level
items.feedback: Trace the demand shock, profit or loss, entry or exit, and the cost condition.

items.stem: Demand falls permanently in a decreasing-cost competitive industry. Which full adjustment statement is correct?
options: Price falls; losses induce exit; the short-run price persists with ongoing economic profit
Price falls; losses induce exit; long-run price ends above its original level
Price rises; profit attracts entry; long-run price ends above its original level
Price falls; losses induce exit; long-run price ends below its original level
items.feedback: Trace the demand shock, profit or loss, entry or exit, and the cost condition.

items.stem: A fixed annual tax rises sharply. Which combined firm-and-market conclusion is defensible?
options: MC rises and output falls immediately
AVC rises and shutdown price rises
Short-run output is unchanged, loss increases, and long-run exit pressure can rise
Profit rises and entry occurs
items.feedback: Classify the cost or market failure and trace the short-run and long-run implications.

items.stem: A per-unit tax is imposed. Which combined firm-and-market conclusion is defensible?
options: ATC alone rises; output is unchanged; shutdown is more likely
MC and AVC fall; output can rise; entry is more likely
AFC alone rises; output falls; exit is impossible
MC and AVC rise; output can fall; shutdown is more likely
items.feedback: Classify the cost or market failure and trace the short-run and long-run implications.

items.stem: Technology raises productivity. Which combined firm-and-market conclusion is defensible?
options: MC and AVC fall; output and profit can rise; entry may follow
AFC alone falls; output stays fixed; entry cannot follow
MC and AVC rise; output falls; profitable firms exit
Demand falls; output and profit fall; entry may follow
items.feedback: Classify the cost or market failure and trace the short-run and long-run implications.

items.stem: The wage rises across the industry. Which combined firm-and-market conclusion is defensible?
options: AFC alone rises; supply is unchanged; long-run price stays fixed
MC and AVC rise; supply contracts; long-run price may rise
MC rises but AVC falls; supply expands; long-run price falls
Firm demand rises; supply is unchanged; long-run profit persists
items.feedback: Classify the cost or market failure and trace the short-run and long-run implications.

items.stem: A lump-sum subsidy is introduced. Which combined firm-and-market conclusion is defensible?
options: MC falls and output rises; the shutdown price falls
AVC falls and output rises; ATC remains unchanged
ATC falls and profit rises; output at a given price is unchanged
Firm demand shifts right; output and the chosen price rise
items.feedback: Classify the cost or market failure and trace the short-run and long-run implications.

items.stem: At the current competitive output, price equals private MC=$18. Each extra unit also imposes $6 of uncompensated harm on others. A proposal uses a $6 per-unit tax instead of an output-independent license payment of equal expected revenue. At that output, how does each policy change the marginal cost faced by the firm?
options: Per-unit tax: MC becomes $24; license payment: MC becomes $24.
Per-unit tax: MC stays $18; license payment: MC becomes $24.
Per-unit tax: MC stays $18; license payment: MC stays $18.
Per-unit tax: MC becomes $24; license payment: MC stays $18.
items.feedback: At the stated output, social MC is $18 + $6 = $24. A $6 per-unit tax makes the firm face that marginal cost. An output-independent license payment changes profit but leaves marginal cost at $18; equal expected revenue does not imply equal marginal incentives.

items.stem: A price-taking firm initially produces at the minimum of ATC, where P=MC=ATC=$18, with no externalities. A temporary mandate forces it farther along rising MC to an output where ATC=$20 and MC=$23; market price stays $18. Which comparison is correct?
options: The original output is productively and allocatively efficient with zero economic profit; the mandated output is neither and creates an economic loss.
Both outputs are productively efficient because the original minimum ATC remains $18; the mandated output earns zero profit.
The mandated output is allocatively efficient because more output is produced, although ATC exceeds price.
The original output is inefficient because profit is zero; the mandated output improves efficiency by raising ATC.
items.feedback: Initially the chosen output actually attains minimum ATC and P=MC. Under the mandate, ATC is above its minimum and MC exceeds marginal value P; P<ATC also means a loss. A minimum somewhere on the curve is not enough to establish efficiency at another output.

items.stem: P=MC and P>min ATC. Which interpretation is strongest?
options: The firm is both allocatively and productively efficient because P=MC is enough to satisfy both efficiency conditions
The output is allocatively efficient, but productive efficiency is not achieved at that firm output
The firm should shut down because price above minimum ATC indicates that output is beyond the efficient scale
The firm earns zero accounting profit because P=MC determines the relationship between price and total cost
items.feedback: Apply the exact efficiency conditions and distinguish behavioral assumptions from welfare assumptions.

items.stem: A price-taking firm faces a temporary output cap of 40 units. At 40 units, ATC is at its minimum of $12 and MC is $12; market price is $18. There are no externalities. If the cap is removed, rising MC reaches $18 at 70 units, where ATC exceeds its minimum. Which comparison correctly evaluates the two outputs?
options: At 40 units production is both productively and allocatively efficient; at 70 units it is neither.
At 40 units production is neither productively nor allocatively efficient; at 70 units it is both.
At 40 units production is productively efficient but not allocatively efficient; at 70 units it is allocatively efficient but not productively efficient.
At 40 units production is allocatively efficient but not productively efficient; at 70 units it is productively efficient but not allocatively efficient.
items.feedback: Minimum ATC establishes productive efficiency at 40. However, P exceeds MC there, so additional output has marginal value above marginal cost. Removing the cap permits P=MC at 70, establishing allocative efficiency even though ATC is above its minimum.

items.stem: P=private MC while social MC is higher. Which interpretation is strongest?
options: Output is below the social optimum because private MC equals price
Output is socially optimal because competition internalizes every cost
Output is socially optimal because zero profit eliminates external harm
Output exceeds the social optimum because social MC exceeds price
items.feedback: Apply the exact efficiency conditions and distinguish behavioral assumptions from welfare assumptions.

items.stem: A firm earns zero economic profit in a market with a binding barrier to entry. What can be concluded about competition in this market?
options: Zero profit alone does not establish free entry or competitive adjustment
Zero profit establishes free entry despite the stated entry barrier
Zero profit establishes both allocative and productive efficiency
Zero profit establishes that accounting profit is also zero
items.feedback: Apply the exact efficiency conditions and distinguish behavioral assumptions from welfare assumptions.

items.stem: Many sellers and standardized products, but severe buyer misinformation. Which interpretation is strongest?
options: Both efficiency conditions always hold
Price-taking may fit while the welfare benchmark fails
The firm must shut down
Accounting profit must be zero
items.feedback: Apply the exact efficiency conditions and distinguish behavioral assumptions from welfare assumptions.

items.stem: What can be inferred when the economy's short-run relationship changes from SRPC1 to SRPC2?
options: Inflation is higher at a given unemployment rate; expectations or a supply disturbance could explain the shift.
Inflation is lower at a given unemployment rate; expectations or a supply disturbance could explain the shift.
Inflation is higher at a given unemployment rate; the graph alone proves that expected inflation rose.
Inflation is higher at a given unemployment rate because stronger demand moved the economy along unchanged SRPC1.
items.feedback: SRPC2 lies above SRPC1. The less favorable short-run tradeoff can result from higher expectations or an adverse supply disturbance; the shift itself does not identify which cause occurred.

items.stem: Refer to the graph with SRPC0, SRPC1, A, and B. Use inflation = expected inflation − 0.6 × (unemployment − 5) + s, where s is the number of percentage points a supply shock adds to inflation. Rates are in percent and differences are in percentage points. At B, s is independently measured as +1.1 percentage points. What expected inflation is consistent with B, and could we determine it from the graph alone without knowing s?
options: Expected inflation is 5.5%; without knowing s, only expected inflation plus s is identified
Expected inflation is 6.6%; without knowing s, only expected inflation plus s is identified
Expected inflation is 5.5%; without knowing s, expected inflation is still separately identified by the curve intercept
Expected inflation is 4.3%; without knowing s, expected inflation is still separately identified by actual inflation
items.feedback: At B, unemployment is 6% and actual inflation is 6%. Thus 6 = expected inflation − 0.6 + 1.1, giving expected inflation of 5.5%. Without knowing the supply shock's contribution s, the graph determines only expected inflation + s = 6.6. The higher curve alone does not show how much expectations changed.

items.stem: In the graph, expected inflation initially equals inflation at A, but the economy is at B. Next period, expectations adjust to B’s inflation, shifting SRPC vertically by the same amount. Its slope, the natural rate, and supply conditions stay fixed. Compare keeping unemployment at B’s rate with keeping inflation at B’s rate. What happens next period?
options: Keeping unemployment at B's 3% requires inflation of 5.5%; holding inflation at 4% instead returns unemployment to 5%.
Keeping unemployment at B's 3% requires inflation of 4.5%; holding inflation at 3.5% instead returns unemployment to 5%.
Keeping unemployment at B's 3% requires inflation of 3.5%; expected inflation cannot alter a point already reached.
Keeping unemployment at B's 3% requires inflation of 4.5%; holding inflation at 3.5% instead permanently lowers the natural rate to 3%.
items.feedback: Expectations rise from 2.5 to 3.5, shifting the curve up one point. At unemployment 3, inflation therefore rises from 3.5 to 4.5. Alternatively, actual inflation equal to the new expectation gives natural unemployment at 5. A fixed unemployment target and a fixed inflation target are different continuations.

items.stem: Refer to the graph with B to the right of A on SRPC0. Initially actual inflation is B’s rate and expected inflation is A’s rate. Each period expectations equal the previous period’s actual inflation; each one-point expectations change shifts SRPC vertically by one point with slope unchanged. Natural unemployment and supply conditions stay fixed. Policy holds unemployment at B’s rate for one additional period, then requires inflation to be nonnegative in the following period. What inflation occurs in the additional period, and what is the highest unemployment rate compatible with that later inflation constraint?
options: Inflation stays 1.5 percent, then unemployment can remain at 7 percent.
Inflation is 0.5 percent, then unemployment can remain at 7 percent without deflation.
Inflation is 2.5 percent, then unemployment can be at most 5 percent.
Inflation is 0.5 percent, then unemployment can be at most 6 percent.
items.feedback: The plotted slope is (1.5 − 2.5)/(7 − 5) = −0.5. Expectations first fall from 2.5 to 1.5, so holding unemployment at 7 gives inflation 0.5. Next expectations are 0.5; nonnegative inflation requires 0.5 − 0.5 × (unemployment − 5) ≥ 0, or unemployment no greater than 6. Maintaining 7 would instead produce −0.5 percent inflation.

items.stem: A temporary supply disruption raises inflation while existing contracts still reflect the original expected inflation. Wage setters update forecasts using the observed inflation, but the disruption ends before the new contracts take effect. Expected inflation nevertheless remains above its original level. With natural unemployment unchanged, what can be concluded about the final SRPC relative to its original position and its position during the disruption?
options: It must return exactly to its original position because the physical disruption ended.
It must lie above the disruption-period curve because any expectations rise exceeds the inflation effect of the supply disruption ending.
It must lie below the original curve because the original supply shock was temporary.
It remains above the original curve; its position relative to the curve during the disruption depends on the sizes of the two effects.
items.feedback: Neither the supply disruption nor the higher expected inflation affected the original curve. The final curve reflects only the higher expected inflation, so it remains above the original curve. Comparing the final curve with the curve during the disruption requires comparing the sizes of those two effects; observed inflation alone does not establish them.

items.stem: A credible target lowers expectations immediately, but nominal wages cannot reset for one year. Officials propose an equally immediate, large demand contraction and promise no output loss. Which sequencing change would most directly address the stated conflict?
options: Coordinate the restraint with contract adjustment; credibility alone does not instantly change locked-in nominal costs
Increase the contraction before wages reset because credibility removes every nominal rigidity
Raise expected inflation back to its old level to shift SRPC down immediately
Treat the old contracts as lower natural unemployment and use the new natural rate as the target
items.feedback: A belief change and a contract-cost change can occur at different times. The no-loss promise overlooks that timing mismatch; coordinating adjustment addresses it without assuming an altered natural rate.

items.stem: A government repeatedly uses surprise demand expansion to hold unemployment below natural. Wage setters begin anticipating the next expansion. Compare continuing the same actual inflation rate with generating a fresh surprise.
options: Anticipated inflation preserves the gain; expectations adjustment permanently lowers natural unemployment.
Anticipated inflation loses the gain; a fresh surprise must fall below updated expectations.
Anticipated inflation preserves the gain; a fresh surprise shifts the long-run curve left.
Anticipated inflation loses the gain; a fresh surprise must exceed updated expectations.
items.feedback: Once the higher rate is expected, the short-run surprise disappears. Repeating the gain requires exceeding the updated expectation; under repeated adjustment this can mean accelerating inflation rather than a stable long-run tradeoff.

items.stem: An adverse supply shock raises actual inflation, then wage setters incorporate it into next year’s contracts. What are the two stages?
options: An initial SRPC shift followed by reinforcement through higher expected inflation
Two movements along one fixed SRPC with no change in the inflation-unemployment relation
An LRPC shift followed by lower expected inflation when contracts renew
A demand contraction followed by an SRPC shift downward at each unemployment rate
items.feedback: The supply shock first shifts SRPC upward even with expectations unchanged. Incorporating the higher observed inflation into contracts adds an expectations-driven upward shift. This reinforces inflation pressure rather than describing the disappearance of a demand-created unemployment gain.

items.stem: An evaluator says, "Option A saves more staff time, so it is the best policy." Which reply separates the testable component from the hidden value premise?
options: Measure the time savings, then ask why that objective should outrank other consequences
Treat the entire sentence as positive because staff time is measurable
Treat the time-saving estimate as normative because it supports a recommendation
Conclude more accurate timing data will uniquely determine the preferred policy
items.feedback: Time savings can be tested. Moving from that estimate to "best" requires a criterion for weighing time against other outcomes.

items.stem: A board ranks plans only by the number of people served and selects A. New evidence shows B serves more people but offers less privacy. Which conclusion distinguishes logic from values?
options: Choosing A would necessarily show the new service count is false
Its stated rule now favors B; preferring A would require changing or qualifying that rule
The privacy difference makes the service-count evidence normative
More people served proves B is morally superior under every criterion
items.feedback: A fixed criterion has implications that evidence can change. Preferring privacy can justify a different criterion, but does not refute the service-count evidence.

items.stem: A forecast says a digitization plan will reduce waiting. A recommendation says it should be adopted only if access for people without internet is protected. Waiting falls but offline access worsens. Which inference is sound?
options: Observed waiting reductions prove the plan satisfies the value criterion
The forecast becomes normative because implementation affected access
The forecast is supported, while the recommendation's stated condition is unmet
The failed access condition refutes the waiting-time forecast
items.feedback: The observed waiting result bears on the positive claim. Protecting offline access is a separate condition in the recommendation; success on one outcome does not satisfy it.

items.stem: A report states that volunteers prefer evening shifts and therefore evening-only service is fair. A representative survey confirms the preference. What remains unresolved?
options: Whether a confirmed preference statement can count as positive
Whether using a survey converts the fairness conclusion into a measured fact
Whether the fairness judgment proves daytime users have no unmet needs
Whether fairness should be judged by volunteer preferences rather than users' access
items.feedback: A preference claim is empirically testable. The move from measured volunteer preferences to fairness requires a value premise about whose interests count.

items.stem: A rule gives priority to people facing the greatest hardship. New data show that a different group meets that description. What change is consistent with keeping the same normative principle?
options: Change the priority group because the evidence changed who satisfies the criterion
Keep the old group because normative principles cannot use evidence
Declare hardship measurement normative solely because it informs policy
Treat the data as proof that greatest-hardship priority is the only fair principle
items.feedback: A stable value criterion can lead to a different recommendation when facts change. Evidence identifies its beneficiaries without uniquely establishing the criterion itself.

items.stem: A researcher predicts that simplifying an application raises completion when eligibility is unchanged. A trial simplifies the form and broadens eligibility; completion rises. Which statement is justified?
options: Only recommendations can be evaluated when two policies change together
The prediction is positive, but the joint change does not isolate the form's effect
The rise proves the form alone caused every added completion
The extra eligibility change makes the original claim normative
items.feedback: The conditional causal prediction is testable. Because eligibility changed too, the observation does not by itself identify the effect of form simplification.

items.stem: A report finds that a shuttle saves travelers time but increases neighborhood noise. It recommends adoption using travelers' gains alone. Which critique is precise?
options: Time savings become normative when expressed in money
Adding more precise effect estimates removes the need to decide whose welfare counts
The effects are testable; excluding neighbors from the recommendation embeds a value choice
Noise estimates are normative because neighbors dislike the outcome
items.feedback: Time and noise effects can be measured. Counting only travelers when recommending a policy assigns standing to one group and excludes another, which is a value choice.

items.stem: Two forecasts disagree about whether a new scheduling rule will shorten next year's queues. Both specify measurable waiting times and comparable staffing. What would change their status as positive claims?
options: The forecast with the larger benefit is positive; the other is normative
Both become normative until next year's data exist
Agreement by the forecasters is required before evidence can test them
Neither disagreement nor the future date changes their testable status
items.feedback: Positive status depends on empirical testability, not agreement, truth, desirability or whether the outcome has occurred. Later evidence can support one forecast over the other.

items.stem: An analyst rejects a delivery plan because predicted delays exceed her stated acceptable limit. Better evidence places delays below that limit, but she still rejects it on privacy grounds. Which interpretation fits?
options: The factual case changed, and the rejection now requires an additional value criterion
The original delay forecast was normative because it supported rejection
The unchanged decision proves the new delay estimate is irrelevant to the original argument
Privacy concerns establish that the revised forecast is false
items.feedback: The delay objection no longer follows from the updated evidence and original threshold. A privacy objection can support rejection, but it is a separate normative premise.

items.stem: A planner defines "optimal" as maximizing visits, then claims the chosen schedule is objectively best. Another schedule serves fewer visitors but reaches people with greater need. Which statement is most defensible?
options: A numerical criterion cannot contain a value judgment
Visit maximization identifies an optimum under one criterion, not a uniquely justified social ranking
Calling a result optimal makes its criterion empirically true
The need difference disproves the measured visit counts
items.feedback: Optimization can be objective conditional on a criterion. Choosing visits rather than need as the social objective remains a normative judgment.

items.stem: An adviser predicts a wage rule raises employed teenagers’ annual income by $8 million but reduces teenage employment by 3%. She recommends it because the income gain is worth the employment loss. A pilot instead finds a 1% job loss. Which conclusion separates evidence from values?
options: The pilot makes the original employment prediction normative because a positive statement cannot be contradicted by data.
The pilot challenges the size of the positive employment prediction; it does not by itself establish the adviser’s tradeoff criterion.
The smaller loss proves the recommendation objectively correct, regardless of how the affected teenagers value work and income.
The recommendation makes both numerical predictions normative, so neither can be evaluated using pilot evidence.
items.feedback: Predictions about income and employment are testable positive claims even when inaccurate. Calling one outcome worth another introduces a value judgment. New evidence informs the tradeoff but cannot supply the normative weighting by itself.

items.stem: A report states: (1) a tax reduces cigarette purchases; (2) the tax burden falls heavily on low-income smokers; (3) therefore the tax is unjust. Which classification is correct?
options: All three are positive, because technical wording removes every value judgment
Only statement 1 is positive
Statements 1 and 2 are positive; statement 3 is normative
Statements 2 and 3 are normative
items.feedback: The first two claims can be tested empirically. The conclusion that the policy is unjust is normative.

items.stem: School plan A is predicted to raise scores by 6 points and reduce free time by 4 hours weekly. Plan B raises scores by 4 points and reduces free time by 1 hour. A board declares A preferable because each extra score point is worth at least 2 hours of free time. Which statement correctly distinguishes the predictions from the board’s value judgment?
options: The outcome predictions are normative; the board’s numerical weighting is positive, and A’s extra 2 points cost 3 hours.
All claims are positive because they contain numbers; A dominates B on both scores and free time.
The weighting is normative, so the score and time predictions cannot be tested against observed outcomes.
The outcome predictions are positive; the board’s weighting is normative, and A’s extra 2 points cost 3 hours relative to B.
items.feedback: Comparative predictions imply A adds 2 score points while costing 3 more hours, or 1.5 hours per extra point. Whether that is worthwhile depends on the board’s stated value criterion, not merely on the accuracy of the predictions.

items.stem: An electricity supplier charges more during evening peaks and less overnight. Some households can delay appliance use, while others need electricity immediately. Which response shows how the price signal can coordinate scarce capacity?
options: Flexible users shift use into the evening, reducing peak pressure because peak prices are higher.
Inflexible users must stop consuming before the price difference can affect peak demand.
Flexible users shift some use overnight, reducing peak pressure without requiring every household to shift.
All households must use less electricity over the full day for timing prices to reduce peak demand.
items.feedback: Higher peak prices encourage users with flexible timing to move consumption. Daily consumption need not fall, and users with urgent needs need not shift for this coordinating effect to occur.

items.stem: A market initially has demand Qd=100−P and supply Qs=20+P. Later price is $45 and quantity is 75. Assume demand and supply retain their original slopes. Which changes at every price are consistent with the observed equilibrium?
options: Demand increases by 20 and supply increases by 10; demand pressure is larger, so both price and quantity rise.
Demand increases by 20 and supply decreases by 10; both changes explain the rise in quantity.
Demand increases by 10 and supply increases by 20; stronger supply pressure raises price.
Demand is unchanged and supply increases by 30; a supply increase raises both price and quantity.
items.feedback: Initially P=40 and Q=60. At P=45, old demand is 55 but observed demand is 75, requiring a +20 shift. Old supply is 65 but observed supply is 75, requiring a +10 shift. Price and quantity alone do not imply only demand changed.

items.stem: Refer to the PPF graph. A proposal values each extra unit of X at 2 units of Y. Comparing the average tradeoff over A to B and D to E, which movement passes that benefit-cost test?
options: A to B passes; D to E fails
Both pass because each ends on the frontier
D to E passes; A to B fails
Neither passes because every frontier movement sacrifices Y
items.feedback: A to B forgoes 5 Y for 8 X, or 0.625 Y per X; D to E forgoes 20 Y for 4 X, or 5 Y per X. A benefit of 2 Y per X exceeds only the first average cost.

items.stem: Refer to the PPF graph. Starting at B, a planner must choose among labeled frontier points while keeping at least 30 units of Y. What is the greatest attainable X among those choices, and what Y is sacrificed?
options: 25 X at E, sacrificing 45 Y
15 X at C, sacrificing 10 Y
21 X at D, sacrificing 25 Y
8 X at B, sacrificing no Y
items.feedback: A, B and C meet the Y floor. C has the most X of those labeled points: 15. Relative to B, Y falls from 45 to 35, a cost of 10.

items.stem: Refer to the PPF graph. An economy at F considers B as an immediate target and G as a longer-run target. Which diagnosis fits both?
options: Reaching B expands the frontier; reaching G merely removes unemployment
Both targets are currently efficient choices because each is desirable
Better resource use can reach B; reaching G requires an expansion of feasible production
Both targets require new technology because both are above F
items.feedback: F is inside the existing frontier, B lies on it and G lies outside. Removing inefficiency can reach B with current capacity; G requires a changed production possibility set.

items.stem: Refer to the PPF. Moving from point C to point D increases production of X but reduces production of Y. Suppose each additional unit of X generates a benefit equivalent to 3 units of Y. What is the net benefit, measured in units of Y, from moving from C to D?
options: 3 Y
items.feedback: The move gains 6 X and forgoes 15 Y. Its benefit is 6 times 3 = 18 Y; deducting the 15 Y opportunity cost leaves 3 Y.

items.stem: Production moves from F to C and then from C to D with resources and technology unchanged. Which explanation, supported by the graph’s output changes, explains why only the second move sacrifices Y for more X?
options: F to C uses idle resources to add 7 X and 15 Y; C to D reallocates fully employed resources, adding 6 X at a cost of 15 Y.
F to C uses idle resources to add 7 X and 10 Y; C to D reallocates fully employed resources, adding 6 X at a cost of 15 Y.
F to C expands productive capacity to add 7 X and 15 Y; C to D uses idle resources to add 6 X at a cost of 15 Y.
F to C expands productive capacity to add 7 X and 10 Y; C to D uses idle resources to add 6 X at a cost of 15 Y.
items.feedback: F=(8,20) lies inside the PPF, while C=(15,35) and D=(21,20) lie on it. F to C uses idle resources to add 7 X and 15 Y without expanding capacity. C to D reallocates fully employed resources: gaining 6 X requires giving up 15 Y.

items.stem: The first ten generators cost two forgone repairs; the next ten cost six more. A buyer offers four repairs in exchange for each ten-generator block. Blocks must be produced in order. Which production choice yields the most net repairs?
options: Produce only the second block because its opportunity cost is higher
Produce neither because any generator production sacrifices repairs
Produce one block, gaining two net repairs
Produce both blocks because their average cost equals the offer
items.feedback: The first block gains 4 - 2 = 2 repairs; the second loses 4 - 6 = -2. Producing both yields zero net gain, so one block is better.

items.stem: From an efficient starting point, reallocating crews to the first four school reopenings forgoes 12 bridge repairs; the next four forgo 20 more. A planner uses the first block's cost to estimate all eight. What is the error?
options: The estimate is correct because equal numbers of schools must cost equal repairs
The estimate is 12 repairs too high because the first block is already planned
The estimate is 20 repairs too low because the first block has no opportunity cost
The estimate is 8 repairs too low because the later marginal tradeoff is steeper
items.feedback: Extrapolating the first block gives 24 repairs for eight schools. Actual cost is 12 + 20 = 32, eight more. The second block has the higher opportunity cost.

items.stem: A factory raises both outputs after reorganizing idle workers. Later, training expands the maximum output possible even when all workers are occupied. Which evidence separates the two improvements?
options: The first can occur within existing capacity; the second changes the efficient production boundary
Any simultaneous output increase proves the frontier shifted
Any training program moves production along an unchanged frontier
Both improvements establish that the original output was outside the frontier
items.feedback: Using idle resources can raise both outputs without changing capacity. A higher maximum under full efficient use establishes a frontier expansion.

items.stem: A straight-line PPF trades one turbine for three pumps. An observed move gains two turbines while pumps stay unchanged, with technology and resources fixed. Which explanation is consistent with both facts?
options: The straight frontier proves every observed move must lose six pumps
The turbine gain by itself proves the PPF shifted outward
The observation establishes zero opportunity cost everywhere on the frontier
The starting point was inside the frontier, so the move could use idle capacity
items.feedback: The three-pump tradeoff describes efficient frontier reallocations. An interior starting point can permit output gains without sacrificing the other good; the observation does not erase frontier opportunity cost.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. After the shift from PPF0 to PPF1, production remains at B. Which statement combines the capacity change with the observed production choice?
options: Capacity expanded, and PPF1 identifies the preferred output combination; unchanged production at B therefore establishes that welfare has increased.
Capacity expanded, but unchanged B is now inside the new frontier; higher welfare is not established by the shift alone
Capacity expanded, but unchanged B remains on the efficient frontier; its earlier efficiency establishes that resources are still fully employed.
Capacity stayed unchanged because production remains at B; the shift to PPF1 changes the selected output mix rather than the feasible set.
items.feedback: The outward frontier makes more output feasible and places the old B inside the new boundary. A capacity change alone does not show that production adjusted or establish a welfare ranking.

items.stem: On an unchanged efficient frontier, moving from 50 drones and 80 scanners to 65 drones and 50 scanners costs 2 scanners per added drone. The next 10 drones would reduce scanners from 50 to 20. A planner claims a constant cost of 2 and wants 10 more drones only if each is worth at least 2.5 scanners. Which evaluation is correct?
options: The next block costs 3 scanners per drone, so it fails the 2.5 threshold and indicates rising opportunity cost.
The next block costs 2 scanners per drone, so it passes the threshold because the previous average applies to every move.
The next block costs 0.33 scanner per drone, so it passes the threshold after inverting the ratio.
The next block costs 30 scanners per drone, so the frontier must have shifted inward rather than displaying changing tradeoffs.
items.feedback: The first cost is (80-50)/(65-50)=2. The next is (50-20)/10=3. At a value of 2.5 scanners per drone, the extra block loses 0.5 scanner-equivalent per drone. Changing slopes can occur along one unchanged bowed frontier.

items.stem: A country starts inside its PPF with idle workers. Hiring them raises both outputs until the old frontier is reached. Later, technology improves only scanner production and the country can produce more scanners at the same drone output. Which diagnosis distinguishes the two changes?
options: Both changes shift the frontier outward equally because any rise in both observed outputs proves general capacity growth.
The first improves resource utilization; the second expands productive capacity asymmetrically, rather than merely moving along the old frontier.
The first is growth and the second is improved utilization because scanner output rises without reducing drones.
Neither changes productive capacity because every increase in one output must reduce the other under scarcity.
items.feedback: Using idle resources can move production to the existing frontier without changing capacity. Sector-specific technology expands feasible production toward scanners, so the later improvement cannot be attributed solely to more efficient use of the old technology.

items.stem: On one efficient frontier, the first 20 solar units sacrifice 5 food units and the next 20 sacrifice 14. A storage innovation then halves the food sacrifice required for each of those solar blocks, leaving maximum food output unchanged. Which conclusion separates the original tradeoff from the innovation?
options: Original marginal cost falls from 4 to about 1.43 food per solar unit; the innovation merely moves production along the same frontier.
Original marginal cost is constant at 0.475 food per solar unit; the innovation eliminates increasing opportunity cost because both blocks improve.
Original marginal cost rises from 0.25 to 0.70 food per solar unit; the innovation expands solar capacity, with the two costs falling to 0.125 and 0.35.
Original marginal cost rises from 5 to 14 food per solar unit; unchanged maximum food means productive capacity cannot expand.
items.feedback: Divide each food sacrifice by 20 solar units: 0.25 and 0.70. Halving sacrifices produces 0.125 and 0.35, still increasing across blocks. The new technology changes the feasible set, unlike movement along the original frontier.

items.stem: With full resource use and constant tradeoffs, an economy can make 100 food units or 50 medical units. Medical-only technology doubles maximum medical output, leaving maximum food unchanged. At 60 food, compare feasible medical output before and after; then assess an observed rise from an interior point to the old frontier.
options: Medical capacity rises from 20 to 50; every output increase from an interior point proves the whole frontier shifted equally.
Medical capacity stays 20 because food technology is unchanged; only a move to a new point on the old line is possible.
Medical capacity rises from 40 to 80; an interior-to-frontier move reduces efficiency because fewer resources remain idle.
Medical capacity at 60 food rises from 20 to 40; the separate interior-to-old-frontier move is improved utilization, not evidence of that technology shift.
items.feedback: The old linear frontier is M=50(1-F/100), giving 20 at F=60. The new one is M=100(1-F/100), giving 40. An interior-to-frontier move under old technology improves utilization without identifying a capacity change.

items.stem: An economy initially produces 60 units of each good inside a frontier that permits 80 of each together. Reemploying idle labor reaches 80 of each. New machinery then permits 100 of each together. A planner attributes the entire increase to growth in productive capacity. Which counterfactual best exposes the error?
options: Without new machinery, reemployment could still reach 80 of each; only the later extension beyond the old feasible set demonstrates added capacity.
Without reemployment, machinery could not affect the frontier, because a frontier is defined by actual rather than possible output.
Without new machinery, output must remain at 60 of each, because any increase in both goods requires an outward frontier shift.
Without reemployment, the old frontier would automatically move inward to the observed 60-unit bundle.
items.feedback: Initial unused resources explain movement from 60 to 80 under the old feasible set. Machinery changes what can be produced, permitting 100 of each. Observed output growth combines utilization and capacity changes; it cannot all be labeled a frontier shift.

items.stem: A plant initially produces 24,000 units using 20 workers who each work 100 hours. Next period, 24 workers each work 80 hours and produce 25,344 units. Which comparison is correct?
options: Output per worker falls 12%; output per hour rises 10%
Both productivity measures rise 5.6%, matching total output
Output per worker rises 10%; output per hour falls 12%
Output per hour is unchanged because the plant hired more workers
items.feedback: Per-worker output falls from 1,200 to 1,056, or 12%. Total hours fall from 2,000 to 1,920; hourly output rises from 12 to 13.2, or 10%. Changes in hours per worker make the productivity measures diverge.

items.stem: An economy initially produces $90 billion using 3 billion labor hours. A plan targets $108 billion while limiting total hours to 3.2 billion. What hourly productivity and increase over the initial level are required?
options: $33.75 per hour, a 12.5% increase
$36 per hour, a 20% increase
$30 per hour, with no productivity gain
$28.125 per hour, a 6.25% decline
items.feedback: Initial productivity is 90/3 = 30 dollars per hour. The target requires 108/3.2 = 33.75, or 12.5% more. Output growth alone overstates the needed productivity increase because hours also expand.

items.stem: A country’s real GDP rises 6% while employment rises 10%. Population is unchanged. How do real GDP per person and output per worker change?
options: Output per person rises 6%; output per worker falls about 3.6%
Both fall about 3.6% because productivity declined
Both rise 6% because GDP increased
Output per person falls 4%; subtract employment growth from GDP growth
items.feedback: With population fixed, GDP per person rises 6%. Output per worker changes by 1.06/1.10 - 1 ≈ -3.6%. A productivity decline does not imply that average output per resident also declined.

items.stem: Output per worker rises from $50,000 to $55,000, but real GDP per resident stays at $30,000. What must happen to the employed share of residents, assuming the measures cover the same output?
options: It falls from 60% to about 54.5%, offsetting the productivity rise
It rises from 60% to 66%, reinforcing the productivity rise
It stays at 60% because output per resident is unchanged
It falls from 50% to 45%, because wages determine employment shares
items.feedback: Workers/residents equals output/resident divided by output/worker. The share changes from 30,000/50,000 = 60% to 30,000/55,000 ≈ 54.5%. This accounting result does not identify why the employment share fell.

items.stem: A plant initially produces 1,000 units in 100 hours. Output then rises 20% while hours rise 25%. Management claims productivity improved and that the current 1,200 units could be produced in the original 100 hours without any further change. Is that plan feasible at observed productivity?
options: Yes. Output grew 20%, so productivity is 12 units per hour regardless of the increase in hours.
No. Productivity fell 4% to 9.6 units per hour;100 hours would produce 960 units, so meeting 1,200 requires a further productivity improvement.
No. Productivity fell 25%, because output growth is irrelevant to output per hour.
Yes. Faster hours growth raises productivity by 5%, enough to maintain the higher output with fewer hours.
items.feedback: Observed output per hour is 1,200/125=9.6, down from 10. With that productivity,100 hours yield 960, not 1,200. A claim about feasible output must use the observed output-per-hour ratio, not total output growth.

items.stem: A firm produces 2,100 units at 10 units per labor hour. Training raises productivity to 12 units per hour while required output rises to 2,520. Management plans to cut total hours because of the training. Can it meet the new output requirement with fewer hours if no further productivity change occurs?
options: Yes. New required hours are 175 because only the productivity change affects labor needs.
No. Both plans require 210 hours; a cut would require further productivity gains or a lower output target.
No. New required hours are 252 because only output growth affects labor needs.
Yes. A rise in productivity guarantees fewer total hours regardless of the quantity required.
items.feedback: Initial hours are 2,100/10=210; new hours 2,520/12=210. The proportional output increase uses the full productivity gain. The output requirement is a constraint that prevents cutting hours under unchanged new productivity.

items.stem: Output per worker changes from A to B, while employment falls by 25%. A report concludes that higher productivity must mean higher total output. Is that conclusion supported?
options: No. Productivity rises about 27.5%, but total output falls about 4.4% after the employment decline.
Yes. Productivity rises about 40%, so total output rises about 5% after the employment decline.
Yes. Productivity rises about 27.5%; subtracting 25% gives a total-output increase of about 2.5%.
No. Productivity itself falls about 4.4%, because employment is part of the vertical-axis measure.
items.feedback: The plotted productivity ratio is 36.37/28.53 ≈ 1.2748. Total output changes by 1.2748 × 0.75 − 1 ≈ −4.4%. A productivity gain and an employment decline can therefore coexist with lower total output.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. An analyst describes the move from a to b as a rightward shift of money demand and says that doubling the money quantity proves a doubling of the price level. Is the analyst’s conclusion correct?
options: MD is unchanged; the price level rises by one-third, so constant output would require velocity to fall.
MD shifts right; the price level doubles, so velocity can remain fixed.
MD is unchanged; the price level falls by one-quarter, so velocity must rise.
MD shifts left; the price level is unchanged because the money supply is vertical.
items.feedback: The same MD contains both a and b. Money doubles from 2,500 to 5,000, while P rises from 1/2 to 2/3, a factor of 4/3. With Y fixed, MV = PY requires velocity to change by (4/3)/2 = 2/3, so it falls.

items.stem: An economy plans for real output to grow 4 percent and the price level to grow 2 percent over one year. A payments change is expected to reduce velocity by 3 percent. Using the exact multiplicative quantity equation, approximately what money-growth rate meets both targets, and why would simply adding 2 and 4 be insufficient?
options: 9.36 percent; money must also offset the velocity decline.
6 percent; velocity has no effect when output growth is given.
3 percent; declining velocity reduces the money needed.
9 percent exactly; percentage growth rates always add exactly.
items.feedback: The required money growth factor is (1.02 × 1.04)/0.97 = 1.093608..., so growth is about 9.36 percent. The sum approximation gives 9 percent, but is not the exact multiplicative result.

items.stem: A country has nominal spending $640. It aims for a 3% price-level increase with real output up 2% and velocity down 1%. What money-growth rate is required, and why is adding 3% and 2% incomplete?
options: Exactly 1% money growth; subtract real growth from the price target
About 6.1% money growth; falling velocity also has to be offset
Exactly 5% money growth; velocity does not affect the target
About 4.0% money growth; falling velocity amplifies the desired spending increase
items.feedback: Solve M factor = P factor × Y factor / V factor = 1.03×1.02/.99≈1.06121, or 6.1%. The velocity decline reduces spending per dollar and requires additional money growth.

items.stem: The money supply is initially $180, velocity is 4, and real output is 360 units. Money rises 10%, velocity falls 10%, and real output is unchanged. Which conclusion corrects the claim that prices must rise 10%?
options: The price level rises 10%; money growth alone determines prices without a velocity assumption
The price level is unchanged; equal opposite percentage changes exactly cancel
The price level falls 10%; ignore the simultaneous money increase
The price level falls 1%; the opposing percentage changes in M and V combine multiplicatively
items.feedback: MV=PY. With Y fixed, P changes by the product of M and V factors: 1.10×0.90=.99, a 1% fall. A constant-velocity shortcut is not valid here.

items.stem: Use MV=PY. In period 1, independently verified money is 200, velocity is 5, and real output is 500; the reported price index is 2.4. In period 2, money rises 20% and velocity falls 10%. Independently verified nominal spending is 1,080 and the price index is 2.16, while reported real output is 600. Which corrections reconcile both periods, and what is the corrected inflation rate?
options: Period-1 price index: 2; period-2 real output: 500; inflation: 8%.
Period-1 price index: 2; period-2 real output: 600; inflation: 8%.
Period-1 price index: 2.4; period-2 real output: 500; inflation: −10%.
Period-1 price index: 2; period-2 real output: 500; inflation: 10%.
items.feedback: Period 1 gives P=200×5/500=2. Period 2 gives M=240 and V=4.5, so MV=1,080, agreeing with independently measured spending. Its verified P=2.16 requires Y=1,080/2.16=500. Corrected inflation is 2.16/2−1=8%; using the erroneous first price index would give a false decline.

items.stem: Money rises 5% and real output is unchanged. Nominal spending is also unchanged. Using MV=PY, what must happen to velocity, and why is money growth alone an insufficient inflation forecast?
options: Velocity falls by the reciprocal factor; it offsets money growth in nominal spending.
Velocity is unchanged; money growth can leave nominal spending fixed at fixed output.
Velocity rises proportionally; two increases offset each other in the product MV.
Velocity falls to zero; unchanged nominal spending means all money ceases circulating.
items.feedback: If M rises by a factor of 1.05 while MV is fixed, V must be divided by 1.05, a fall of about 4.76%. With Y also fixed, P is unchanged. A money-growth-only forecast omitted the velocity response.

items.topic: Real Exchange Rates and Purchasing Power
items.stem: The nominal exchange rate rises from 1.20 to 1.26 foreign units per domestic unit. Domestic prices rise 4% and foreign prices 10%. An exporter says nominal appreciation must make domestic goods relatively dearer abroad. Does the real exchange rate support that claim?
options: Yes. A 5% nominal appreciation guarantees a 5% real appreciation regardless of relative inflation.
Yes. Adding the nominal and domestic price increases gives 9% real appreciation; foreign prices do not enter.
No. Its factor is 1.05×1.04/1.10, a slight real depreciation; faster foreign inflation outweighs the nominal appreciation.
No. It depreciates 10% because only foreign inflation matters for international competitiveness.
items.feedback: The real factor is 1.26/1.20×1.04/1.10≈0.9927, a 0.7% depreciation. The nominal exchange-rate direction alone is insufficient: relative prices slightly reverse its competitive implication.

items.topic: Real Exchange Rates and Purchasing Power
items.stem: A domestic basket costs 200 domestic units and a comparable foreign basket costs 300 foreign units. Initially e is 1.50 foreign units per domestic unit. Later e falls to 1.35 and the foreign basket rises 8 percent. What domestic basket price would keep ε = eP/P* unchanged, and what if the actual price were 230?
options: 216 domestic units; at 230, ε is below its initial value
240 domestic units; at 230, ε is below its initial value
240 domestic units; at 230, ε is above its initial value
200 domestic units; at 230, ε is above its initial value
items.feedback: Initial ε=1. The later foreign basket is 324 foreign units, so maintaining ε requires P=324/1.35=240 domestic units. At P=230, ε=1.35×230/324≈0.9583, a real depreciation.

items.topic: Real Exchange Rates and Purchasing Power
items.stem: Country A has 9% inflation and Country B has 3% inflation. Let e be units of B currency per unit of A currency, and define A’s real exchange rate as e×P_A/P_B. Use the approximation that its percentage change is the percentage change in e plus A’s inflation minus B’s inflation. About how much must e fall to leave the real exchange rate unchanged? If e instead falls 2%, what happens to A’s real exchange rate and the relative price of A’s goods?
options: A 6% fall is needed; a 2% fall means about 4% real appreciation, making A’s goods relatively dearer.
A 6% rise is needed; a 2% fall means about 4% real depreciation, making A’s goods relatively cheaper.
A 12% fall is needed; a 2% fall means about 10% real appreciation, making A’s goods relatively dearer.
A 6% fall is needed; a 2% fall means about 4% real depreciation, making A’s goods relatively cheaper.
items.feedback: Using percentage changes, real stability requires the nominal exchange-rate change plus 9 minus 3 to equal zero, so e must fall about 6%. With only a 2% fall, the real exchange rate rises about −2+9−3=4%. Under the stated quotation, that is real appreciation: A’s goods become more expensive relative to B’s.

items.topic: Real Exchange Rates and Purchasing Power
items.stem: In common currency, identical traded goods have equal prices across two countries, but broad consumer baskets remain differently priced. An analyst predicts that removing shipping costs alone must equalize the broad baskets. Which missing evidence matters most?
options: Whether the nominal exchange rate is quoted reciprocally, since taking a reciprocal removes real basket gaps
Whether domestic saving equals investment, since balanced trade is sufficient for broad-basket PPP
Whether traded-goods PPP holds, since that alone requires every consumer basket to match
Whether remaining basket gaps come from nontraded services, quality differences or local taxes that shipping reform does not remove
items.feedback: Traded-goods arbitrage can coexist with broad-basket differences. Shipping reform does not remove nontraded components, basket composition or local taxes; identifying the sources of the remaining gap is necessary.

items.topic: Real Exchange Rates and Purchasing Power
items.stem: Relative PPP predicts depreciation of a domestic currency, but it depreciates less over the observed interval. The report gives no horizon or evidence about traded-goods price gaps. Which follow-up best distinguishes short-run deviation from persistent limits to PPP?
options: Replace the nominal quote with its reciprocal and treat the discrepancy as resolved
Examine the horizon and whether gaps are concentrated in nontraded or costly-to-arbitrage goods
Infer that inflation data are wrong because depreciation differed from the benchmark
Infer that capital flows cannot matter because PPP already predicts a direction
items.feedback: A short interval can reflect asset-demand or policy forces, while persistent nontradable or trade-cost gaps can limit arbitrage. The discrepancy alone identifies neither measurement error nor the source and persistence of the deviation.

items.topic: Real Exchange Rates and Purchasing Power
items.stem: The real exchange rate is initially 1. Use ε = eP/P*, where e is foreign currency per domestic currency, P is the domestic price level and P* is the foreign price level. In year one, the nominal exchange rate rises 12 percent, domestic prices fall 3 percent and foreign prices rise 4 percent. In year two, both price levels are fixed. What year-two change in the nominal exchange rate restores the initial real exchange rate?
options: A decline of about 4.27 percent
A decline of exactly 5 percent
A rise of about 4.46 percent
A decline of about 4.46 percent
items.feedback: Year-one ε factor is 1.12×0.97/1.04=1.04461538. Year two must multiply e by its reciprocal, 1.04/(1.12×0.97), a decline of about 4.27 percent. The recovery percentage uses the new base.

items.topic: Real Exchange Rates and Purchasing Power
items.stem: Let e be foreign currency per unit of domestic currency and let the real exchange rate be ε = eP/P*, where P and P* are the domestic and foreign basket prices. The domestic basket price rises from 250 to 270 domestic currency units, the foreign basket price rises from 400 to 408 foreign currency units, and e falls from 1.60 to 1.50. Would keeping the domestic basket price at 250 instead of 270 make the real depreciation larger or smaller?
options: Weaken it. The actual real exchange rate falls from 1.00 to about 0.993 because domestic inflation reinforces nominal depreciation.
Leave it unchanged. The real exchange rate depends only on e, which falls from 1.60 to 1.50 in both cases.
Reverse it into appreciation. Lower domestic prices necessarily make domestic goods more expensive relative to foreign goods.
Strengthen it. The actual real exchange rate falls from 1.00 to about 0.993; domestic inflation offsets much of the nominal depreciation.
items.feedback: Actual ε is 1.50×270/408≈0.9926 versus initial 1.00. Without domestic inflation it would be 1.50×250/408≈0.9191, a larger depreciation. Rising domestic prices partially offset the competitiveness effect of the cheaper currency.

items.topic: Real Exchange Rates and Purchasing Power
items.stem: Country A’s currency rises 3 percent in B currency per A currency, while A’s prices rise 7 percent and B’s rise 2 percent. A second policy can reduce only A’s nominal currency value, measured from that new quote. Approximately how much nominal depreciation is needed to prevent any net real appreciation over both stages?
options: At least 8 percent
At least 3 percent
At least 7.45 percent
At least 4.76 percent
items.feedback: The first-stage real factor is 1.03×1.07/1.02≈1.08049. To keep the two-stage factor at or below one, the next nominal factor must be at most 1.02/(1.03×1.07)≈0.92551. That requires depreciation of at least about 7.45 percent from the new quote.

items.stem: A country’s nominal GDP is $468 billion and its deflator is 130. Next year real GDP rises 10%, but nominal GDP is $475.2 billion. Which new deflator and interpretation reconcile these facts?
options: 120; real output rises while the domestic price level falls
132; nominal and real growth must move together
145.2; add real growth to the old deflator
120; the lower deflator proves real production fell
items.feedback: Initial real GDP is 468/1.30 = 360. It grows to 396; the new deflator is 475.2/396 × 100 = 120. Output grew despite a decline in the price index from 130 to 120.

items.stem: A workshop economy makes pumps and repair visits. Base prices are $40 and $20. Current quantities are 60 pumps and an unreported number of visits; current prices are $50 and $30. Current nominal GDP is $6,000. What real GDP and deflator follow?
options: $4,400 real GDP; deflator about 136.4
$6,000 real GDP; deflator 100
$4,000 real GDP; deflator 150
$4,400 real GDP; deflator about 73.3
items.feedback: Pumps account for 60 × 50 = 3,000 nominal dollars, leaving 3,000/30 = 100 visits. At base prices real GDP is 60 × 40 + 100 × 20 = 4,400. The deflator is 6,000/4,400 × 100 ≈ 136.4.

items.stem: Two new domestic goods have current prices of $12 and $30 and base prices of $10 and $20. Output of the first is 80 units; total real GDP is $2,400. What is current nominal GDP, and why does it differ from real GDP?
options: $3,360; recover 80 units of the second good and value both at current prices
$2,880; raise all real output by the first good’s price increase
$2,400; real and nominal GDP use the same quantities, so they are equal
$4,320; current prices must be applied to the dollar value of real GDP
items.feedback: Base-price output of the first good is 800, leaving 1,600/20 = 80 units of the second. Nominal GDP is 80 × 12 + 80 × 30 = 3,360. The same quantities have different values at different price vectors.

items.stem: Nominal GDP grows 8% and the GDP deflator grows 12.5%. Population is unchanged. Which conclusion best evaluates the claim that average real production rose?
options: Real GDP per person falls 4%; nominal growth does not establish output growth
Real GDP per person falls 4.5%; subtracting rates gives an exact result
Real GDP per person rises 8%; population did not change
Real GDP per person rises 20.5%; combine both positive rates
items.feedback: The real-output ratio is 1.08/1.125 = 0.96, a 4% fall. With population fixed, real GDP per person falls by the same proportion. Nominal output rose only because the price increase exceeded the real contraction.

items.stem: Nominal GDP rises 32% over two years. Real GDP rises 10% in the first year and is unchanged in the second. The deflator started at 125. Which final deflator and cumulative price change follow?
options: 150; the domestic price level rose 20%
165; the domestic price level rose 32%
152.5; subtracting growth rates gives an exact 22% price rise
150; the domestic price level rose 50% during these two years
items.feedback: Real GDP’s cumulative factor is 1.10. The price factor is 1.32/1.10 = 1.20, giving deflator 125 × 1.20 = 150. A level of 150 is 50% above the base year, but only 20% above the initial 125.

items.stem: Nominal GDP rises 8 percent while the GDP deflator rises 5 percent. The measured unemployment rate falls, but employment and participation data are not supplied. Using the usual approximate real-growth calculation, which conclusion is supported?
options: Real output rose about 3 percent; measured unemployment fell, but labor-force exits could explain the rate decline
Real output rose about 3 percent; measured unemployment fell, which establishes that employment increased
Real output rose about 13 percent; measured unemployment fell, but labor-force exits could explain the rate decline
Real output was unchanged; measured unemployment fell, which establishes that employment increased
items.feedback: Approximate real growth is 8−5 = 3 percent (the exact ratio gives about 2.9 percent). A lower unemployment rate alone does not prove stronger employment: unemployed workers may have stopped searching. Employment and participation evidence would distinguish the possibilities.

items.stem: Nominal GDP rises from $715 billion to $756 billion while a common-base deflator rises 130 to 140. A report subtracts the 10 index-point increase from nominal growth of about 5.7%, claiming real GDP fell about 4.3%. What is the error?
options: It treats index points as percentage inflation; correct deflation gives real GDP 550 then 540 billion, a decline of about 1.8%.
It should add the 10 index points to nominal growth, giving real growth of about 15.7%.
It should use nominal growth alone because common-base deflators cannot change real-output comparisons.
It correctly measures inflation as 10%; the only error is rounding the nominal growth rate.
items.feedback: The price factor is 140/130, not 1.10. Real levels are 715/1.30=550 and 756/1.40=540. Their decline is 10/550≈1.8%; subtracting index points from a growth percentage mixes incompatible measures.

items.stem: An economy reports nominal GDP $1560 and real GDP $1300. Next year nominal GDP remains $1560 while its deflator falls from 120 to 100. Which inference is valid?
options: Real GDP falls 20%; lower prices reduce real output at any nominal spending
Real GDP rises 16.7%; divide the output change by the final output level
Real GDP rises 20%; unchanged nominal GDP can conceal increased output when prices fall
Real GDP is unchanged; equal nominal spending implies equal physical output
items.feedback: Initial real GDP is 1300; next real GDP is 1560/1 = 1560. Growth uses initial real output: (1560−1300)/1300 = 20%.

items.stem: Initially 160 books cost $4 each and 80 meals cost $10 each. Both quantities rise 10% and both prices 20%, so nominal GDP rises 32%. An analyst says using different positive base prices could change real growth from 10% to 32%. Is that possible here?
options: Yes. Choosing current prices as fixed weights always turns nominal growth into real growth.
No. Because both quantities rise by the same 10%, any fixed positive price weights give 10% real growth;32% includes price growth.
No. Real growth is 12% under every weighting because 32 minus 20 is exact deflation.
Yes. A higher weight on either good changes its quantity growth from 10% to 32%.
items.feedback: With uniform quantity growth, the whole fixed-price sum is multiplied by 1.10 regardless of the chosen positive weights. Nominal growth is 1.10×1.20−1=32%. This weight-invariance depends on uniform quantity growth; it is not a general rule for changing output composition.

items.stem: A lender charged a fixed 8% nominal rate to target a 3% expected real return. CPI subsequently moved from 160 to 172.8. What realized real rate and forecast error follow using approximate real interest?
options: 0% realized real return; inflation was 3 percentage points above expected
3% realized real return; the target guarantees the outcome
-4.8% realized real return; the CPI-point increase is inflation
5% realized real return; actual inflation was below expected
items.feedback: The target implies expected inflation of 8 - 3 = 5%. Observed inflation is (172.8 - 160)/160 = 8%, so realized real interest is 0%. Inflation exceeded the expectation by 3 percentage points.

items.stem: A lender wants a 2% approximate real return and forecasts CPI rising from 125 to 130. The resulting fixed nominal contract is signed, but CPI ends at 135. What nominal rate and realized real return follow?
options: 6% nominal; -2% realized real return
7% nominal; -1% realized real return
6% nominal; 2% realized real return
10% nominal; 2% realized real return
items.feedback: Expected inflation is 5/125 = 4%, so the target nominal rate is 2 + 4 = 6%. Actual inflation is 10/125 = 8%, giving approximate realized return 6 - 8 = -2%. Use the stated approximation, not the exact Fisher ratio.

items.stem: A lender wants a 3% expected real return on a $200 loan. Expected inflation rises from 2% to 5% before a new fixed-rate contract is signed. Actual inflation then turns out to be 7%. Using the approximation, which nominal rate and realized return follow?
options: The new nominal rate is 8%; realized real return is 3%
The new nominal rate is 8%; realized real return is 1%
The new nominal rate is 5%; realized real return is 3%
The new nominal rate is 10%; realized real return is 3%
items.feedback: The new nominal rate uses expected inflation: 3+5=8%. Realized return then uses actual inflation: 8−7=1%. Actual inflation cannot retroactively set the signed nominal rate.

items.stem: Two fixed-rate loans each advance $230. In economy A the nominal rate is 7% and expected inflation is 2%; in B they are 9% and 5%. Actual inflation is 4% in both economies. Using real interest ≈ nominal interest minus inflation, how do the lenders’ expected and realized rankings compare, and which borrowers benefit relative to their original expectations?
options: A initially ranks higher (5% versus 4%), but B realizes more (5% versus 3%); borrower B gains, while borrower A loses.
B initially ranks higher (9% versus 7%) and still realizes more (5% versus 3%); both borrowers gain from positive inflation.
A initially ranks higher (5% versus 4%), but B realizes more (5% versus 3%); borrower A gains, while borrower B loses.
A initially ranks higher (5% versus 4%) and still realizes more (5% versus 3%); neither borrower is affected by forecast errors.
items.feedback: Expected real returns are A:7−2=5% and B:9−5=4%; realized returns are A:7−4=3% and B:9−4=5%. A’s inflation exceeds expectations, reducing its borrower’s real burden and its lender’s return relative to their bargain.
