items.feedback: Untaxed Q is 12 and TS is $144. With the tax, Q = 8, buyers pay $22 and sellers receive $14: CS = $32, PS = $32 and revenue = $64, totaling $128. The ceiling also supports 8 supplied units; efficient allocation gives CS = $96 and PS = $32. Each loses $16 of gains, but consumers receive $64 more under the ceiling. This equality depends on the stated allocation and cost assumptions.

items.stem: Refer to the movie-tax graph. A review finds that CS plus PS falls by $480,000 after the displayed tax. With no externalities or collection costs, how should that change be reconciled with incidence and total surplus?
options: $480,000 is lost surplus, while the $400,000 revenue is an additional loss
$400,000 becomes revenue, $80,000 is lost surplus, and each side bears $2 per unit
$560,000 becomes revenue, total surplus rises $80,000, and each side bears $2
$400,000 becomes revenue, $80,000 is lost surplus, and buyers bear all $4 per unit
items.feedback: Read the old price $12, buyer price $14, seller receipt $10 and taxed quantity 100,000. The $4 wedge raises $400,000. Subtracting that transfer from the $480,000 private loss leaves $80,000 of lost surplus, also 0.5 × 40,000 × $4. Each side bears $2 on each remaining unit.

items.stem: A market faces Qd=1,000−20Pb and Qs=20Ps, where Pb and Ps are buyer and seller prices. A $10 per-unit tax creates Pb−Ps=10. An official forecasts tax revenue using the untaxed quantity. Which corrected revenue and forecast error follow?
options: Actual revenue $4,000 rather than $5,000; quantity falls from 500 to 400.
Actual revenue $4,000 rather than $5,000; quantity stays 500 but some tax is a transfer.
Actual revenue $5,000 rather than $4,000; the legal tax rate fixes quantity.
Actual revenue $6,000 rather than $5,000; adding a tax increases the supply price and quantity.
items.feedback: Without tax, 1,000−20P=20P gives P=25 and Q=500. With Pb=Ps+10, 1,000−20(Ps+10)=20Ps gives Ps=20, Pb=30, and Q=400. Revenue is 10×400=$4,000, $1,000 below the unchanged-quantity forecast.

items.stem: Untaxed price is $30. A $7 tax makes buyers pay $34 and sellers receive $27. Lawmakers propose collecting the same tax from buyers instead of sellers in the same competitive market, with unchanged demand, supply and enforcement. Which prediction correctly combines the observed burdens with the proposed change?
options: Buyers bear $4 and sellers $3 per unit; collecting from buyers shifts the full $7 burden to buyers.
Buyers bear $4 and sellers $3 per unit; changing the statutory payer alone does not change those economic burdens.
Buyers bear $3 and sellers $4 per unit; changing the statutory payer alone does not change those burdens.
Buyers bear $7 and sellers $0 per unit; collecting from sellers would reverse those burdens.
items.feedback: The buyer-price increase is $4 and seller-receipt decrease is $3, summing to $7. Moving collection between sides does not change the equilibrium wedge or relative responsiveness in the stated competitive setting.

items.stem: In a competitive market, a per-unit tax initially raises buyer price, lowers seller receipts and reduces trades. Several years later suppliers can adjust output much more easily, while demand responsiveness is unchanged. Which statement correctly distinguishes the initial effect from the later burden comparison?
options: Initially buyers bear the full wedge; as supply becomes more elastic, sellers necessarily bear the full wedge.
Initially both sides bear part of the wedge; more elastic supply tends to move a larger share onto sellers.
Initially both sides bear part of the wedge; as supply becomes more elastic, a larger share tends to fall on buyers.
Initially seller receipts rise; later statutory collection determines which side bears the wedge.
items.feedback: The initial wedge separates a higher buyer price from a lower seller receipt. In the later comparison, suppliers have better adjustment options, so the relatively less responsive demand side tends to bear more of the tax.

items.stem: A $10 tax reduces equilibrium quantity only slightly in Market A but sharply in Market B. What is the strongest inference?
options: Market A likely has less elastic demand and/or supply around equilibrium
Market A must have more elastic demand and supply
Tax revenue must be zero in Market A
The statutory side paying the tax differs across markets
items.feedback: Less elastic curves produce a smaller quantity response to a given tax wedge.

items.stem: A survey begins with 132 employed,12 unemployed and 56 adults outside the labor force. Then 4 unemployed find jobs,3 stop searching,5 adults enter the labor force without finding work, and 2 employed retire. All job seekers are available. Participation ends unchanged. Does that prove nobody entered or left the labor force?
options: No. Five entries offset five exits; participation remains 72% while unemployment falls to about 6.9%.
Yes. An unchanged participation rate means every individual kept the same labor-force status.
No. Participation rises to 75.5% because people who stop searching must remain counted as unemployed.
Yes. Retirements and discouraged exits are ignored in both participation and unemployment statistics.
items.feedback: Employment becomes 134 and unemployment 10, so the labor force stays 144 of 200. Five entrants offset three search exits and two retirements. An unchanged aggregate participation rate can hide substantial flows; unemployment is 10/144≈6.9%.

items.stem: Among 200 adults, participation is 75% and unemployment 8%. Next month 6 unemployed stop searching,6 employed retire, and 4 adults enter the labor force but find no work. Other statuses are unchanged and seekers are available. A report calls the lower unemployment rate evidence of net job creation. Is that justified?
options: No. Employment falls to 132; unemployment is about 7.0% and participation 71%.
Yes. Any lower unemployment rate means the number of employed people increased.
No. Employment stays 138 and participation 75%, because retirees remain employed for this calculation.
Yes. Employment rises to 144 when the four new job seekers and six retirees are added to the initial workforce.
items.feedback: Initially LF=150, U=12 and E=138. Employment becomes 132; unemployment 12−6+4=10; LF=142. Thus unemployment is about 7.0% and participation 71%. A falling unemployment rate can accompany employment losses when participation also declines.

items.stem: A population of 200 adults is unchanged. The unemployment rate stays at 6%, while participation falls from 75% to 70%. Which employment change and interpretation follow?
options: Employment falls by 9.4 despite the unchanged unemployment rate
Employment stays at 141; a stable rate fixes employment
Employment falls by 10; every labor-force exit must be an employed worker
Employment rises by 9.4; lower participation indicates more jobs
items.feedback: The labor force falls from 150 to 140. Employment is 94% of each total: 141 initially and 131.6 afterward, a decline of 9.4. The unchanged unemployment rate is a ratio, not an unchanged employment count.

items.stem: Unemployment fell from 20 to 12 while employment rose from 180 to 184. Adult population is fixed at 250, and the only flows were unemployed people finding jobs or stopping search. How many unemployed people found jobs, how many stopped searching, and how did labor-force participation change?
options: 4 found jobs and 4 left search; participation fell from 80% to 78.4%
8 found jobs; participation stayed at 80%
4 found jobs and 8 left search; participation fell to 76.8%
4 left search and none found jobs; the employment rise is unrelated
items.feedback: The employment rise identifies 4 job findings. Of the 8-person unemployment decline, the remaining 4 are exits. LF falls from 200 to 196, so participation falls from 80% to 78.4%. Both hiring and withdrawal contributed to the lower headline rate.

items.stem: Two districts have the same unemployment rate and population. One has lower participation and a larger share of employed people working part time because full-time work is unavailable. Which additional comparison is best before calling their labor markets equally strong?
options: Compare employment per adult and desired versus actual hours; the headline rate omits both differences
Compare only total unemployment; equal unemployment rates guarantee equal counts
Count all involuntary part-time workers as unemployed before applying the official definition
Exclude discouraged workers from every indicator because they are outside the labor force
items.feedback: Unemployment divides job seekers by the labor force. Lower participation can lower employment per adult even at the same rate, while involuntary part-time workers remain employed. Additional participation and hours evidence is needed for the broader assessment.

items.stem: Initially 150 million adults are employed, 12 million are unemployed and 88 million are outside the labor force. Four million unemployed people find jobs. Then six million other unemployed people stop searching and leave the labor force. Adult population is unchanged. Which calculation and interpretation are correct?
options: The new unemployment rate is about 1.28%; employment rises, but discouraged exits also contribute to the rate decline
The new unemployment rate is about 4.94%; employment rises, and the denominator remains the original labor force
The new unemployment rate is about 0.80%; employment rises, and adult population is the unemployment-rate denominator
The new unemployment rate is about 5.13%; employment rises, and the six exits are subtracted from employment
items.feedback: Employment becomes 154 million. Unemployment becomes 12−4−6 = 2 million, and the labor force is 154+2 = 156 million. Thus UR = 2/156×100 ≈ 1.28%. Job finding improves employment, while discouraged exits separately lower both unemployment and participation; the rate decline is not solely job creation.

items.stem: Of 230 employed workers, ten full-time workers lose half their hours but retain paid jobs. No one enters or leaves the labor force. Which observation would reveal the deterioration that the official unemployment rate misses?
options: Employment falls by five; two half-time jobs equal one employed person.
Unemployment rises by ten; each loss of full-time hours counts as joblessness.
Participation falls by ten; paid part-time workers leave the labor force.
Hours fall; employment, unemployment and participation remain unchanged.
items.feedback: A paid part-time worker is employed. Head-count employment, UR and LFPR can stay constant while hours and underemployment worsen; hours-based evidence supplies the missing margin.

items.stem: Initially 240 adults are employed and 24 unemployed. A recession causes 12 employed workers to lose jobs and actively search, while an equal number of previously unemployed people stop searching. Which joint result can occur?
options: Employment is fixed because layoffs and exits cancel; the unemployment rate is fixed
Employment falls and unemployment head count falls; the unemployment rate necessarily falls
Employment and labor-force participation fall; unemployment head count stays fixed and its rate rises
Employment falls but participation is fixed; unemployment head count doubles
items.feedback: Layoffs move employed people to unemployment; discouraged exits remove an equal number from unemployment. U is unchanged, E and the labor force fall, so U/LF rises. Equal flows do not cancel employment or participation effects.

items.stem: In Year 1, employed = 150 million, unemployed = 10 million, and not in labor force = 90 million. In Year 2, employed = 152 million, unemployed = 8 million, and not in labor force = 95 million. What is the best interpretation?
options: Employment rose, unemployment rose, and labor-force participation rose
Employment fell because not-in-labor-force increased
Employment rose, the unemployment rate fell, but labor-force participation fell
The unemployment rate stayed constant because the labor force stayed at 160 million
items.feedback: Employment rises from 150 to 152. The unemployment rate falls from 10/160 to 8/160. But participation falls because adult population rises while the labor force stays at 160.

items.stem: An economy has 120 employed and 12 unemployed adults. Two separate policy evaluations observe the same fall in unemployed people. In A, they find jobs; in B, they stop searching. With adult population fixed, which extra indicator distinguishes the cases?
options: Employment and participation fall in both because fewer people are unemployed
Employment rises with unchanged participation in A; employment is unchanged and participation falls in B
Employment is unchanged and participation falls in A; employment rises with unchanged participation in B
Employment and participation rise in both because measured unemployment falls
items.feedback: Job finding moves people within the labor force from unemployed to employed. Discouragement moves people out of unemployment and the labor force without raising employment. The same unemployment change can conceal different labor outcomes.

items.stem: Of 130 employed workers, ten full-time workers lose half their hours but retain paid jobs. No one enters or leaves the labor force. Which observation would reveal the deterioration that the official unemployment rate misses?
options: Hours fall; employment, unemployment and participation remain unchanged.
Employment falls by five; two half-time jobs equal one employed person.
Unemployment rises by ten; each loss of full-time hours counts as joblessness.
Participation falls by ten; paid part-time workers leave the labor force.
items.feedback: A paid part-time worker is employed. Head-count employment, UR and LFPR can stay constant while hours and underemployment worsen; hours-based evidence supplies the missing margin.

items.stem: After a regional downturn ends, one group has suitable job offers but needs time to choose; another cannot meet credentials for expanding occupations. A third group has already accepted paid part-time work while seeking full-time jobs. Which diagnosis respects both cause and official status?
options: The first group is frictionally unemployed, the second structurally unemployed, and the third employed
All three are structurally unemployed because each wants a different job
The first is cyclical, the second frictional, and the third outside the labor force
All three are unemployed until they obtain their preferred full-time jobs
items.feedback: Normal matching among suitable jobs is frictional; a persistent credential mismatch is structural. A paid part-time job makes the third group employed under the official measure, even though underemployment may remain.

items.stem: Spending and total vacancies recover after a downturn, but vacancies concentrate in licensed occupations while displaced workers lack the credentials. Which evidence would most directly strengthen a structural diagnosis over a purely cyclical one?
options: Credential training is followed by placements into the unfilled occupations while overall spending changes little
All vacancies disappear when spending weakens again
Workers have suitable offers and are briefly choosing among them
Unemployment falls only when economy-wide spending rises sharply, with no change in skills
items.feedback: The mismatch between expanding occupations and worker credentials points to a structural barrier. Placements after relevant training, with demand broadly unchanged, strengthen that mechanism rather than a claim based only on weak spending or ordinary search.

items.stem: A city’s jobless population includes skilled movers choosing among local openings and workers whose occupation disappeared. A single faster job-listing service is proposed for both. Which prediction is best supported?
options: Listings can resolve the obsolete-qualification mismatch; skilled movers additionally need new qualifications before any matching can occur
Listings can shorten matching for both groups; information alone removes the missing-qualification constraint just as it removes search friction
Listings cannot affect either group; both need aggregate-demand expansion rather than matching or qualification changes
Listings can shorten matching for skilled movers; workers with obsolete qualifications may additionally need retraining or mobility support
items.feedback: The first group faces search frictions among suitable jobs. The second faces a durable mismatch that information alone may not remove. Diagnosis should guide the intervention without assuming guaranteed placement.

items.stem: An initially cyclical recession lasts long enough that displaced workers lose relevant skills. Demand later recovers fully. A forecast assumes the old natural rate must immediately return. Which counterfactual best reveals the forecast’s weakness?
options: With identical recovered demand, neither economy can have any unemployment
With identical recovered demand, an economy that preserved skills can have lower structural unemployment than one that lost them
With identical recovered demand, both economies must have the same natural rate regardless of skills
With identical recovered demand, the economy with lost skills must have lower frictional unemployment and lower total unemployment
items.feedback: Demand recovery can remove cyclical weakness while skill loss leaves a structural legacy. Comparing otherwise similar recoveries isolates that mechanism; the old natural rate is not assured.

items.stem: Demand is at its normal level. Each week, 40 qualified workers start searching for suitable existing vacancies. Average search lasts 6 weeks. A job-information service cuts that duration to 3 weeks without changing entries into search or job requirements. Another 180 job seekers lack the skills vacancies require. Assume steady flows, so the frictionally unemployed equal weekly entries times average search duration. What does the service change, and what would address the remaining mismatch?
options: Frictional unemployment falls by 240; retraining addresses the 180 mismatched workers, while demand stimulus alone need not do so.
Frictional unemployment falls by 120; the information service also removes all structural unemployment without retraining.
Frictional unemployment falls by 120; retraining addresses the 180 mismatched workers, while demand stimulus alone need not do so.
Frictional unemployment stays unchanged; only stronger aggregate demand can shorten search when suitable vacancies already exist.
items.feedback: The steady search stock falls from 40×6=240 to 40×3=120. Better information reduces search time and frictional unemployment. It does not supply missing skills, so the separate structural mismatch calls for a skill response. At normal demand, an aggregate-demand increase is not a substitute for these targeted changes.

items.stem: Two plans address unemployed workers after a recession and permanent automation. Plan A restores spending immediately; Plan B retrains workers but starts next year. A report calls either plan sufficient for every worker immediately. Which correction recognizes mechanism and timing?
options: A fixes skill mismatch now; B restores current aggregate demand before training starts.
A helps demand layoffs now; B addresses skill mismatch after training takes effect.
Both eliminate both causes now; spending and training have identical immediate mechanisms.
Neither affects either cause; cyclical and structural unemployment cannot coexist in one economy.
items.feedback: The plans operate through different channels and on different schedules. A demand response and a delayed skill response are complements for the mixed case, not interchangeable immediate cures.

items.stem: Automation raises output per worker and lowers production costs, but some workers in the old process lose jobs and need retraining. Which statement best describes the combined effect?
options: Productivity must fall when workers are displaced, even if output per worker rises and unit costs fall
Productivity can rise while displaced workers face only frictional search, even when their old skills no longer fit vacancies
Productivity and potential living standards can rise while displaced workers face a structural skill mismatch requiring adjustment
Productivity can rise while displaced workers face only cyclical unemployment that disappears as soon as the new machines operate
items.feedback: Technology can raise productivity and living standards over time while displacing some workers whose skills no longer match the market.
